docs.title: ml-toolkit
docs.text: Prepare data, choose a model and metric, then train, evaluate and record an experiment with the same workflow across tasks. Splitter and evaluator objects control data partitions and additional reports.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Getting started: installation and one complete training run.
  • Task recipes: model, metric and report choices for your target.
  • Data: prepare a Pool and preserve row alignment when slicing.
  • Training: run the workflow and interpret its result.
  • Models: fit, predict, save and load a supported adapter.

docs.title: Follow the workflow
docs.text:
1. A splitter supplies train/validation pairs.
  2. Each pair independently selects features, tunes parameters and fits a model. Selection and tuning are optional.
  3. A fresh main model uses the last pair's selected settings and splitter.get_test().train, including former validation and gap rows.
  4. With test data, the test stage evaluates the held-out pool. Without test, this fit is named final_fit and uses all eligible rows.
  5. With fit_on_test=True, a separate final_fit includes test and returns result.final_model. Without test, requesting this option is an error. Metrics, reports and model artifacts are recorded in MLflow.

Built-in splitters reserve chronological windows and refit on all non-test rows. Custom splitters define their own windows and final training data. The caller prepares features and targets and selects the MLflow experiment.

docs.title: Inspect and customize
docs.text:
Task Guide Choose a diagnostic and understand its graph Evaluation Analyze input distributions or drift Data analysis Supply custom data metrics or artifacts Build a data analyzer Supply extra prediction metrics or artifacts Build an evaluator Define validation windows Data splitting Select or rank model features Feature selection Search model parameters Parameter tuning Implement model fitting and serving Build a model adapter Choose or implement a training metric Metrics Find experiment results Tracking Configure shared settings Configuration

Each guide includes executable usage and the relevant API reference. Use the version selector to switch between stable (the latest release), dev (unreleased changes), and archived releases. Source and examples are in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Task recipes
docs.text:
When ReportingConfig.psi=True, every model saved by the existing tracking flags includes its fitted PSI baseline. ReportingConfig.on_* switches govern report generation; they do not disable this model attachment. features=() disables levels and baseline packaging. No additional tracking flag is needed. See PSI baseline loading.

Choose the model, primary metric and reports for your target, then pass them to train_model. The short recipes share the setup below. A complete Frequency example spells out selection, tuning, reporting and model packaging without requiring that setup.

docs.title: Choose a recipe
docs.text: Task Model Primary metric Binary classification CatBoostClassificationModel metrics_classification Regression CatBoostRegressionModel metrics_regression Frequency CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel metrics_frequency Severity CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel Tweedie deviance with fixed power Positive–unlabeled CatBoostPUClassificationModel PUMetric with a population prior

docs.title: Prepare source data
docs.text:
From an installed repository checkout, run python -m examples.prepare_data once. The examples read cached sources and do not download data implicitly.

Source Target Partition UCI Bike Sharing, 17,379 recorded hours Rentals/hour, or high demand for binary classification Three chronological folds and the latest 20% as test UCI Online Retail, fixed 10% invoice sample Positive unit price in GBP/item Train before September 2011, validate in September, test from October Your PU project Known positives and unlabeled observations Recorded project timestamps and an independently justified prior

See the Bike setup and retail setup for features, units and sampling. The PU recipe is a function requiring your own pool.

docs.title: Shared setup
docs.text:
Run this block, choose one short task recipe, then use Run the chosen recipe. Set the MLflow tracking URI and experiment before training. Compact recipes disable model packaging and leave selection and tuning off; PSI, prediction evaluators and data analyzers still write reports.

from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout, TimeSeriesCV
from dataclasses import replace
from ml_toolkit.config import (
    FeatureLevelConfig,
    ReportingConfig,
    TrackingConfig,
    TrainingConfig,
)
from ml_toolkit.metrics import (
    MetricsSeverity,
    PUMetric,
    metrics_classification,
    metrics_frequency,
    metrics_severity,
)
from ml_toolkit.models import (
    CatBoostClassificationModel,
    CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    CatBoostPUClassificationModel,
    CatBoostRegressionModel,
)
from ml_toolkit.types import FloatArray

base_config = TrainingConfig(tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False))
base_params = {
    "iterations": 20,
    "depth": 2,
    "random_seed": 42,
    "thread_count": 2,
    "verbose": False,
    "allow_writing_files": False,
}
common = ReportingConfig(psi=True)
See Configuration for settings, data splitting for partition rules, Evaluation for prediction reports, and Data analysis for distributions and drift.

docs.title: Binary classification
docs.text:
The example labels an observed hour as high demand when its recorded rental count is at least 100. This fixed operational threshold is chosen before splitting; the count and its components are excluded from features. Include both classes in evaluated splits for finite ROC AUC; single-class splits return NaN.

from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import NumericalFeatureDistributions
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import (
    PrecisionRecall,
    F1Threshold,
    Calibration,
    Gains,
    Lift,
    ObservedFitted,
    TimeObservedFitted,
)
from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
import polars as pl

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
data = data.with_target((data.y >= 100).cast(pl.Float64))
classification_config = replace(base_config, reporting=common)
splitter = TimeSeriesCV(data, n_splits=3, test_size=0.2)
config = classification_config
model_factory = CatBoostClassificationModel
params = {**base_params, "loss_function": "Logloss"}
metric = metrics_classification
feature_selector = None
param_space = None
prediction_evaluators = [
    PrecisionRecall(),
    F1Threshold(),
    Calibration(),
    Gains(),
    Lift(),
    ObservedFitted(),
    TimeObservedFitted(),
]
data_analyzers = [NumericalFeatureDistributions()]

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
Ordinary regression supports signed targets. metrics_regression returns weighted MAE, MSE, RMSE, R² and mean error (prediction minus target).

from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import NumericalFeatureDistributions
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import (
    ObservedFitted,
    TimeObservedFitted,
)
from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)

from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_regression

regression_config = replace(base_config, reporting=common)
splitter = TimeSeriesCV(data, n_splits=3, test_size=0.2)
config = regression_config
model_factory = CatBoostRegressionModel
params = {**base_params, "loss_function": "RMSE"}
metric = metrics_regression
feature_selector = None
param_space = None
prediction_evaluators = [
    ObservedFitted(),
    TimeObservedFitted(),
]
data_analyzers = [NumericalFeatureDistributions()]

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Use the recorded positive retail unit prices as monetary targets, with stock_code, country and quantity as inputs. The test starts on 1 October 2011; the holdout uses September for validation and earlier invoices for training. The validation row count comes from the canonical calendar split, so whole invoices stay together. Feature diagnostics use quantity.

Use a Tweedie power consistent with the model loss and metric. Here power=1.5 allows zero targets and requires positive predictions and positive weighted observed totals. Gamma deviance (power=2) requires strictly positive targets.

For strictly positive severity, set loss_function="Gamma" on the same CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel and set the reporting metric's power=2.0. See Gamma regression for CPU/GPU configuration, predictions, validation requirements and saving models.

from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import NumericalFeatureDistributions
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import (
    Gains,
    Lift,
    ObservedFitted,
    TimeObservedFitted,
)
from examples.retail_data import load_retail_pool, load_retail_splits

data = load_retail_pool(download_if_missing=False)
retail_splits = load_retail_splits(download_if_missing=False)


def severity_metric(
    observed: FloatArray, prediction: FloatArray, weight: FloatArray
) -> MetricsSeverity:
    return metrics_severity(observed, prediction, weight, power=1.5)


severity_config = replace(
    base_config,
    reporting=replace(
        common, features=(FeatureLevelConfig("quantity", "numerical"),)
    ),
)
splitter = Holdout(
    data, val_size=len(retail_splits.validation), test_size="2011-10-01"
)
config = severity_config
model_factory = CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel
params = {**base_params, "loss_function": "Tweedie:variance_power=1.5"}
metric = severity_metric
feature_selector = None
param_space = None
prediction_evaluators = [
    Gains(),
    Lift(),
    ObservedFitted(),
    TimeObservedFitted(),
]
data_analyzers = [NumericalFeatureDistributions()]

docs.title: Positive–unlabeled classification
docs.text:
Use 1 for known positives and 0 for unlabeled observations. Both groups need positive weight in training and evaluated samples. prior is the positive fraction in the population, not the fraction of labeled rows. Supply a prepared project Pool and call train_pu(data, prior=your_prior) after setting up MLflow. The function uses the same prior in the model and metric.

from ml_toolkit import Pool, TrainingResult, train_model
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import PUScoreDistribution, PUPositiveCapture


def train_pu(data: Pool, *, prior: float) -> TrainingResult:
    return train_model(
        splitter=TimeSeriesCV(data, n_splits=3, test_size=0.2),
        params={**base_params, "loss": "uPU", "pu_prior": prior},
        model_factory=CatBoostPUClassificationModel,
        metric=PUMetric(prior, loss="uPU"),
        run_name="project-pu",
        config=replace(base_config, reporting=common),
        prediction_evaluators=[PUScoreDistribution(), PUPositiveCapture()],
    )

The PU report guide explains what the two plots show.

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text:
Use nonnegative targets with a positive weighted total in every evaluated split. The log-link adapter fits a training-only baseline and returns positive rates.

from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import NumericalFeatureDistributions
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import (
    Gains,
    Lift,
    ObservedFitted,
    TimeObservedFitted,
)
from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
frequency_config = replace(base_config, reporting=common)
splitter = TimeSeriesCV(data, n_splits=3, test_size=0.2)
config = frequency_config
model_factory = CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel
params = {**base_params, "loss_function": "Poisson"}
metric = metrics_frequency
feature_selector = None
param_space = None
prediction_evaluators = [
    Gains(),
    Lift(),
    ObservedFitted(),
    TimeObservedFitted(),
]
data_analyzers = [NumericalFeatureDistributions()]

docs.title: Run the chosen recipe
docs.text:
This call uses the variables from your chosen short recipe. Executing this page in order uses Frequency, the final recipe above. PU uses its explicit train_pu function instead.

import mlflow

from ml_toolkit import train_model

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("ml-toolkit-task-recipes")
result = train_model(
    splitter=splitter,
    params=params,
    model_factory=model_factory,
    metric=metric,
    run_name="task-example",
    config=config,
    feature_selector=feature_selector,
    param_space=param_space,
    prediction_evaluators=prediction_evaluators,
    data_analyzers=data_analyzers,
)
print(
    {
        name: round(value, 4)
        for name, value in result.validation.mean_metrics.items()
    }
)
assert result.test_metrics is not None
print({name: round(value, 4) for name, value in result.test_metrics.items()})

{'mean_absolute_error': 144.2219, 'mean_squared_error': 42249.5587, 'root_mean_squared_error': 205.547, 'r2_score': 0.1309, 'mean_error': -75.6556, 'mean_poisson_deviance': 159.3838, 'd2_poisson_score': 0.1984, 'prediction_over_observed': 0.6959, 'lift_at_10': 1.7831, 'gain_at_10': 0.1783, 'normalized_gini': 0.7351}

The two dictionaries contain validation averages and independent test scores. Metrics, configuration and evaluator artifacts are written to a local MLflow store. See workflow results and Tracking to inspect a run.

docs.title: Complete Frequency example
docs.text:
This standalone configuration enables RFE, two Optuna trials per fold, PSI, SHAP, the listed evaluators and main-model packaging. Install the shap extra. The small budgets keep the demonstration reproducible; choose production budgets for your own task. RFE's min_features is a lower bound, not a promised result.

from ml_toolkit.training import TimeSeriesCV
from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import NumericalFeatureDistributions
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import (
    Gains,
    Lift,
    ObservedFitted,
    TimeObservedFitted,
)
from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
from optuna import Trial
from ml_toolkit.config import (
    FigureConfig,
    ReportingConfig,
    ShapConfig,
    TrackingConfig,
    TrainingConfig,
    TuningConfig,
)
from ml_toolkit.feature_selection import RFESelector
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_frequency
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import importance_ranker
from ml_toolkit.types import ModelParams

frequency_config = TrainingConfig(
    tuning=TuningConfig(
        metric="mean_poisson_deviance",
        direction="minimize",
        n_trials=2,
        timeout_seconds=None,
        seed=42,
    ),
    reporting=ReportingConfig(
        figure=FigureConfig(figsize=None, dpi=150, format="png"),
        features=None,
        psi=True,
        period="month",
        n_bins=10,
        epsilon=1e-06,
        shap=ShapConfig(
            max_samples=500, seed=42, max_display=10, dependence_features=()
        ),
    ),
    tracking=TrackingConfig(
        log_trial_models=False,
        log_validation_models=False,
        log_test_model=True,
        log_final_model=True,
        input_example_rows=5,
        model_name="model",
        registered_model_name=None,
        conda_env=None,
    ),
)
splitter = TimeSeriesCV(
    data,
    n_splits=3,
    val_size=None,
    test_size=0.2,
    gap=0,
    max_train_size=None,
    skip_splits=0,
)
config = frequency_config
model_factory = CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel
params = {
    "iterations": 20,
    "depth": 2,
    "random_seed": 42,
    "thread_count": 2,
    "verbose": False,
    "allow_writing_files": False,
    "loss_function": "Poisson",
}
metric = metrics_frequency
feature_selector = RFESelector(
    min_features=1,
    metric="mean_poisson_deviance",
    direction="minimize",
    ranker=importance_ranker,
    max_fits=2,
    score_tolerance=0.0,
    protected_features=(),
)


def param_space(trial: Trial) -> ModelParams:
    return {
        "depth": trial.suggest_int("depth", 1, 3),
        "learning_rate": trial.suggest_float(
            "learning_rate", 0.03, 0.1, log=True
        ),
    }


prediction_evaluators = [
    Gains(),
    Lift(),
    ObservedFitted(),
    TimeObservedFitted(),
]
data_analyzers = [NumericalFeatureDistributions()]

docs.title: Inspect the complete run
docs.text:
Run the complete Frequency block immediately above, then this example. It prints the selected settings and independent test metric, and renders SHAP importance from at most 500 test rows. Contributions are in the native raw log-rate units.

from pathlib import Path
import mlflow
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.explainability import calculate_shap_values
from ml_toolkit.plots.explainability import shap_importance

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("ml-toolkit-task-recipes")
result = train_model(
    splitter=splitter,
    params=params,
    model_factory=model_factory,
    metric=metric,
    run_name="frequency-full-example",
    config=config,
    feature_selector=feature_selector,
    param_space=param_space,
    prediction_evaluators=prediction_evaluators,
    data_analyzers=data_analyzers,
)
assert result.feature_selection is not None
assert result.tuning is not None
assert result.test_metrics is not None
print("Selected features:", result.features)
print(
    "Visited subset sizes:",
    [len(step.features) for step in result.feature_selection.steps],
)
print("Best trial:", result.tuning.best_trial)
print(
    "Test Poisson deviance:",
    round(result.test_metrics["mean_poisson_deviance"], 4),
)
test = splitter.get_test().heldout
assert test is not None
selected_test = test.select_features(result.features)
shap_config = config.reporting.shap
explanation = calculate_shap_values(
    result.model.native_model, selected_test.X, config=shap_config
)
shap_importance(
    explanation, Path("frequency-full-shap.png"), config=shap_config
)

Selected features: ('temperature', 'feels_like_temperature', 'humidity', 'wind_speed', 'hour', 'working_day', 'weekday', 'holiday', 'season', 'weather', 'month')
Visited subset sizes: [11, 1]
Best trial: 0
Test Poisson deviance: 114.3487

steps includes every subset tried in the last fold; the winning subset can contain more than min_features. best_trial is zero-based. The main model reuses the last fold's selected settings. Its packaged form preserves the prediction behavior shown in the Models guide.

Find fold results, tuning trials, configuration and reports in the MLflow run hierarchy. See feature selection, parameter tuning and SHAP for independent usage and customization.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Python 3.11 or later is required. Install a specific release using Git:

python -m pip install 'ml-toolkit @ git+https://github.com/sssqweeeed/ml-toolkit.git@v0.5.0'

The distribution is named ml-toolkit; the Python import is ml_toolkit. CatBoost, Polars, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, scikit-learn, Optuna, Numba, and MLflow are installed by default.

Alternatively, install a downloaded wheel from GitHub Releases with python -m pip install /path/to/ml_toolkit-0.5.0-py3-none-any.whl; this does not require Git. The package is distributed through GitHub, not PyPI or Conda.

Optional integrations use these extra names:

Integration Extra Purpose SHAP shap Diagnostic SHAP explanations LightGBM lightgbm LightGBM integration Both all SHAP and LightGBM CUDA cuda Single-GPU CatBoost uPU training

For example, install both SHAP and LightGBM with:

python -m pip install 'ml-toolkit[all] @ git+https://github.com/sssqweeeed/ml-toolkit.git@v0.5.0'

CUDA training requires a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. CPU training does not require CUDA, and the all extra does not include it.

docs.title: Train a model
docs.text:
Predict hourly rental counts from the original UCI Bike Sharing dataset. The reusable loader lives in the repository's examples/ directory. Check out the matching release and explicitly download the source once:

git clone --branch v0.5.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/sssqweeeed/ml-toolkit.git
cd ml-toolkit
python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike

The loader caches hour.csv under .cache/uci-bike-sharing. It keeps all 17,379 recorded hours from 2011–2012 with their original timestamps and rental counts. Weather and calendar fields are predictors; casual and registered are excluded because their sum reveals the target. Each hour has weight one.

July–December 2012 is held out for testing. The last 20% of earlier observations forms validation; the main model refits on all pre-test hours. No test observations are used to choose training iterations.

from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from datetime import datetime

import numpy as np
import mlflow

from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.config import TrackingConfig, TrainingConfig
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_frequency
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel

# Run the explicit preparation command above once before reading the cache.
data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("ml-toolkit-quickstart")

result = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(data, val_size=0.2, test_size="2012-07-01"),
    params={
        "iterations": 100,
        "depth": 5,
        "loss_function": "Poisson",
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    },
    model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    metric=metrics_frequency,
    run_name="hourly-rentals",
    config=TrainingConfig(tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False)),
)
print(
    f"Validation deviance: {result.validation.mean_metrics['mean_poisson_deviance']:.2f}"
)
assert result.test_metrics is not None
print(f"Test deviance: {result.test_metrics['mean_poisson_deviance']:.2f}")
test = data.take(np.flatnonzero((data.time >= datetime(2012, 7, 1)).to_numpy()))
predictions = result.model.predict_pool(test)
print("Observed rentals:", test.y.head(5).to_list())
print("Predicted rentals:", predictions[:5].round(1).tolist())

Validation deviance: 70.59
Test deviance: 72.23
Observed rentals: [149.0, 93.0, 90.0, 33.0, 4.0]
Predicted rentals: [48.7, 48.0, 47.8, 47.2, 47.5]

Poisson deviance summarizes count prediction error; lower is better. The first five predictions are genuine future-period observations, in rentals per hour. Validation and test cover different seasons, so their scores need not match. This small model demonstrates the workflow; it is not a tuned demand forecast.

Pool is included in the installed package. Pass your own prepared data to its constructor; see the data guide for fields and operations. The example creates a local mlflow.db and logs metrics and configuration. Model packaging is disabled here; TrackingConfig(log_test_model=True) also saves the main model and its inference dependencies.

docs.title: Reproduce the other examples
docs.text:
From the checkout, install optional integrations and the example-only Excel reader, then prepare the remaining sources explicitly:

python -m pip install -e '.[all]' -r requirements-examples.txt
python -m examples.prepare_data

Bike Sharing supports count and demand-classification workflows; the gallery also uses bundled handwritten digits and original Cora citation records. UCI Online Retail (CC BY 4.0; Daqing Chen, 2015) provides recorded invoice timestamps and item prices in sterling for monetary and inflation examples. Its source workbook is approximately 23 MB. openpyxl is required only to read that workbook; it is not a package runtime dependency.

python -m examples.render_examples --check executes the recipes and checks captured results and figures. Dataset caches stay local; recipe execution does not implicitly download missing sources. Remove --check to regenerate output.

docs.title: Prepare your own data
docs.text:
• Keep features, targets, timestamps, and weights aligned and nonempty.
  • Sort observations by ascending time. Use Polars Date or Datetime timestamps.
  • Supply finite targets and finite, nonnegative weights with positive total.
  • List categorical and numerical features explicitly when needed. Keep IDs and reporting groups outside X unless they are intentional model inputs.
  • Configure your own MLflow URI and experiment before training.

Pool.take, select_features, and with_target return new pools with aligned metadata. See the data API for the complete contract.

docs.title: Choose the next step
docs.text:
• Task recipes choose a model, metric and reports for your target.
  • Training explains the result and execution order.
  • Data splitting supplies validation and final-fit pools.
  • Evaluation covers prediction reports.
  • Data analysis covers distributions, PSI and custom data reports.
  • Models covers prediction, packaging and custom adapters.
  • Configuration lists shared settings and defaults.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: TrainingConfig controls console verbosity, tuning, shared reporting, model packaging and optional training including test via fit_on_test=False. Enabling this flag returns an additional result.final_model and requires a held-out test sample. See the training scenarios. A splitter supplies validation and final-fit data. Model factories, metrics, selectors and report objects are explicit train_model arguments.

docs.title: Start with a small configuration
docs.text:
from dataclasses import replace
from ml_toolkit.config import ReportingConfig, TrackingConfig, TrainingConfig
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import ObservedFitted, TimeObservedFitted
from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import NumericalFeatureDistributions

config = TrainingConfig(tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False))
with_reports = replace(config, reporting=ReportingConfig(psi=True))
prediction_evaluators = [ObservedFitted(), TimeObservedFitted(period="month")]
data_analyzers = [NumericalFeatureDistributions(period="month")]

Configurations are immutable keyword-only dataclasses; replace produces a modified copy. Pass evaluator objects separately to select individual reports. Their execution, sample selection and shared feature levels are described in Evaluation and Data analysis. Pass prediction_evaluators= and data_analyzers= separately to train_model. PSI and O/F share ReportingConfig.features and n_bins, including auxiliary columns stored in Pool.auxiliary_features; each independently fits a LevelTransformer on the same training rows. See how levels are shared.

Setting Responsibility TrainingConfig Console verbosity, tuning, reporting and model packaging settings TuningConfig Objective name/direction, trial budget and seed ReportingConfig Stage switches, PSI/SHAP and common report options FeatureLevelConfig Numerical or categorical feature levels and bounds FigureConfig Figure size, resolution and output format ShapConfig Explanation sampling and displayed features TrackingConfig Which models to package and how to package them

See Task recipes for complete configuration in a training call, Build an evaluator for custom prediction reports, and Build a data analyzer for custom data reports.

docs.title: Console verbosity
docs.text:
Set TrainingConfig(verbosity="normal") to see training progress without configuring a Python logger. normal is the default. Each setting applies only to the current train_model call, including its selection, tuning and reports.

Level Output silent No automatic progress or result output from ml-toolkit. Warnings and exceptions remain visible. normal Run name, original dataset row/feature counts, stage and split milestones, selection/tuning summaries, and a final metric table. verbose Everything in normal, plus each split's row/feature counts and date range, selected feature count, best iteration, train/validation/test metrics, and each tuning trial's objective. debug Everything in verbose, plus selected feature names, built-in selection candidates, and internal model, PSI, SHAP, report and artifact diagnostics. 
normal_config = replace(config, verbosity="normal")
detailed_config = replace(config, verbosity="verbose")
quiet_config = replace(config, verbosity="silent")
debug_config = replace(config, verbosity="debug")

Pass the chosen configuration as train_model(..., config=detailed_config). Unknown levels raise ValueError. There is no numeric interval or per-tree progress bar. The selected level is recorded in MLflow's configuration/requested.json together with the other training settings.

The plain-text output goes to stderr, including in notebooks and redirected terminal output. Tables use six significant digits; returned metrics retain their original precision. A compact final summary looks like this (illustrative values):

Evaluation summary (test scores belong to the main model)
metric | validation mean | test
-------+-----------------+-----
mae    | 9               | 12
Completed training run example

The test column is omitted when the splitter has no test sample. With fit_on_test=True, test scores still describe the main model evaluated before the additional fit. Its train-only metrics appear separately in verbose and debug. Missing best iterations are shown as —; available iterations use the model's zero-based best_iteration. Undefined existing metrics display as nan or inf. Empty metric dictionaries produce a short no metrics message.

Dataset counts describe splitter.data; per-stage tables describe the actual pools supplied by the splitter. Splits appear as they are processed, with their original indices. Output uses existing results and inexpensive metadata; it does not calculate extra metrics, repeat predictions, or collect all split pools in memory. Evaluator/analyzer metrics remain in their existing reports.

docs.title: Python logging and backend output
docs.text:
Console verbosity does not change CatBoost parameters (such as verbose=False), Optuna verbosity, MLflow output, or experiment recording. Consequently, silent does not suppress messages from those libraries or from your callbacks.

Standard records under the ml_toolkit Python logger remain independent and retain application-controlled levels and handlers. When a standard stream handler delivers a record to stdout or stderr, automatic output omits its duplicate. File handlers and handlers that reject a record leave automatic output available at the selected verbosity. Dataset and metric tables still follow that verbosity. Use verbosity="silent" to disable automatic output while retaining your application's logging. Standalone model, selector, tuning and diagnostic calls keep their existing Python logging behavior; this setting does not enable automatic output outside train_model.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: TimePeriod supports minute, hour, day, week, month, quarter and year. Temporal reports preserve input timezones. Standalone PSI also accepts these settings through its own API.

docs.title: Build a model adapter
docs.text:
Implement Model when your project needs its own fitting or prediction policy. The example below trains a CatBoost RMSE model in thousands of hourly bike rentals and returns predictions in rentals per hour. It composes a new adapter around a built-in model and preserves that transformation when logging to MLflow.

The complete runnable files are examples/custom_model.py and examples/custom_model_serving.py in the repository checkout. They use the built-in Pool to hold prepared data.

docs.title: Run the complete example
docs.text:
From the installed repository checkout, download the source data once with python -m examples.prepare_data, then run:

python -m examples.custom_model

Or run it from Python:

from examples.custom_model import demo

demo()

native predictions (thousands): [0.1959, 0.1918, 0.1883, 0.2361, 0.2308]
observed rentals: [283.0, 253.0, 261.0, 306.0, 445.0]
predicted rentals: [195.9, 191.8, 188.3, 236.1, 230.8]
validation MAE: 92.736
test MAE: 91.174
serving predictions match: True

The example uses all 17,379 original UCI Bike Sharing hours from 2011–2012, with weather/calendar features, recorded rental counts and timestamps, and unit weights. It reserves the latest 20% for test and validates on the last 25% of the remaining rows. The normal workflow refits on non-test observations; the example logs that exact final adapter, reloads it, and checks prediction equality on the untouched test tail. The displayed test MAE and serving predictions therefore describe the same fitted adapter. MLflow uses a temporary local database and artifact directory that are removed after the check. No remote tracking service or registry is required.

docs.title: Implement the training contract
docs.text:
Explicit inheritance from Model is unnecessary. A factory accepts a ModelParams dictionary and returns a fresh object with these operations:

Operation What the example does Contract to preserve fit(train, validation) Divides both targets by the fixed scale; delegates fitting Preserve row metadata, use validation only for selection, return the fitted adapter predict_pool(data) Multiplies native predictions back by the scale Return one finite prediction per row in the metric's target units native_model Exposes the fitted CatBoostRegressor Supply the native backend used by supported diagnostics best_iteration Delegates the validation-selected iteration Return a zero-based index or None feature_importances(data) Delegates native feature ranking Return one finite value for every current feature name get_refit_params() Reuses the selected iteration budget and disables early stopping Return copied constructor settings, without learned state log(sample, config=...) Saves native weights, scale settings, and serving source Preserve the adapter's complete prediction behavior

To support PSI baseline packaging, implement the optional keyword argument extra_artifacts: Mapping[str, str] | None = None in log. Merge those artifacts with the adapter's native files and pass them to mlflow.pyfunc.log_model before registration. Reject duplicate artifact names rather than overwriting model state. The complete example demonstrates this contract. Existing workflow calls omit this keyword when no baseline is attached; custom adapters enabling PSI packaging must accept and preserve it.

fit uses Pool.with_target, so timestamps, weights, IDs, and categorical metadata stay aligned. The scale is fixed project configuration; it is never estimated from the validation or test rows. The factory supplies that same scale to every fresh adapter. Selection and tuning therefore compare predictions in the original target units.

Complete adapter and factory source 
from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Mapping

from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

import json
from importlib.metadata import version
from math import isfinite
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from typing import Self

import catboost
import mlflow
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
from mlflow.models import infer_signature
from mlflow.models.model import ModelInfo

from ml_toolkit import Pool, train_model
from ml_toolkit.config import TrackingConfig, TrainingConfig
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.tracking.model_artifacts import merge_artifacts
from ml_toolkit.types import FloatArray, ModelParams


class TargetScaledRegressor:
    """Fit a CatBoost RMSE regressor in scaled target units.

    Parameters
    ----------
    params : ModelParams
        Native CatBoost RMSE settings, copied by the wrapped adapter.
    target_scale : float, default 1000.0
        Positive finite conversion factor. Training divides targets by this
        factor; prediction multiplies outputs back into original units.

    Notes
    -----
    The factory must reuse the same target_scale for validation and final
    fitting. Native SHAP contributions describe scaled targets. Logged serving
    predictions retain the complete inverse transformation.
    """

    def __init__(self, params: ModelParams, *, target_scale: float = 1000.0) -> None:
        if not isfinite(target_scale) or target_scale <= 0:
            raise ValueError("target_scale must be finite and positive")
        self.target_scale = target_scale
        self._inner = CatBoostRegressionModel(params)

    @property
    def native_model(self) -> catboost.CatBoostRegressor:
        """Return the fitted backend, whose outputs are in scaled target units."""
        return self._inner.native_model

    @property
    def best_iteration(self) -> int | None:
        """Return the zero-based iteration chosen on validation, when available."""
        return self._inner.best_iteration

    def fit(self, train: Pool, validation: Pool | None = None) -> Self:
        """Fit on transformed targets while preserving aligned row metadata.

        Parameters
        ----------
        train : Pool
            Aligned training rows with targets in original units.
        validation : Pool or None, default None
            Optional holdout rows transformed using the same fixed scale.

        Returns
        -------
        Self
            Fitted adapter.
        """
        scaled_train = train.with_target(train.y.cast(pl.Float64) / self.target_scale)
        scaled_validation = (
            None
            if validation is None
            else validation.with_target(
                validation.y.cast(pl.Float64) / self.target_scale
            )
        )
        self._inner.fit(scaled_train, scaled_validation)
        return self

    def predict_pool(self, data: Pool) -> FloatArray:
        """Return one prediction per row in original target units.

        Parameters
        ----------
        data : Pool
            Rows containing the fitted feature columns.

        Returns
        -------
        FloatArray
            Predictions of shape (n_samples,) in original units.
        """
        return self._inner.predict_pool(data) * self.target_scale

    def feature_importances(self, data: Pool) -> dict[str, float]:
        """Return the wrapped backend's importance for each current feature.

        Parameters
        ----------
        data : Pool
            Current feature subset in fitted order.

        Returns
        -------
        dict[str, float]
            Importance for every supplied feature, suitable for importance_ranker.
        """
        return self._inner.feature_importances(data)

    def get_refit_params(self) -> ModelParams:
        """Return fresh constructor settings with the fitted iteration budget.

        Returns
        -------
        ModelParams
            Copied backend parameters with early stopping disabled. The factory
            supplies target_scale separately; learned state is never reused.
        """
        return self._inner.get_refit_params()

    def log(
        self,
        sample: Pool,
        *,
        config: TrackingConfig | None = None,
        extra_artifacts: Mapping[str, str] | None = None,
    ) -> ModelInfo:
        """Log native artifacts and an entrypoint that reverses target scaling.

        Parameters
        ----------
        sample : Pool
            Representative serving rows in fitted feature order.
        config : TrackingConfig or None, default None
            Artifact name, registry, example size, and optional environment file.

        extra_artifacts : Mapping[str, str] or None, default None
            Additional files or directories bundled with the model. Names must
            not conflict with the adapter's own artifacts.

        Returns
        -------
        ModelInfo
            Logged complete adapter's serving URI.

        Notes
        -----
        Call inside an active MLflow run. The serving entrypoint uses CatBoost,
        pandas, NumPy, and MLflow; it does not import the training example.
        """
        config = TrackingConfig() if config is None else config
        frame = sample.to_model_input(
            n_rows=config.input_example_rows, categorical_as_strings=True
        )
        frame = frame.loc[:, self._inner.feature_names]
        prediction = self._inner.predict_frame(frame) * self.target_scale
        with TemporaryDirectory(prefix="target-scaled-model-") as directory:
            root = Path(directory)
            model_path = root / "model.cbm"
            self.native_model.save_model(str(model_path))
            state_path = root / "settings.json"
            state_path.write_text(
                json.dumps(
                    {
                        "target_scale": self.target_scale,
                        "feature_names": self._inner.feature_names,
                        "cat_features": self._inner.cat_features,
                    }
                ),
                encoding="utf-8",
            )
            return mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
                name=config.model_name,
                python_model=str(Path(__file__).with_name("custom_model_serving.py")),
                artifacts=merge_artifacts(
                    {"model": str(model_path), "settings": str(state_path)},
                    extra_artifacts,
                ),
                signature=infer_signature(frame, prediction),
                input_example=frame,
                params={},
                metadata={"target_scale": self.target_scale},
                code_paths=[],
                registered_model_name=config.registered_model_name,
                conda_env=None if config.conda_env is None else str(config.conda_env),
                pip_requirements=(
                    [
                        f"{package}=={version(package)}"
                        for package in ("mlflow", "catboost", "numpy", "pandas")
                    ]
                    if config.conda_env is None
                    else None
                ),
            )


def model_factory(params: ModelParams) -> TargetScaledRegressor:
    """Create an independent adapter using the same project target scale.

    Parameters
    ----------
    params : ModelParams
        Backend settings for a fresh fit.

    Returns
    -------
    TargetScaledRegressor
        Unfitted adapter with a new inner CatBoost model.
    """
    return TargetScaledRegressor(params, target_scale=1000.0)

The source uses the built-in regressor for CatBoost's categorical preparation, early stopping, feature importance, and refit policy. A custom implementation can perform those operations itself, provided it keeps the same contracts. Create new nested models and learned preprocessing objects in each factory call; do not close over a fitted estimator or reuse mutable learned state.

docs.title: Connect the factory to training
docs.text:
The demo() function shows the complete call, including data preparation:

Executable workflow source 
from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae


def demo() -> None:
    """Run deterministic validation, final fitting, and serving parity checks.

    Notes
    -----
    Uses cached UCI Bike Sharing observations and a temporary local MLflow
    store. Prepare the cache with python -m examples.prepare_data, then run
    python -m examples.custom_model. The model fitted without test rows is
    logged and checked on the untouched future test tail; artifacts are removed
    after the check.
    """
    from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool

    data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
    splitter = Holdout(data, val_size=0.25, test_size=0.2)
    partition = splitter.get_test()
    assert partition.heldout is not None
    params: ModelParams = {
        "iterations": 40,
        "depth": 4,
        "loss_function": "RMSE",
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    }
    with TemporaryDirectory(prefix="custom-model-demo-") as directory:
        root = Path(directory)
        mlflow.set_tracking_uri(f"sqlite:///{root / 'tracking.db'}")
        experiment = mlflow.create_experiment(
            "custom-model-demo", artifact_location=(root / "artifacts").as_uri()
        )
        mlflow.set_experiment(experiment_id=experiment)
        result = train_model(
            splitter=splitter,
            params=params,
            model_factory=model_factory,
            metric=weighted_mae,
            run_name="scaled-regression",
            config=TrainingConfig(
                tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False)
            ),
        )
        fitted = result.model
        with mlflow.start_run(run_name="serving-parity"):
            logged = fitted.log(partition.train)
        info = logged[1] if isinstance(logged, tuple) else logged
        served = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(info.model_uri)
        expected = fitted.predict_pool(partition.heldout)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(
            served.predict(
                partition.heldout.to_model_input(categorical_as_strings=True)
            ),
            expected,
        )
        native_predictions = fitted.native_model.predict(
            partition.heldout.to_model_input()
        )
        np.testing.assert_allclose(expected, native_predictions * 1000.0)
        print(
            "native predictions (thousands):", native_predictions[:5].round(4).tolist()
        )
        print("observed rentals:", partition.heldout.y.head(5).to_list())
        print("predicted rentals:", expected[:5].round(1).tolist())
        print(f"validation MAE: {result.validation.mean_metrics['mae']:.3f}")
        assert result.test_metrics is not None
        print(f"test MAE: {result.test_metrics['mae']:.3f}")
        print("serving predictions match: True")

Pass model_factory to train_model together with your ordinary metric and TrainingConfig. The metric receives predictions after the inverse scale transformation. The same factory is used for feature selection, tuning trials, validation, and the final fresh fit. get_refit_params transfers the selected iteration budget to that last fit; the factory supplies the target scale again.

docs.title: Preserve predictions in serving
docs.text:
Logging only the inner CatBoost model would return values in scaled units. The example's log writes the native model plus a concrete JSON settings file, then uses MLflow Models From Code with this separate serving entrypoint:

Complete serving entrypoint 
"""MLflow Models From Code entrypoint for the target-scaled example."""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from pathlib import Path
from typing import TypedDict, cast

import catboost
import mlflow
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from mlflow.pyfunc.model import PythonModel, PythonModelContext
from numpy.typing import NDArray


class Settings(TypedDict):
    target_scale: float
    feature_names: list[str]
    cat_features: list[str]


class TargetScaledServingModel(PythonModel):
    def load_context(self, context: PythonModelContext) -> None:
        self.settings = cast(
            Settings, json.loads(Path(context.artifacts["settings"]).read_text())
        )
        self.model = catboost.CatBoostRegressor()
        self.model.load_model(context.artifacts["model"])

    def predict(
        self,
        context: PythonModelContext | None,
        model_input: pd.DataFrame,
        params: dict[str, object] | None = None,
    ) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
        """Return original-unit predictions after native categorical preparation.

        Parameters
        ----------
        context : PythonModelContext or None
            MLflow serving context; unused during prediction.
        model_input : pandas.DataFrame
            Fitted feature columns; categorical values are converted to strings.
        params : dict or None, default None
            Unused inference parameters.

        Returns
        -------
        numpy.ndarray
            One original-unit prediction per input row.
        """
        frame = model_input.loc[:, self.settings["feature_names"]].copy()
        for feature in self.settings["cat_features"]:
            frame[feature] = frame[feature].astype("string").fillna("unknown").astype(str)
        return np.asarray(self.model.predict(frame), dtype=np.float64) * self.settings["target_scale"]


mlflow.models.set_model(TargetScaledServingModel())

The entrypoint restores feature order and categorical conversion, then applies the inverse scale transformation. It depends only on pinned CatBoost, pandas, NumPy, and MLflow packages. An explicit TrackingConfig.conda_env can supply your own serving environment.

docs.title: Backend and diagnostic constraints
docs.text:
Model shrinking is an optional capability, separate from Model. Implement n_iterations, shrink(k) returning an independent fitted adapter, and predict_pool to support model shrink curves. Preserve fitted preprocessing and inverse transformations in the copy; its predictions must stay in the task metric's target units. Existing custom adapters remain usable without this capability unless a shrink report runs.

Training adapters expose a CatBoost or LightGBM backend through native_model; generic scikit-learn estimators do not satisfy this contract. LightGBMServingModel packages an already trained model and does not implement the complete training adapter interface.

Observed/fitted reports use the adapter's predictions in original units. Native SHAP diagnostics and ShapRanker inspect native_model and see scaled raw outputs in this example. Multiplication by a fixed positive scale preserves relative feature rankings, but raw contributions must be multiplied by the scale before interpreting them as original-unit contributions.

Before adopting your own adapter, check metadata alignment, finite one-value predictions, fresh factory instances, selected iteration reuse, and serving prediction equality. The reference below lists the full method signatures.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: Pool is the toolkit's ready-to-use data container for aligned Polars features, targets, dates, weights, and row metadata. Instantiate it with your prepared data; row operations and backend conversions are included in the package.

docs.title: Prepare a pool
docs.text:
After installing the package, create a pool directly. This small constructed fixture demonstrates container operations; it is not an evaluation dataset:

from datetime import date, timedelta

import polars as pl

from ml_toolkit.data import Pool

n_rows = 24
frame = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "age": [20 + i % 10 for i in range(n_rows)],
        "region": ["north", "south"] * (n_rows // 2),
        "target": [float(i % 3) for i in range(n_rows)],
        "date": [date(2025, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=i) for i in range(n_rows)],
        "weight": [1.0] * n_rows,
        "business_type": ["new", "renewal"] * (n_rows // 2),
        "insured_value": [50_000.0 + i * 25_000 for i in range(n_rows)],
    }
).sort("date")
data = Pool(
    X=frame.select("age", "region"),
    y=frame["target"],
    time=frame["date"],
    weight=frame["weight"],
    cat_features=("region",),
    numerical_features=("age",),
    auxiliary_features=frame.select("business_type", "insured_value"),
)

There are 24 rows and two model features. Targets, timestamps, weights, IDs, and reporting groups stay outside X unless they are model features.

docs.title: Slice without losing alignment
docs.text:
first_week = data.take(range(7))
age_only = first_week.select_features(["age"])

print("Selected rows and features:", len(age_only), age_only.X.columns)
reordered = data.take([2, 0, 2])
print("Aligned (age, target, date):")
for age, target, time in zip(reordered.X["age"], reordered.y, reordered.time):
    print(age, target, time)
print("Original rows:", len(data))

Selected rows and features: 7 ['age']
Aligned (age, target, date):
22 2.0 2025-01-03
20 0.0 2025-01-01
22 2.0 2025-01-03
Original rows: 24

The selection repeats row 2 around row 0; their ages, targets, and dates move together. Weights and optional IDs and reporting groups follow the same order. Feature selection filters feature declarations as well as X. Both operations return new containers, leaving the original 24 rows intact. Reordered data is useful for inspection; training still requires ascending timestamps.

Contiguous nonnegative row selections, including ranges and arrays of consecutive indices, share the source buffers. Reordered, repeated or noncontiguous positions allocate gathered rows. Feature selection also shares column buffers. A small slice can therefore keep its larger source allocation alive.

docs.title: Replace a target without changing rows
docs.text:
For example, prepare a log-transformed target while keeping original counts available for comparison:

transformed = data.with_target(data.y.cast(pl.Float64).log1p())
print("Original targets:", data.y.head(3).to_list())
print("Log1p targets:", transformed.y.head(3).round(4).to_list())
print("Dates preserved:", transformed.time.equals(data.time))

Original targets: [0.0, 1.0, 2.0]
Log1p targets: [0.0, 0.6931, 1.0986]
Dates preserved: True

A model fitted to this transformed target predicts on the transformed scale; convert predictions back before comparing them with original counts. The original pool remains available with unchanged targets.

docs.title: Convert features and baseline for a backend
docs.text:
This conversion example includes a missing category. Use a small copy of the prepared pool so the shared data keeps its original values:

from dataclasses import replace

with_missing = replace(
    data.take([0, 1, 2]),
    X=data.X.head(3).with_columns(
        pl.Series("region", ["north", None, "south"])
    ),
)
model_input = with_missing.to_model_input()
print("Backend categories:", model_input["region"].tolist())
print("Source categories:", with_missing.X["region"].to_list())
native = with_missing.to_catboost(baseline=0.25)
print("Backend features:", native.get_feature_names())
print("Raw-score baseline:", native.get_baseline().reshape(-1).tolist())

Backend categories: ['north', 'unknown', 'south']
Source categories: ['north', None, 'south']
Backend features: ['age', 'region']
Raw-score baseline: [0.25, 0.25, 0.25]

to_model_input() returns pandas feature columns with dictionary-encoded categories whose labels are strings, and fills missing categories with "unknown". For MLflow serving or serialization, use to_model_input(categorical_as_strings=True) to expand categories to strings. to_catboost() also carries targets, weights, and timestamps, broadcasting a scalar baseline to every row. The baseline is a raw model score, not a prediction on the response scale; a log-link model interprets 0.25 on the log scale.

Training reserves the literal category "unknown" for missing values. Raw categorical columns in training and validation inputs must not already contain that value after string conversion, even when they have no missing values. Training reports the offending column. Prepared model inputs, prediction and serving continue to accept "unknown"; ordinary missing values are still filled.

docs.title: Auxiliary features for diagnostics
docs.text:
auxiliary_features is an optional Polars DataFrame containing categorical or continuous values. It has the same row count and positional order as X, with disjoint column names. There is no implicit join on IDs. A frame without columns is normalized to None. All optional constructor arguments are keyword-only.

take() slices auxiliary columns with all other row fields, including reordered and repeated positions. select_features() and with_target() preserve them. Train/held-out pools must have the same auxiliary schema, including column order and dtypes; missing columns are not filled or silently cast.

Select diagnostic columns across both tables with to_analysis_frame():

analysis = data.to_analysis_frame(["age", "business_type", "insured_value"])
assert analysis.columns == ["age", "business_type", "insured_value"]
assert data.to_analysis_frame().columns == [
    "age", "region", "business_type", "insured_value"
]
assert data.to_model_input().columns.to_list() == ["age", "region"]

The method preserves requested column order and reports missing or duplicate names. With no selection it includes X followed by auxiliary columns, sharing their buffers. Backend conversion and serving examples contain only X. cat_features and numerical_features describe only columns of X.

docs.title: Categories and continuous values
docs.text:
ObservedFitted and PSI use FeatureLevelConfig for either table. Numeric dtypes are inferred as numerical; strings and booleans as categorical. Explicit rules can mark integer codes as categorical. features=None infers model and auxiliary columns; features=() disables level diagnostics.

Numerical levels use unweighted train quantiles (n_bins=10 by default), then reuse the exact boundaries on validation/test. Ties may reduce the interval count; constant or entirely missing reference columns have one ordinary interval. Internal boundaries belong to the interval on their right. Finite values outside the observed train range enter the extreme intervals unless they violate explicit lower_bound/upper_bound. Nulls, NaNs and missing sentinels become __NULL__; error sentinels and out-of-bound values become __ERROR__. Other infinities are rejected in both reference and current data. Source columns are not modified.

NumericalFeatureDistributions uses original numerical values for unweighted time summaries, omitting null and nonfinite values; it does not use level bins.

docs.title: Grouping by prepared bands
docs.text:
TimeObservedFitted(by=...) and GroupedMetrics(by=...) group exact values, including combinations of columns. They do not learn numerical intervals. Prepare an auxiliary categorical band for a continuous grouping variable:

from ml_toolkit.evaluation import GroupedMetrics, TimeObservedFitted
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_regression

band = (
    pl.when(pl.col("insured_value").is_null() | pl.col("insured_value").is_nan())
    .then(pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.String))
    .when(pl.col("insured_value") < 100_000)
    .then(pl.lit("less_than_100k"))
    .when(pl.col("insured_value") < 500_000)
    .then(pl.lit("100k_to_500k"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("at_least_500k"))
    .alias("insured_value_band")
)
banded = replace(
    data,
    auxiliary_features=data.auxiliary_features.with_columns(band),
)
grouped_reports = [
    TimeObservedFitted(by=("insured_value_band",)),
    GroupedMetrics(
        metric=metrics_regression,
        by=("business_type", "insured_value_band"),
        min_rows=30,
    ),
]

These fixed business thresholds are independent of the observed data. Learned thresholds must be fitted separately on each fold's training rows and then applied to its held-out rows; do not learn them on the full dataset. Pass reports through prediction_evaluators. Both grouped reports limit distinct combinations to max_groups=50 by default and raise an error when exceeded. Null/NaN form a missing group, distinct from ordinary strings such as "missing".

docs.title: Use the shared container
docs.text:
The same class is available from ml_toolkit and ml_toolkit.data for construction and type annotations:

from ml_toolkit import Pool

docs.title: Row fields
docs.text:
Fields Contract X, y, time, weight Aligned, nonempty Polars frame/series; one value per row cat_features, numerical_features Tuples of feature names present in X object_id Aligned string/integer IDs or None; optional for evaluators that join external data auxiliary_features Aligned categorical/numerical diagnostic frame or None; names disjoint from X

Training validates ascending non-null Date/Datetime timestamps, finite targets, and finite nonnegative weights with a positive total. Optional metadata defaults to None. Fields cannot be reassigned; contained frames and series are not deeply immutable.

docs.title: Row and feature operations
docs.text: take preserves requested row order, including repeated indices. select_features preserves all row metadata and filters feature declarations. with_target preserves rows and their metadata. Each method returns the same concrete container type, so chronological splitting and selection retain your container type.

docs.title: Backend conversion
docs.text: The bundled CatBoost adapters call to_catboost for fitting and to_model_input for named feature frames and serving examples. Preserve fitted feature names and categorical handling in both conversions. A scalar baseline must be broadcast across rows; array baselines must stay aligned.

docs.title: Array types
docs.text: Import FloatArray and IntArray from ml_toolkit.types when annotating your functions. They mean NumPy float64 and int64 arrays; individual APIs describe the required shape. ModelParams is the backend parameter dictionary.

docs.title: Feature selection
docs.text: Selectors choose input columns using training and validation pools. A ranker scores columns of an already fitted adapter; RFE and Top-K use that ordering. The final model is fitted with the last validation split's selected columns.

docs.title: Prepare a selection experiment
docs.text:
Run from an installed checkout after python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike. The imported prepare_training() loads the original Bike Sharing hours, model parameters and local MLflow settings described in the training example. Targets are rentals per hour; weights are one per recorded hour.

from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_frequency
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
splitter = Holdout(data, val_size=0.25, test_size=0.2)
from ml_toolkit.feature_selection import (
    ForwardSelector,
    RFESelector,
    TopKSelector,
)
from ml_toolkit.training import importance_ranker

docs.title: Choose a selector
docs.text:
The selector owns its settings and ranker. Run the setup above first. Omit feature_selector to keep all columns. Each validation window uses fresh models, and the final fit reuses the last window's selected columns.

partition = next(splitter.get_validation())
selectors = (
    RFESelector(
        min_features=3,
        metric="mean_poisson_deviance",
        direction="minimize",
        ranker=importance_ranker,
        max_fits=2,
    ),
    TopKSelector(k=3, ranker=importance_ranker),
    ForwardSelector(
        metric="mean_poisson_deviance",
        direction="minimize",
        max_features=2,
        max_fits=21,
    ),
)
for selector in selectors:
    selection = selector.select(
        train=partition.train,
        validation=partition.heldout,
        params=params,
        model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
        metric=metrics_frequency,
    )
    print(
        type(selector).__name__,
        "features:",
        len(selection.features),
        "candidates:",
        len(selection.steps),
    )

RFESelector features: 11 candidates: 2
TopKSelector features: 3 candidates: 2
ForwardSelector features: 2 candidates: 21

RFE repeatedly removes low-ranked columns and chooses the smallest visited subset within score_tolerance of the best result. Top-K ranks once and keeps exactly k, including protected features, even if its quality is worse. Forward compares every remaining single-feature addition and accepts it only when the absolute gain exceeds min_improvement (default zero). It does not begin a round that exceeds max_fits; too little budget for its first comparison is an error. With no protected columns it starts by comparing every singleton.

protected_features are mandatory and count toward every size limit. Ties prefer the original feature order. steps contains all evaluated candidates, including rejected ones, with metrics and timings; selected_step identifies the returned subset. No fitted models are retained. settings records concrete JSON-compatible configuration; executable rankers are excluded. Its public type, ml_toolkit.feature_selection.SelectionSettings, is a flat dictionary with string keys and values of type str, int, float, bool, None, or tuple[str, ...]. Use it for a custom selector's configuration; the tuple form records feature names.

Each validation run stores concrete settings and every evaluated subset in selection/history.json, including scores, timings, available importances and selected_step. The selected scores are logged under selection/metrics/<name>; fit count, feature count and selected index have separate selection/ entries.

docs.title: Automatic selection plots
docs.text:
train_model also writes diagnostic figures from each split's single search history in that same selection/ artifact folder:

Selector Artifact (default format) Contents RFE selection/rfe_progress.png Validation objective against decreasing feature count, best and selected subsets, and the score tolerance band. Top-K selection/top_k_ranking.png All full-model ranking values, with selected, excluded and protected features distinguished. Forward selection/forward_progress.png All evaluated candidates by subset size, accepted additions, protected baseline when present, and the stopping reason. Forward selection/forward_improvement.png The best candidate's improvement over the preceding accepted subset in each comparable round, with the strict min_improvement threshold. All three selection/best_iteration.png Recorded best iteration against feature count, with the selected subset highlighted when its iteration is available.

Forward improvement is positive when quality improves, for either optimization direction. The initial singleton round without protected features establishes the baseline; it has no improvement against an artificial zero score. With protected features, the protected-only fit supplies the baseline. If there are no comparable rounds, the improvement figure is skipped.

Best iterations are zero-based; zero is valid. Missing iterations are omitted and break connecting lines instead of being plotted as zero. If every iteration is missing, the figure is skipped. Forward displays all available candidates as points, without connecting alternative subsets. RFE progress limits axis labels on long schedules while retaining every evaluated point.

These search diagnostics are always generated when a built-in selector runs, including when ReportingConfig.on_validation=False. They use the stored history without additional fits, predictions or rankings. ReportingConfig.figure controls size, DPI and format; SVG/PDF settings replace the filename extension. Top-K has no before/after quality plot. Protected Top-K features can be below the ranking cutoff, so a global Top-K line is shown only without protected features. Selection scores describe the search, not independent performance.

Calling selector.select() directly only returns the result; it does not plot or log artifacts. To draw an existing built-in result manually, use ml_toolkit.plots.feature_selection.rfe_progress(result, save_fig), top_k_ranking(result, save_fig), or forward_progress(result, save_fig). The same module provides forward_improvement(result, save_fig) and best_iteration_progress(result, save_fig) for the additional diagnostics. Each accepts an optional keyword-only figure=FigureConfig(...) and closes the figure after saving. Custom selector identifiers are skipped by automatic plotting; their history and metrics are still recorded as before.

docs.title: Implement a selector
docs.text:
Implement FeatureSelector.select with the documented keyword arguments and return a FeatureSelectionResult. The workflow checks the selected history entry and input-column order. Create a fresh model for every fit, copy parameter dictionaries, and keep learned state local to each call. The same selector instance is reused across splits; it must not accumulate fitted estimators.

This reusable example evaluates a project-approved feature subset:

Complete custom selector source 
"""A project-owned selector that evaluates an approved feature subset."""

from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from time import perf_counter

import numpy as np

from ml_toolkit import Pool
from ml_toolkit.feature_selection import FeatureSelectionResult, FeatureSelectionStep
from ml_toolkit.metrics import Metric
from ml_toolkit.models.base import Model
from ml_toolkit.types import ModelParams


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FixedFeatureSelector:
    """Evaluate a nonempty, unique subset, preserving original input order."""

    features: tuple[str, ...]

    def select(
        self,
        *,
        train: Pool,
        validation: Pool,
        params: ModelParams,
        model_factory: Callable[[ModelParams], Model],
        metric: Metric,
    ) -> FeatureSelectionResult:
        """Fit and evaluate the subset; retain no learned state between calls."""
        if not self.features or len(set(self.features)) != len(self.features):
            raise ValueError("features must be nonempty and unique")
        if not set(self.features) <= set(train.X.columns):
            raise ValueError("Requested features must exist in training data")
        names = tuple(name for name in train.X.columns if name in self.features)
        train = train.select_features(names)
        validation = validation.select_features(names)
        started = perf_counter()
        model = model_factory(params.copy()).fit(train, validation)
        fit_seconds = perf_counter() - started
        started = perf_counter()
        prediction = model.predict_pool(validation)
        if prediction.shape != (len(validation),) or not np.isfinite(prediction).all():
            raise ValueError("Predictions must be finite and aligned")
        scores = dict(
            metric(
                validation.y.to_numpy().astype(float),
                prediction,
                validation.weight.to_numpy().astype(float),
            ).to_dict()
        )
        step = FeatureSelectionStep(
            names,
            scores,
            {},
            (),
            fit_seconds,
            perf_counter() - started,
            0.0,
            model.best_iteration,
        )
        return FeatureSelectionResult(
            names, 0, (step,), {"selector": "fixed", "features": names}
        )

from examples.custom_selector import FixedFeatureSelector

custom_selection = train_model(
    splitter=splitter,
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    metric=metrics_frequency,
    run_name="custom-selector",
    config=config,
    feature_selector=FixedFeatureSelector(("temperature", "hour")),
)
print(custom_selection.features)
assert custom_selection.feature_selection is not None
print(custom_selection.feature_selection.settings)

('temperature', 'hour')
{'selector': 'fixed', 'features': ('temperature', 'hour')}

The normal workflow performs validation, optional tuning and a fresh final fit using those columns. Prediction, refitting and model packaging remain the model adapter's responsibility: serve inputs in result.features order through that adapter. The selector itself owns no learned model state and is not a serving artifact. See model packaging for saving and reloading the final model. Custom selectors must use the supported Pool and Model contracts; they do not extend backend or prediction-shape support.

The selected final model can be packaged and checked independently of the selector. Continue with custom_selection above; this creates an MLflow model artifact and verifies its reloaded predictions on the selected input schema.

import numpy as np
import mlflow

development = splitter.get_test()
assert development.heldout is not None
selected_train = development.train.select_features(custom_selection.features)
selected_test = development.heldout.select_features(custom_selection.features)
expected = custom_selection.model.predict_pool(selected_test)
with mlflow.start_run():
    logged = custom_selection.model.log(selected_train)
model_info = logged[1] if isinstance(logged, tuple) else logged
reloaded = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(model_info.model_uri)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    reloaded.predict(selected_test.to_model_input(categorical_as_strings=True)),
    expected,
)
print("Selected model predictions preserved after reload")

Selected model predictions preserved after reload

docs.title: Choose a ranker
docs.text:
Ranker What its score means importance_ranker Importance supplied by the fitted adapter's native backend ShapRanker Weighted mean absolute native raw-output SHAP contribution Custom callable Your score for each current validation column

ShapRanker supports CatBoost and LightGBM and does not require the shap extra. It samples positive-weight validation rows deterministically. Native raw outputs may have different units from adapter predictions.

from ml_toolkit.training import ShapRanker

shap_selection = TopKSelector(
    k=3, ranker=ShapRanker(max_samples=500, seed=42)
).select(
    train=partition.train,
    validation=partition.heldout,
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    metric=metrics_frequency,
)
print("SHAP-selected features:", shap_selection.features)

SHAP-selected features: ('temperature', 'feels_like_temperature', 'hour')

The selected names retain their original input order. SHAP affects ranking; the candidate subset is still evaluated with the supplied task metric.

docs.title: Implement a ranker
docs.text:
A FeatureRanker is callable as ranker(model, data). The model is already fitted; data contains the current validation columns. Return exactly one finite value per column name. Higher values rank higher, and signed values are allowed. Preserve both inputs and retain no learned state between calls.

This custom ranker measures the increase in weighted validation MAE after permuting one feature. A fresh seeded generator makes repeated calls reproducible. Each perturbation starts from the original features, leaving labels, weights, timestamps and IDs aligned:

Complete implementation 
"""A project-owned permutation ranker using weighted validation MAE."""

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

import numpy as np

from ml_toolkit.data import Pool
from ml_toolkit.models import Model


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PermutationMAERanker:
    """Rank columns by the rise in weighted MAE after one seeded permutation.

    Higher scores identify columns whose disruption hurts predictions more.
    Values may be negative. The model remains fitted; only a copy of one feature
    column changes for each prediction. Targets, weights, timestamps and row
    metadata stay in their original order. No predictions or models are stored.
    """

    seed: int = 42

    def __call__(self, model: Model, data: Pool) -> dict[str, float]:
        """Return one finite importance for every current validation column."""
        target = data.y.to_numpy()
        weights = data.weight.to_numpy()
        baseline = float(
            np.average(np.abs(target - model.predict_pool(data)), weights=weights)
        )
        rng = np.random.default_rng(self.seed)
        importance: dict[str, float] = {}
        for name in data.X.columns:
            shuffled = data.X[name].gather(rng.permutation(len(data)))
            perturbed = replace(data, X=data.X.with_columns(shuffled))
            error = float(
                np.average(
                    np.abs(target - model.predict_pool(perturbed)), weights=weights
                )
            )
            importance[name] = error - baseline
        return importance

A high score means the fitted model relies on that feature for accurate predictions. Correlated features can share predictive information, and a single permutation is noisy; these scores are not causal effects. The example ranks by MAE even though the workflow reports Poisson deviance.

from examples.custom_ranker import PermutationMAERanker

ranked = train_model(
    splitter=splitter,
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    metric=metrics_frequency,
    run_name="permutation-selection",
    config=config,
    feature_selector=TopKSelector(k=3, ranker=PermutationMAERanker(seed=42)),
)
print("Permutation-selected features:", ranked.features)
assert ranked.test_metrics is not None
print(
    "Test Poisson deviance:",
    round(ranked.test_metrics["mean_poisson_deviance"], 4),
)

Permutation-selected features: ('temperature', 'feels_like_temperature', 'hour')
Test Poisson deviance: 112.9418

TopKSelector creates the fitted model supplied to the ranker, applies the returned ordering and evaluates the chosen subset. No model is fitted inside the ranker. Explicit inheritance from FeatureRanker is unnecessary.
