docs.title: Inflation
docs.text: Inflation strategies convert monetary values between price dates. Use a constant annual rate for a supplied assumption, a monthly index for historical or planned levels, or a learned common index estimated from project observations.

docs.title: Convert to a later price date
docs.text:
from datetime import date

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from ml_toolkit.inflation import ConstantRateInflation

from_dates = pl.Series([date(2025, 1, 1)])
to_dates = pl.Series([date(2026, 1, 1)])
inflation = ConstantRateInflation(annual_rate=0.08)
adjusted = inflation.adjust(np.array([100.0]), from_dates, to_dates)
print("Later price level:", adjusted.round(2).tolist())
restored = inflation.adjust(adjusted, to_dates, from_dates)
print("Original price level:", restored.round(2).tolist())
np.testing.assert_allclose(restored, [100.0])

Later price level: [107.99]
Original price level: [100.0]

0.08 means 8% annual compound growth. The result is slightly below 108 because elapsed years use 365.25 days. Each row can have its own amount and date pair; reversing the dates converts back to an earlier price level.

docs.title: Use a monthly index
docs.text:
from ml_toolkit.inflation import ManualInflation

monthly = ManualInflation({date(2025, 1, 1): 1.0, date(2025, 3, 1): 1.21})
adjusted = monthly.adjust(
    np.array([100.0]),
    pl.Series([date(2025, 1, 15)]),
    pl.Series([date(2025, 2, 28)]),
)
print(adjusted.round(2).tolist())

[110.0]

Continuing with the imports above, February's interpolated index is 1.1. Every date within a month uses that month's level. Missing months between anchors are interpolated in log space; requested months must stay within the anchor range.

docs.title: Learn a common price index
docs.text:
LogLinearInflation and SplineInflation estimate a weighted Gamma mean with a log link:

log(E[amount | features, date]) = intercept + feature effects + trend(date)

The first strategy has a linear time effect, giving a constant compound growth rate inside training. The second uses a regularized cubic B-spline to represent a changing growth rate. Both fit original positive amounts, rather than a regression on log-transformed targets.

The proportional price change is shared by all objects. Features help distinguish a change in product composition from price growth: an increasing share of expensive products need not imply inflation. When comparing the same object at two dates, its feature effect cancels, leaving the multiplier exp(trend(to_date) - trend(from_date)). Features are required only for fitting; factor() and adjust() still accept dates without features.

Numeric controls have standardized linear effects; categorical controls use sparse one-hot encoding according to Pool.cat_features. Numeric missing values use training medians; all-missing numeric columns are dropped. Interactions, object-specific trends and separate seasonal components are not modeled. Missing price-determining characteristics or a strong relationship between time and the available characteristics can limit interpretation of the estimated trend.

The following reproducible data is synthetic, with Gamma price variation, changing product composition and a known time effect; it is not measured inflation. Continue with the NumPy, Polars and date imports above:

import json

from examples.inflation_benchmark import synthetic_pool
from ml_toolkit.inflation import (
    LogLinearInflation,
    SplineInflation,
    inflation_from_config,
)

training = synthetic_pool(months=36, rows_per_month=25)
linear = LogLinearInflation(control_features=["size", "category"]).fit(training)
smooth = SplineInflation(
    n_knots=5,
    alpha=0.001,
    extrapolation="damped",
    damping_half_life_years=1.0,
).fit(training)
original = pl.Series([date(2017, 1, 1)])
requested = pl.Series([date(2018, 1, 1)])
for strategy in (linear, smooth):
    changed = strategy.adjust(np.array([100.0]), original, requested)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        strategy.adjust(changed, requested, original), [100.0]
    )

saved = json.loads(json.dumps(smooth.to_config(), allow_nan=False))
restored = inflation_from_config(saved)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    restored.factor(original, requested), smooth.factor(original, requested)
)

fit(data) takes a Pool. control_features=None uses every available column, an explicit sequence chooses controls, and control_features=[] fits dates only. Every preprocessing step uses positive-weight training rows only. Targets must be finite and strictly positive; weights must be finite and nonnegative with positive total. Zero-weight rows do not set the fitted time range or knots. The linear method needs at least two distinct positive-weight timestamps; the spline needs at least n_knots (default five). These target and weight restrictions do not apply to the fixed strategies' no-op fit.

Both methods use elapsed time in 365.25-day years, including fractional days. Timezone-aware timestamps refer to UTC instants. Defaults are alpha=0.001 (L2 regularization of time and control coefficients), extrapolation="linear", and damping_half_life_years=1.0; the spline degree is fixed at three.

docs.title: Choose an extrapolation policy
docs.text:
The forecast horizon is determined by the requested dates; there is no fixed one-year limit. extrapolation selects behavior outside positive-weight training:

Policy Behavior linear Continue the boundary log-index tangent, preserving its growth rate constant Hold the boundary index level error Reject dates outside the fitted range damped After the last training date, exponentially decay the boundary log-index slope toward zero; before the first date, extrapolate linearly

For damped, the future slope halves every damping_half_life_years. This approaches a constant price level, not a long-run inflation target. The spline polynomial is never continued beyond its training boundaries. Policies define one index function, so conversions remain reversible and agree when performed through an intermediate date. Unrepresentable factors raise ValueError.

docs.title: Prepare recorded retail prices
docs.text:
Run from the installed repository checkout and prepare the source explicitly:

python -m pip install -r requirements-examples.txt
python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset retail

The reusable loader reads UCI Online Retail (Daqing Chen, 2015; CC BY 4.0). UnitPrice is sterling per item and InvoiceDate is the recorded transaction time. The approximately 23 MB workbook and normalized records stay in .cache/uci-online-retail; reading Excel requires openpyxl, an example dependency rather than a package runtime dependency.

We exclude cancelled invoices and lines with nonpositive quantity or price. A reproducible approximately 10% invoice sample retains all eligible lines of each selected invoice: the first eight bytes of its ID's SHA-256 digest, interpreted big-endian, must have remainder zero modulo ten. Original values and timestamps are retained. December 2011 is excluded because it is incomplete. Training ends before September 2011, validation covers September, and testing covers October–November. Invoice groups never cross those partitions.

from examples.retail_data import load_retail_splits

retail = load_retail_splits(download_if_missing=False)
print(
    "Train / validation / test lines:",
    len(retail.train),
    len(retail.validation),
    len(retail.test),
)
print("First held-out prices (GBP/item):", retail.test.y.head(5).to_list())

Train / validation / test lines: 29847 4282 15210
First held-out prices (GBP/item): [0.85, 7.08, 4.95, 4.25, 4.95]

The three predictors are product code, country, and purchased quantity. Invoice IDs, customer IDs, timestamps, and target-derived amounts are excluded from model features. Each invoice line has weight one, so metrics describe line-level prices.

docs.title: Fit an inflation-adjusted regressor
docs.text:
Continue with retail above and the NumPy, Polars, date, and inflation imports from the first calculation. Fit at a common reference price date, then predict held-out transaction prices at their recorded dates:

from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel, InflationAdjustedModel

adjusted_model = InflationAdjustedModel(
    CatBoostRegressionModel(
        {
            "iterations": 60,
            "depth": 4,
            "loss_function": "RMSE",
            "random_seed": 42,
            "thread_count": 2,
            "verbose": False,
            "allow_writing_files": False,
        }
    ),
    inflation=ConstantRateInflation(annual_rate=0.08),
    reference_date=date(2011, 9, 1),
).fit(retail.train, retail.validation)
predictions = adjusted_model.predict_pool(retail.test)
print("Predicted prices (GBP/item):", predictions[:5].round(2).tolist())
print(
    "Held-out MAE (GBP/item):",
    round(float(np.mean(np.abs(predictions - retail.test.y.to_numpy()))), 2),
)

# Hold product, country, and quantity fixed; vary only the requested price date.
requested_dates = pl.Series(
    "prediction_date", [date(2011, 9, 1), date(2012, 9, 1)]
)
future = retail.test.X[[0, 0]].with_columns(requested_dates)
date_predictions = adjusted_model.predict_frame(future)
assert date_predictions[1] > date_predictions[0] > 0
print("Same item at requested price dates:", date_predictions.round(2).tolist())
conversion = adjusted_model.inflation.factor(
    requested_dates.head(1), requested_dates.tail(1)
)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    date_predictions[1:], date_predictions[:1] * conversion
)

Predicted prices (GBP/item): [1.42, 5.08, 4.87, 7.22, 9.98]
Held-out MAE (GBP/item): 2.18
Same item at requested price dates: [1.41, 1.52]

The 8% annual rate is an assumed conversion policy, not a historical UK inflation estimate.

Pool predictions use each row's observation date. Frame predictions require prediction_date, whose name can be configured on the adapter. With ManualInflation, all training, reference, and requested months must lie within the supplied index range.

docs.title: Use a learned strategy in a model factory
docs.text:
Keep strategy settings in the factory, and create a fresh strategy on every call. The workflow can then refit it independently for feature selection, validation and final fitting. Continue with retail, adjusted_model and the model imports above:

from ml_toolkit.types import ModelParams


def learned_model(params: ModelParams) -> InflationAdjustedModel:
    return InflationAdjustedModel(
        CatBoostRegressionModel(params),
        inflation=LogLinearInflation(alpha=0.001),
        reference_date=date(2011, 9, 1),
    )


learned_retail = learned_model(adjusted_model.model.params).fit(
    retail.train, retail.validation
)
assert np.isfinite(learned_retail.predict_pool(retail.test)).all()

InflationAdjustedModel passes only the original training pool to the strategy. Validation amounts are normalized using that fitted index. With control_features=None, feature selection also determines the controls available to each strategy fit. Explicit controls must be present in each supplied pool. Do not pass strategy settings as native CatBoost parameters.

docs.title: Compare strategies at calendar forecast horizons
docs.text:
Start with the linear strategy and compare the spline and extrapolation settings on chronological validation. The benchmark holds CatBoost parameters fixed for four methods: no adjustment, an assumed constant rate, a learned linear trend, and a learned spline trend. Each origin fits on preceding observations only.

python -m examples.inflation_benchmark --output inflation-benchmark.csv
python -m examples.inflation_benchmark --extrapolation damped --damping-half-life-years 1
python -m examples.inflation_benchmark --dataset retail --min-train-months 6 --step-months 1 --horizons 1 3

The default synthetic benchmark tests 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. Horizon 12 evaluates the twelfth month after the training cutoff, rather than accumulating twelve months of observations. Incomplete horizons are skipped. The real-data command requires the explicitly prepared Online Retail cache above and never downloads implicitly. Its history is shorter than a year and cannot establish twelve-month forecast quality.

Individual fold results include weighted MAE, RMSE, Gamma deviance and predicted over observed total amounts. Synthetic results also measure error in the known log-index, relative to the final training date. Printed summaries average fold metrics equally across origins. The constant rate defaults to an assumed 8%, not an estimate. There is no guarantee a learned adjustment improves the final regressor, and synthetic index recovery is not evidence of real-world superiority.

For reference, running the synthetic and retail commands above with --iterations 60 and the default strategy settings produced these mean fold MAEs. Synthetic monetary units are arbitrary; retail units are GBP per item.

Strategy Synthetic, 12 months Retail, 1 month Retail, 3 months No adjustment 113.360 1.879 2.061 Assumed 8% rate 88.364 1.852 2.063 Learned linear 72.337 1.805 1.941 Learned spline 93.952 1.846 2.067

These settings illustrate a tradeoff: the retail linear adjustment reduced MAE but its predicted/observed amount ratio moved further below one (from 0.900 to 0.850 at one month and from 0.888 to 0.783 at three months). The spline did not outperform the linear strategy. Select settings using the metric appropriate to the project rather than assuming any adjustment is uniformly better.

docs.title: Log and reload for serving
docs.text:
Continue with the fitted adjusted_model, retail, and future above. log() returns the native model first and the adjusted serving model second. Load the second artifact to retain date-dependent predictions:

import mlflow

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("ml-toolkit-inflation")
with mlflow.start_run():
    native_info, adjusted_info = adjusted_model.log(retail.train)

loaded = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(adjusted_info.model_uri)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    loaded.predict(future.to_pandas()),
    adjusted_model.predict_frame(future),
)

This writes a local tracking database and model artifacts. The assertion checks that the reloaded model preserves both requested price-date predictions. The same logging API supports the two learned strategies: their settings, temporal coefficients, spline knots and fitted boundaries are saved as JSON. Feature transformers and the Gamma estimator are not needed for serving, and loading does not refit either estimator.

docs.title: Implement an inflation strategy
docs.text:
Subclass InflationAdjuster and implement factor(from_dates, to_dates): return one finite positive multiplier per aligned date pair. The inherited adjust() multiplies amounts by these factors. Override fit() when learning parameters from fit(data: Pool), using only its training pool; keep learned state in that strategy instance. A model factory must create a fresh strategy for each fit, including final refitting.

This project implementation accepts a separate compound rate for each calendar year. A full year applies exactly 1 + rate, including leap years; a partial year compounds by the fraction of that year's calendar days. Datetime inputs use their local dates. Requested dates must lie within the supplied consecutive years, including the following January 1 boundary.

Complete strategy source 
"""Calendar-year conversion policies supplied by a project."""

from datetime import date
from math import isfinite, log1p

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from ml_toolkit.inflation import InflationAdjuster
from ml_toolkit.types import FloatArray


class AnnualRateTable(InflationAdjuster):
    """Compound a different supplied rate in each calendar year.

    Parameters
    ----------
    annual_rates : dict[int, float]
        Consecutive calendar years mapped to finite rates greater than -1.
        A rate of 0.08 represents 8% growth over that complete year.

    Notes
    -----
    Partial years use elapsed calendar days divided by days in that year.
    Datetimes use their local calendar date. The range includes January 1
    after the final configured year. Rates are fixed policy inputs; inherited
    fit(data) validates data.time and does not estimate parameters from targets.
    """

    def __init__(self, annual_rates: dict[int, float]) -> None:
        years = sorted(annual_rates)
        if not years or years != list(range(years[0], years[-1] + 1)):
            raise ValueError("Supply consecutive calendar years")
        if years[0] < 1 or years[-1] > 9998:
            raise ValueError("Years must be between 1 and 9998")
        if any(not isfinite(rate) or rate <= -1 for rate in annual_rates.values()):
            raise ValueError("Annual rates must be finite and greater than -1")
        self.annual_rates = annual_rates.copy()
        self._start = date(years[0], 1, 1)
        self._end = date(years[-1] + 1, 1, 1)

    def factor(self, from_dates: pl.Series, to_dates: pl.Series) -> FloatArray:
        """Return price-level ratios for equally sized, non-null date series."""
        if len(from_dates) != len(to_dates):
            raise ValueError("Date series must have equal lengths")
        factors = np.exp(self._log_level(to_dates) - self._log_level(from_dates))
        if not np.isfinite(factors).all() or (factors <= 0).any():
            raise ValueError("Conversion factors must be finite and positive")
        return factors

    def _log_level(self, dates: pl.Series) -> FloatArray:
        if dates.dtype != pl.Date and dates.dtype.base_type() != pl.Datetime:
            raise TypeError("Dates must have Date or Datetime dtype")
        if dates.null_count():
            raise ValueError("Dates must not contain nulls")
        calendar_dates = dates.dt.date()
        if ((calendar_dates < self._start) | (calendar_dates > self._end)).any():
            raise ValueError("Dates are outside the configured years")
        levels = np.zeros(len(dates), dtype=float)
        for year, rate in self.annual_rates.items():
            start, end = date(year, 1, 1), date(year + 1, 1, 1)
            elapsed = (calendar_dates - start).dt.total_days().to_numpy()
            fraction = np.clip(elapsed / (end - start).days, 0.0, 1.0)
            levels += log1p(rate) * fraction
        return levels

These rates illustrate a supplied conversion policy, not measured inflation. Continue with the NumPy, Polars and date imports from the first calculation:

from examples.custom_inflation import AnnualRateTable

annual = AnnualRateTable({2024: 0.03, 2025: 0.07})
original_dates = pl.Series([date(2024, 1, 1)])
later_dates = pl.Series([date(2026, 1, 1)])
converted = annual.adjust(np.array([100.0]), original_dates, later_dates)
print("After 3% then 7%:", converted.round(2).tolist())
restored = annual.adjust(converted, later_dates, original_dates)
print("Reversed conversion:", restored.round(2).tolist())
np.testing.assert_allclose(restored, [100.0])

After 3% then 7%: [110.21]
Reversed conversion: [100.0]

docs.title: Fit with a project strategy
docs.text:
Continue with retail, mlflow and the model imports above. This example uses the same recorded retail observations and chronological boundaries as the built-in strategy. Rates are fixed inputs; inherited fit() validates dates without learning from prices. The normal workflow creates separate strategy instances for validation and final fitting.

from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from examples.retail_data import load_retail_pool
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.config import TrackingConfig, TrainingConfig
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from ml_toolkit.types import ModelParams


def annual_model(params: ModelParams) -> InflationAdjustedModel:
    return InflationAdjustedModel(
        CatBoostRegressionModel(params),
        inflation=AnnualRateTable({2010: 0.02, 2011: 0.08, 2012: 0.05}),
        reference_date=date(2011, 9, 1),
    )


retail_data = load_retail_pool(download_if_missing=False)
annual_result = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(
        retail_data,
        val_size=len(retail.validation),
        test_size="2011-10-01",
    ),
    params={
        "iterations": 30,
        "depth": 4,
        "loss_function": "RMSE",
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    },
    model_factory=annual_model,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    run_name="retail-annual-policy",
    config=TrainingConfig(tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False)),
)
annual_predictions = annual_result.model.predict_pool(retail.test)
assert annual_result.test_metrics is not None
print(
    "Custom-policy test MAE (GBP/item):",
    round(annual_result.test_metrics["mae"], 2),
)
print("Predicted prices (GBP/item):", annual_predictions[:5].round(2).tolist())

Custom-policy test MAE (GBP/item): 2.08
Predicted prices (GBP/item): [1.09, 3.9, 5.45, 7.21, 7.74]

The final model includes September's validation rows and predicts prices at October–November transaction dates. Metrics and configuration are logged to the local MLflow store configured above.

Bundled model packaging reconstructs ConstantRateInflation, ManualInflation, LogLinearInflation, and SplineInflation. A custom strategy such as AnnualRateTable works for fitting and prediction, but InflationAdjustedModel.log() raises ValueError for it. Keep trial, validation and final model logging disabled, as above, or provide your own serving implementation that saves and restores the strategy. See the model adapter guide for an executable persistence pattern.

Notes

docs.title: ConstantRateInflation
docs.text:
ConstantRateInflation(annual_rate: float)

Bases: InflationAdjuster

Convert price levels using constant annual compound inflation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default annual_rate float

Annual proportional rate greater than -1; 0.08 means 8% annual inflation.

required Notes

Elapsed years are computed using 365.25 days, including fractional days.

Examples:

Express 100 monetary units at a later price level, then reverse the conversion. These small amounts illustrate the calculation, not an observed price index.

>>> from datetime import date
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import polars as pl
>>> from ml_toolkit.inflation import ConstantRateInflation
>>> from_dates = pl.Series([date(2025, 1, 1)])
>>> to_dates = pl.Series([date(2026, 1, 1)])
>>> inflation = ConstantRateInflation(annual_rate=0.08)
>>> later = inflation.adjust(np.array([100.0]), from_dates, to_dates)
>>> later.round(2).tolist()
[107.99]
>>> inflation.adjust(later, to_dates, from_dates).round(2).tolist()
[100.0]

The forward value is slightly below 108 because these dates are 365 days apart and the annual compounding convention uses 365.25 days.

docs.title: ManualInflation
docs.text:
ManualInflation(monthly_index: dict[date, float])

Bases: InflationAdjuster

Convert prices using a sparse monthly index with log-linear interpolation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default monthly_index dict[date, float]

At least two distinct anchor months mapped to finite, strictly positive index values. Keys are interpreted at month granularity.

required

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

Too few anchors are supplied, a month occurs twice, or an index value is nonpositive or non-finite.

Notes

Missing months between anchors are filled by linear interpolation in log(index), producing constant compound growth between anchors. Every day in a month uses that month's index. Extrapolation outside the supplied anchor range is forbidden.

Examples:

>>> from datetime import date
>>> import polars as pl
>>> from ml_toolkit.inflation import ManualInflation
>>> inflation = ManualInflation({date(2026, 1, 1): 1.0, date(2026, 3, 1): 1.21})
>>> factor = inflation.factor(
...     pl.Series([date(2026, 1, 15)]),
...     pl.Series([date(2026, 2, 28)]),
... )
>>> round(float(factor[0]), 2)
1.1

docs.text:
LogLinearInflation(
    *,
    alpha: float = 0.001,
    control_features: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    extrapolation: Extrapolation = "linear",
    damping_half_life_years: float = 1.0
)

Bases: _LearnedInflation

Learn a constant compound trend while controlling for object composition.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default alpha float

Nonnegative L2 regularization of both temporal and control effects.

0.001 control_features sequence of str or None

Controls from Pool.X. None uses every available column; an empty sequence fits a date-only model. Categories follow Pool.cat_features.

None extrapolation ('linear', 'constant', 'error', 'damped')

Outside training, continue the boundary log-index slope, hold the level, reject the date, or exponentially damp the future slope toward zero. Damped extrapolation before the first training date remains linear.

'linear' damping_half_life_years float

Positive number of years for the extrapolated future slope to halve.

1.0 Notes

Fits a Gamma mean with log-link to positive targets, with linear numeric and one-hot categorical controls. The inferred temporal effect is a common index, not an object-specific or causal inflation estimate. Missing controls and time-correlated characteristics can limit its interpretation. Dates use elapsed time in 365.25-day years; timezone-aware datetimes use UTC instants. At least two distinct dates with positive weight are required.

docs.text:
SplineInflation(
    *,
    n_knots: int = 5,
    alpha: float = 0.001,
    control_features: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    extrapolation: Extrapolation = "linear",
    damping_half_life_years: float = 1.0
)

Bases: _LearnedInflation

Learn a changing common price trend with a regularized cubic B-spline.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_knots int

Number of uniformly spaced knots over positive-weight training dates. Must be at least two; at least n_knots distinct dates are required.

5 alpha float

Nonnegative L2 regularization of temporal basis and control effects.

0.001 control_features sequence of str or None

Controls from Pool.X; None uses every column and an empty sequence uses dates only. Numeric effects are linear, categories are one-hot encoded.

None extrapolation ('linear', 'constant', 'error', 'damped')

Same boundary policy as LogLinearInflation. The spline polynomial is never continued outside training; linear uses its boundary tangent.

'linear' damping_half_life_years float

Positive number of years for the extrapolated future slope to halve.

1.0 Notes

Uses the same weighted Gamma mean and shared-index assumption as LogLinearInflation. Only time is spline-transformed; feature/time interactions, separate group trends and seasonality are not modeled.

docs.title: Migrating custom strategies
docs.text: InflationAdjuster.fit(dates, y, sample_weight) has been replaced by fit(data: Pool). Update overrides to read data.time, data.y, data.weight, and optionally data.X. Fixed strategies can continue inheriting the no-op fit, which now validates data.time. There is no fit_pool compatibility method; the date-pair APIs and existing fixed-strategy artifact formats are unchanged.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: Metrics evaluate aligned targets, predictions, and weights. The small arrays below illustrate calculations, not model performance on a real dataset. Use them directly for existing predictions or pass a compatible callable to training. Numerical FloatArray parameters mean one-dimensional NumPy float64 arrays; use np.array([...], dtype=float) when preparing inputs.

docs.title: Choose a metric
docs.text:
Data and purpose Entry point Result General numeric targets, including signed values metrics_regression MetricsRegression Confirmed binary labels and probabilities metrics_classification MetricsClassification Binary labels after applying a cutoff confusion_matrix (TN, FP, FN, TP) weighted counts Poisson frequency rates with exposure metrics_frequency MetricsFrequency Severity predictions with a Tweedie power metrics_severity MetricsSeverity Ranking outcomes by exposure capacity ranking_metrics RankingMetrics curves and selected points Known positive and unlabeled rows PUMetric, positive_capture_curve Named scores or two curve arrays

Regression, classification, frequency, severity, and PU score objects expose to_dict(). RankingMetrics instead contains curves and attributes for inspection and ranking plots; it is not itself a training metric result with to_dict().

docs.title: Evaluate general regression
docs.text:
metrics_regression supports signed targets and uses equal weights when sample_weight is omitted. Frequency and severity results include these same five metrics alongside their specialized scores.

import numpy as np
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_regression

scores = metrics_regression(
    np.array([-2.0, 0.0, 2.0]),
    np.array([-1.0, -2.0, 3.0]),
    np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0]),
)
assert scores.mean_absolute_error == 1.5
assert scores.mean_squared_error == 2.5
assert scores.root_mean_squared_error == np.sqrt(2.5)
assert scores.r2_score == -0.25
assert scores.mean_error == -0.5
print("Weighted MAE:", scores.mean_absolute_error)

Weighted MAE: 1.5

Positive mean error means overprediction; negative means underprediction. R² is NaN with fewer than two positive-weight observations. For constant targets it is 1 for perfect predictions and 0 otherwise. Zero-weight rows contribute to neither errors nor the R² observation count. Inputs must be nonempty, finite, aligned one-dimensional arrays; weights must be finite and nonnegative with positive total.

docs.title: Evaluate binary probabilities
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from ml_toolkit.metrics import confusion_matrix, metrics_classification

observed = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0])
probabilities = np.array([0.1, 0.6, 0.4, 0.9])
weight = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0])
for cutoff in (0.3, 0.7):
    scores = metrics_classification(
        observed,
        probabilities,
        threshold=cutoff,
        sample_weight=weight,
    )
    print(
        f"cutoff={cutoff}: precision={scores.precision:.3f}, recall={scores.recall:.3f}"
    )
labels = (probabilities >= 0.7).astype(float)
print(
    "Weighted (TN, FP, FN, TP):",
    confusion_matrix(observed, labels, sample_weight=weight),
)

cutoff=0.3: precision=0.600, recall=1.000
cutoff=0.7: precision=1.000, recall=0.667
Weighted (TN, FP, FN, TP): (3.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0)

At cutoff 0.3, predicted positives have total weight 5 and positive weight 3, so precision is 3 / 5; all positive weight is captured. Raising the cutoff to 0.7 removes the false positive but misses positive weight 1 out of 3. Weights affect counts, precision, and recall. ROC AUC, average precision, and log loss use probabilities directly. confusion_matrix requires predicted labels instead of probabilities. Pass finite, nonnegative weights with positive total for weighted scores. ROC AUC is NaN when only one target class is present.

docs.title: Evaluate frequency and severity
docs.text:
Continue with the NumPy import above. Frequency targets and predictions are rates; exposure supplies row weights and ranking capacity. Do not multiply the rates by exposure before calling the metric.

from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_frequency, metrics_severity

# Annual claim rates and policy-year exposure, not claim counts.
frequency_observed = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
frequency_prediction = np.array([0.2, 1.2, 1.5])
exposure = np.array([0.5, 1.0, 2.0])
frequency = metrics_frequency(
    frequency_observed, frequency_prediction, exposure
)
print(
    f"Frequency MAE: {frequency.mean_absolute_error:.4f} claims per policy-year"
)
print(f"Poisson deviance: {frequency.mean_poisson_deviance:.4f}")
print(f"Predicted / observed claims: {frequency.prediction_over_observed:.4f}")

# Average claim amounts in dollars, weighted by claim counts.
severity_observed = np.array([100.0, 200.0, 300.0])
severity_prediction = np.array([120.0, 180.0, 240.0])
claim_count = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
severity = metrics_severity(
    severity_observed, severity_prediction, claim_count, power=2.0
)
print(f"Severity MAE: ${severity.mean_absolute_error:.2f} per claim")
print(f"Gamma deviance: {severity.mean_tweedie_deviance:.4f}")
print(f"Predicted / observed cost: {severity.prediction_over_observed:.4f}")

Frequency MAE: 0.3714 claims per policy-year
Poisson deviance: 0.1534
Predicted / observed claims: 0.8600
Severity MAE: $40.00 per claim
Gamma deviance: 0.0359
Predicted / observed cost: 0.8571

The frequency totals are 4.3 predicted and 5.0 observed claims, hence 14% underprediction. Weighting gives more influence to the final row's rate error. Severity predicts $1,200 versus $1,400 observed, with $40 weighted absolute error per claim. Gamma deviance is dimensionless. Export the complete named score dictionary with frequency.to_dict() or severity.to_dict().

Frequency predictions must be strictly positive and targets nonnegative. Severity inputs must satisfy the chosen Tweedie power; power=2.0 uses Gamma deviance and requires positive targets and predictions. Both metrics also calculate ranking scores, so the exposure-weighted observed total must be positive. Their gain_at_10 and lift_at_10 describe the highest-scored 10% of exposure; normalized Gini is NaN when perfect-ranking Gini is close to zero.

Bind the extra severity argument before passing it to training:

from functools import partial

severity_metric = partial(metrics_severity, power=2.0)
bound_scores = severity_metric(
    severity_observed, severity_prediction, claim_count
)
print(round(bound_scores.mean_tweedie_deviance, 4))

0.0359

docs.title: Inspect gains, lift, and Gini
docs.text:
from ml_toolkit.metrics import ranking_metrics

ranking = ranking_metrics(
    np.array([1.0, 4.0, 2.0, 3.0]),
    np.array([0.1, 0.8, 0.9, 0.5]),
    np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0]),
    selected_percents=(25.0, 50.0),
)
print(f"Normalized Gini: {ranking.normalized_gini:.4f}")
for point in ranking.selected_points:
    print(
        f"Exposure={point.percent:.0f}%: gain={point.gain:.4f}, lift={point.lift:.4f}"
    )
print("Cumulative exposure:", ranking.cumulative_exposure.round(4).tolist())
print("Cumulative observed:", ranking.cumulative_observed.round(4).tolist())

Normalized Gini: 0.4286
Exposure=25%: gain=0.2353, lift=0.9412
Exposure=50%: gain=0.5882, lift=1.1765
Cumulative exposure: [0.0, 0.1667, 0.5, 0.8333, 1.0]
Cumulative observed: [0.0, 0.1176, 0.5882, 0.9412, 1.0]

The score puts the row with observed rate 2 above the row with rate 4, so ranking is imperfect. Half of the exposure captures 10 / 17 of the observed amount: 58.82%, or 1.1765 times uniform selection. At 25% exposure, capture is slightly worse than uniform selection; the point interpolates within a row.

Each selected point exposes percent, gain, and lift. Gain is the fraction of total exposure-weighted observed outcome captured; lift divides gain by the exposure fraction. Results interpolate at the requested capacity percentages. Rows are sorted by descending prediction; tied scores retain input order and zero-exposure rows are omitted. The cumulative arrays include an initial zero. These are supervised outcomes; use PU metrics for positive/unlabeled labels.

docs.title: Evaluate positive-unlabeled predictions
docs.text:
from ml_toolkit.metrics import PUMetric, positive_capture_curve

pu_labels = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0])
pu_probabilities = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.2])
pu_metric = PUMetric(prior=0.1, loss="nnPU")
pu_scores = pu_metric(pu_labels, pu_probabilities)
pu_values = pu_scores.to_dict()
print("Known-positive capture:", pu_values["known_positive_capture_at_10pct"])
print(
    "Actual unlabeled fraction flagged:",
    pu_values["unlabeled_flagged_at_10pct"],
)
capacity, capture = positive_capture_curve(pu_labels, pu_probabilities)
print(capacity.tolist())
print(capture.tolist())

Known-positive capture: 0.5
Actual unlabeled fraction flagged: 0.5
[0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0]
[0.0, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0]

With only two unlabeled rows, reaching the requested 10% requires flagging one whole row: actual capacity is 50%, and the same cutoff captures 50% of known positives. Always inspect actual flagged capacity alongside capture.

Here 1 means known positive and 0 means unlabeled. The prior is population positive prevalence, not the labeled fraction; match it and the loss to the model's configuration. Both groups need positive total weight. nnPU clips estimated negative risk at zero when calculating total risk; uPU retains it.

The returned curve arrays contain fractions, whereas the corresponding plot uses percentages. All tied scores enter together. Capacity cutoffs can therefore flag more unlabeled rows than the requested percentage. Capture estimates recall only if labeled positives represent the positive population.

docs.title: Supply a custom training metric
docs.text:
The reusable metric below returns weighted MAE in the same units as the target. It owns no fitted state and can be called for any split.

Complete metric source 
"""A project-owned metric shared by training and adapter examples."""

import numpy as np

from ml_toolkit.metrics import MetricScores
from ml_toolkit.types import FloatArray


def weighted_mae(
    observed: FloatArray, prediction: FloatArray, weight: FloatArray
) -> MetricScores:
    """Return weighted absolute error in the target's units under ``mae``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    observed, prediction, weight : FloatArray
        Aligned one-dimensional values. Weights must be finite, nonnegative,
        and have positive total; training validates that data boundary.

    Returns
    -------
    MetricScores
        Named scalar error usable for reporting and minimization.
    """
    error = abs(observed - prediction)
    return MetricScores({"mae": float(np.average(error, weights=weight))})

from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from ml_toolkit.metrics import Metric

metric: Metric = weighted_mae
print(
    {
        name: round(value, 4)
        for name, value in metric(observed, probabilities, weight)
        .to_dict()
        .items()
    }
)

{'mae': 0.35}

Training passes three aligned arrays and validates weights at its data boundary. Return an object satisfying MetricResult, with to_dict() mapping score names to floats; MetricScores is a simple implementation. Use the same key ("mae" here) in selection or tuning configuration when optimizing it, and choose the appropriate optimization direction.

docs.title: Use the metric in training
docs.text:
Run from the installed repository checkout after python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike. This uses all original UCI Bike Sharing hours, recorded rental counts and timestamps, and unit weights; see the dataset and features. The latest 20% is test; validation is the latest quarter of the remaining rows.

The metric's mae key is the tuning objective below. direction="minimize" selects lower error. CatBoost still fits its RMSE objective; this callable controls toolkit evaluation and trial selection.

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import mlflow
from optuna import Trial

from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.config import TrackingConfig, TrainingConfig, TuningConfig
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from ml_toolkit.types import ModelParams


def search_depth(trial: Trial) -> ModelParams:
    return {"depth": trial.suggest_int("depth", 2, 3)}


bike = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
previous_uri = mlflow.get_tracking_uri()
with TemporaryDirectory(prefix="custom-metric-") as directory:
    mlflow.set_tracking_uri(f"sqlite:///{Path(directory) / 'tracking.db'}")
    experiment_id = mlflow.create_experiment(
        "custom-metric",
        artifact_location=(Path(directory) / "artifacts").as_uri(),
    )
    mlflow.set_experiment(experiment_id=experiment_id)
    result = train_model(
        splitter=Holdout(bike, val_size=0.25, test_size=0.2),
        params={
            "loss_function": "RMSE",
            "iterations": 30,
            "random_seed": 42,
            "thread_count": 2,
            "verbose": False,
            "allow_writing_files": False,
        },
        model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
        metric=weighted_mae,
        run_name="bike-mae",
        param_space=search_depth,
        config=TrainingConfig(
            tuning=TuningConfig(
                metric="mae", direction="minimize", n_trials=2, seed=42
            ),
            tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False),
        ),
    )
mlflow.set_tracking_uri(previous_uri)
assert result.tuning is not None and result.test_metrics is not None
print("Chosen depth:", result.tuning.best_params["depth"])
print("Test MAE (rentals/hour):", round(result.test_metrics["mae"], 3))

Chosen depth: 3
Test MAE (rentals/hour): 94.121

The final model is refitted using the selected depth. The displayed test error uses future hours that neither trial fitted on. The temporary store contains run metrics and configuration during execution; model packaging is disabled for this example, and the store is removed on exit.

    sample_weight: FloatArray | None = None,
    *,
    threshold: float = 0.5
) -> MetricsClassification

Evaluate binary labels and predicted positive-class probabilities.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default y_target numpy.ndarray of shape (n_samples,)

Observed binary labels, containing only 0 and 1.

required y_prob numpy.ndarray of shape (n_samples,)

Finite positive-class probabilities in [0, 1].

None threshold float

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_classification
>>> observed = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0])
>>> probability = np.array([0.1, 0.6, 0.4, 0.9])
>>> weight = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0])
>>> for cutoff in (0.3, 0.7):
...     scores = metrics_classification(
...         observed, probability, threshold=cutoff, sample_weight=weight,
...     )
...     print(f"{cutoff}: precision={scores.precision:.3f}, recall={scores.recall:.3f}")
0.3: precision=0.600, recall=1.000
0.7: precision=1.000, recall=0.667

In this small calculation example, increasing the cutoff removes false positives but also misses one third of the positive weight.

Calculate exposure-weighted Tweedie and ranking metrics.

docs.title: ranking_metrics
docs.text:
ranking_metrics(
    y_target: FloatArray,
    y_pred: FloatArray,
    exposure: FloatArray,
    selected_percents: tuple[float, ...] = (10.0,),
) -> RankingMetrics

Calculate gains, lift, and Gini after ranking by descending prediction. Supply aligned finite vectors: observed rates in y_target, ordering scores in y_pred, and nonnegative row exposures with positive total in exposure. The exposure-weighted observed total must be positive. selected_percents contains capacity percentages in (0, 100]; an empty tuple requests only the full curves and Gini values.

Returns RankingMetrics, with cumulative arrays and selected gain/lift points in request order. Zero-exposure rows are omitted, tied scores retain input order, and selected points use linear interpolation. Normalized Gini is NaN when perfect-ranking Gini is close to zero. Invalid shapes, non-finite values, negative exposures, nonpositive totals, or out-of-range percentages raise ValueError. See the ranking recipe for an executable example and the following result attributes for their meanings.

docs.title: PUMetric dataclass
docs.text:
PUMetric(prior: float, loss: str = 'nnPU')

Evaluate positive-unlabeled risk without treating unlabeled rows as negative.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default prior float

Finite population positive prevalence strictly between zero and one, rather than the labeled-positive fraction.

required loss (uPU, nnPU)

uPU retains estimated negative risk; nnPU clips it at zero when computing total risk.

'uPU' Notes

Callable metric for the training workflow. Match prior and loss to the model settings. Capture at capacity uses a score cutoff set by the unlabeled population. Ties at that cutoff are all included, so actual capacity can be larger. Known-positive capture is a recall proxy only under representative labeling.

Examples:

>>> from ml_toolkit.metrics import PUMetric
>>> scores = PUMetric(prior=0.1)([1, 0, 1, 0], [0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.2])
>>> values = scores.to_dict()
>>> values["known_positive_capture_at_10pct"], values["unlabeled_flagged_at_10pct"]
(0.5, 0.5)

This tiny calculation has only two unlabeled rows. Reaching the requested 10% capacity requires selecting one whole row, so actual capacity is 50%; the same score cutoff captures one of the two known positives.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: CatBoost adapters share fitting, prediction, feature importance, and MLflow packaging operations. Fit an adapter directly, or pass its class as model_factory to train_model, which creates fresh instances. The optional LightGBM wrapper packages an already fitted native regressor.

docs.title: Choose an adapter
docs.text: Adapter Use it for CatBoostRegressionModel General regression with CatBoost's native loss and initialization CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel Poisson, Tweedie or Gamma regression with a fitted log-mean baseline CatBoostClassificationModel Binary classification with probability and label predictions CatBoostPUClassificationModel Positive-unlabeled learning with an explicit population prior InflationAdjustedModel A regressor composed with an inflation strategy

docs.title: Prepare real observations
docs.text:
Run these examples from an installed source checkout after python -m examples.prepare_data. The regression and classification examples use all 17,379 recorded hourly observations from the UCI Bike Sharing dataset. Targets are rentals per recorded hour; weights are one per hour. The eleven weather/calendar features exclude counts that reveal the target. Timestamps come from the original date and hour columns.

from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
splitter = Holdout(data, val_size=0.25, test_size=0.2)
development = splitter.get_test()
split = next(splitter.get_validation())
test = development.heldout

The last 20% of hours are untouched test rows. The preceding observations are split chronologically into training and validation. The following examples show predictions on those test rows; validation chooses fitting settings.

docs.title: Gamma regression
docs.text:
Use loss_function="Gamma" (or loss="Gamma") for a strictly positive target, such as claim severity conditional on a claim. Both regression adapters accept it. Prefer CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel for its fitted initial log mean:

import numpy as np

from examples.retail_data import load_retail_splits
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_severity
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel

retail = load_retail_splits(download_if_missing=False)
gamma = CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel(
    {
        "loss_function": "Gamma",
        "task_type": "CPU",
        "iterations": 40,
        "learning_rate": 0.05,
        "depth": 3,
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    }
)
gamma.fit(retail.train, retail.validation)
predicted_means = gamma.predict_pool(retail.test)
scores = metrics_severity(
    retail.test.y.to_numpy(),
    predicted_means,
    retail.test.weight.to_numpy(),
    power=2.0,
)
print("Observed unit prices (GBP):", retail.test.y.head(5).round(2).to_list())
print("Predicted unit prices (GBP):", predicted_means[:5].round(2).tolist())
print("Test Gamma deviance:", round(scores.mean_tweedie_deviance, 4))
assert np.isfinite(predicted_means).all() and (predicted_means > 0).all()

Observed unit prices (GBP): [0.85, 7.08, 4.95, 4.25, 4.95]
Predicted unit prices (GBP): [1.33, 3.93, 4.58, 5.9, 5.9]
Test Gamma deviance: 0.5101

The shared retail preparation uses recorded sterling unit prices and invoice timestamps. It keeps a deterministic approximately 10% sample of eligible invoice groups, excludes cancellations and nonpositive prices or quantities, trains before September 2011, validates in September, and tests in October–November. Stock code, country and quantity are inputs; price is excluded.

Gamma minimizes log(mu) + y / mu. The toolkit creates its custom objective only for training; constructor and refit parameters retain the string "Gamma". CPU derivatives and deviance are compiled with Numba. Defaults are Plain boosting, Newton leaf estimation and one leaf estimation iteration. Explicit compatible parameters override these defaults.

Targets must remain finite and strictly positive after CatBoost's float32 conversion, even for zero-weight rows. Weights must be finite, nonnegative and have a positive total after conversion. Values are not clipped to satisfy these requirements. Use Tweedie with 1 < variance_power < 2 when zero targets belong in the problem.

The default eval_metric (also selected by eval_metric="Gamma") is weighted Gamma deviance. Early stopping and best-iteration selection use this metric. An explicitly supplied alternative metric receives the raw log means, following CatBoost's custom-objective convention. For toolkit validation/reporting, use functools.partial(metrics_severity, power=2.0) from ml_toolkit.metrics.

Predictions default to positive means, with the log-link baseline applied once. Set the adapter's prediction_type="RawFormulaVal" to request log means instead; prediction_type="Exponent" explicitly requests means. A raw native CatBoost model with this custom objective defaults to raw scores: when calling gamma.native_model.predict directly, pass prediction_type="Exponent" for means. The general CatBoostRegressionModel uses native initialization and rejects boost_from_average=True for Gamma; use the log-link adapter for mean initialization.

For one CUDA GPU, use the following training parameters. This block only constructs an adapter; fitting it requires the GPU setup described below:

gpu_gamma = CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel(
    {"loss_function": "Gamma", "task_type": "GPU", "devices": "0"}
)

GPU derivatives run in a CUDA kernel. Gamma deviance is evaluated on CPU and requires transferring predictions from GPU. Install the cuda extra and use a compatible CUDA toolkit and driver, as for uPU. Multiple devices and automatic CPU fallback are not supported.

Native .cbm plus toolkit state, MLflow models, and InflationAdjustedModel preserve the prediction mode. Bundled inference does not require Numba or CUDA. Older version-1 model states remain loadable; refitting a restored Gamma model recreates the training objective from its saved string parameters.

docs.title: Fit and predict directly
docs.text:
Continue with the Bike split and test prepared above. This fits an RMSE regressor and predicts held-out hours from features alone. Observed counts are shown beside the predictions in the same units.

import polars as pl

from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel

model = CatBoostRegressionModel(
    {
        "iterations": 40,
        "depth": 4,
        "loss_function": "RMSE",
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    }
).fit(split.train, split.heldout)
preview = test.take([0, 8, 16, 24, 32])
future = preview.X
predictions = model.predict_frame(future)
print("Observed rentals:", preview.y.to_list())
print("Predicted rentals:", predictions.round(1).tolist())

Observed rentals: [283.0, 448.0, 7.0, 280.0, 500.0]
Predicted rentals: [197.3, 273.0, 14.1, 200.0, 293.3]

predict_frame accepts Polars or pandas features; predict_pool takes a pool. Both require the fitted feature columns. Extra columns are ignored and fitted feature order is restored. model.native_model exposes the fitted backend for operations such as SHAP contributions.

For binary classification, predict_pool returns positive-class probabilities; use predict_labels_pool for labels at the adapter's decision threshold.

from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostClassificationModel

# A high-demand hour means at least 100 recorded rentals.
binary_train = split.train.with_target((split.train.y >= 100).cast(pl.Float64))
binary_validation = split.heldout.with_target(
    (split.heldout.y >= 100).cast(pl.Float64)
)
classifier = CatBoostClassificationModel(
    {
        "iterations": 40,
        "depth": 4,
        "loss_function": "Logloss",
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    }
).fit(binary_train, binary_validation)
probabilities = classifier.predict_frame(future)
labels = classifier.predict_labels(future)
print("Observed high demand:", (preview.y >= 100).cast(pl.Int64).to_list())
print("Probabilities:", probabilities.round(3).tolist())
print("Decision threshold:", round(classifier.threshold, 3))
print("Predicted labels:", labels.tolist())
assert (labels == (probabilities >= classifier.threshold)).all()

Observed high demand: [1, 1, 0, 1, 1]
Probabilities: [0.963, 0.969, 0.053, 0.962, 0.978]
Decision threshold: 0.171
Predicted labels: [1, 1, 0, 1, 1]

Without an explicit decision_threshold, binary validation labels choose the classifier's cutoff using weighted F1. CrossEntropy also accepts soft targets in [0, 1]; with soft validation labels the cutoff stays at 0.5 and F1 tuning is skipped. Explicit thresholds work with either kind of label. Labels use probability >= threshold; ties in F1 choose the higher threshold. Zero-weight rows do not affect the choice. With no positive-class validation weight, the cutoff is 0.5 and F1 is 0. classifier.threshold and classifier.validation_f1 expose these fitted values, which are preserved when the model is saved and reloaded. The latter is None when threshold tuning is skipped: an explicit threshold, no validation, soft validation labels, or PU training. Positive-unlabeled training uses CatBoostPUClassificationModel with an explicit population prior; see its constructor constraints below. For monetary targets across dates, follow the inflation composition example.

docs.title: Log and reload for serving
docs.text:
Continue with the fitted regression model, split, and future above. Configure MLflow before logging and keep the returned model URI to load later.

import mlflow
import numpy as np

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("ml-toolkit-model-examples")
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="direct-regression"):
    info = model.log(split.train)

served = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(info.model_uri)
served_predictions = served.predict(future.to_pandas())
np.testing.assert_allclose(served_predictions, model.predict_frame(future))

Logging writes native model artifacts, a serving example, and inference dependencies. The loaded model's predict accepts a pandas frame; call predict_frame or predict_pool on local adapters. TrackingConfig controls artifact naming, registration, and the example size.

docs.title: Optional LightGBM integration
docs.text:
Install the lightgbm extra. Fit LightGBM with its own training API, then wrap the fitted estimator for logging and inference. LightGBMServingModel is not a train_model factory. Continue with the Bike training and test split above:

import lightgbm as lgb
import mlflow
import numpy as np

from ml_toolkit.models.lightgbm import LightGBMServingModel

native = lgb.LGBMRegressor(
    n_estimators=10,
    min_child_samples=2,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=2,
    verbosity=-1,
)
features = split.train.to_model_input()
for column in split.train.cat_features:
    features[column] = features[column].astype("category")
native.fit(
    features,
    split.train.y.to_numpy(),
    sample_weight=split.train.weight.to_numpy(),
)
wrapper = LightGBMServingModel(
    native,
    numerical_features=split.train.numerical_features,
    cat_features=split.train.cat_features,
)
serving_input = test.to_model_input(categorical_as_strings=True)
predictions = wrapper.predict(None, serving_input)

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("ml-toolkit-model-examples")
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="lightgbm-regression"):
    lightgbm_info = wrapper.log(split.train)

loaded = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(lightgbm_info.model_uri)
np.testing.assert_allclose(loaded.predict(serving_input), predictions)
print("Held-out predictions preserved:", predictions[:5].round(1).tolist())

Held-out predictions preserved: [164.2, 164.2, 164.2, 164.2, 245.6]

Numerical and categorical feature names must partition the native model's features exactly. The wrapper restores feature order and converts configured categorical columns to pandas categories before prediction. Pass ordinary string columns to the loaded MLflow model; its saved input signature validates them before the wrapper performs categorical conversion.

docs.title: CatBoostPUClassificationModel
docs.text:
CatBoostPUClassificationModel(
    params: ModelParams | None = None,
)

Bases: CatBoostClassificationModel

Train positive-unlabeled CatBoost with a population-prior baseline.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default params dict or None

Copied parameters: loss is uPU (default) or nnPU; pu_prior must be finite and strictly between zero and one. uPU supports CPU and a single CUDA GPU; nnPU requires CPU. Both label groups need positive total weight, and class-weight options are not supported. Labels mean known positive (1) and unlabeled (0). Hard-label prediction requires an explicit decision_threshold; F1 is never tuned.

None Notes

uPU uses Numba-compiled derivatives and risk on CPU. With task_type='GPU', derivatives run in a CUDA kernel; risk evaluation remains on CPU and transfers predictions from the GPU. CUDA training requires a compatible CUDA toolkit and Numba CUDA support. The first fit compiles the kernels. nnPU evaluates the complete training risk before each tree, reversing the negative-risk gradient when needed (beta=0, gamma=1).

Examples:

>>> model = CatBoostPUClassificationModel(
...     {"loss": "uPU", "pu_prior": 0.1, "task_type": "CPU"})
>>> gpu_model = CatBoostPUClassificationModel(
...     {"loss": "uPU", "pu_prior": 0.1, "task_type": "GPU", "devices": "0"})

docs.text: Build a model adapter covers the complete contract, a reusable implementation and factory, and a saved/reloaded prediction check. Factories create fresh adapters for selection, tuning, validation and final fitting. For an inflation-adjusted adapter, each call also creates a fresh wrapped model and strategy; see custom inflation.

docs.title: PSI and feature levels
docs.text: Part of Data analysis, Population Stability Index (PSI) measures how feature distributions change between a reference sample and a current sample. Fit categories and numerical bins on the reference once, then reuse them for every comparison.

docs.title: Compare two samples
docs.text:
This small calculation makes the level counts easy to inspect; four rows per sample are not enough to establish population drift. For monitoring real observations, see the recorded-hour comparison.

import polars as pl

from ml_toolkit.config import FeatureLevelConfig
from ml_toolkit.psi import PSIAnalysis, PSIConfig

reference = pl.DataFrame(
    {"age": [20, 30, 40, 50], "region": ["north", "north", "south", "south"]}
)
current = pl.DataFrame(
    {"age": [45, 55, 65, 75], "region": ["north", "south", "west", "west"]}
)
analysis = PSIAnalysis(
    PSIConfig(
        features=(
            FeatureLevelConfig("age", "numerical", lower_bound=0),
            FeatureLevelConfig("region", "categorical"),
        ),
        n_bins=2,
    )
).fit(reference)
comparison = analysis.compare(current)
print(
    comparison.psi.sort("feature")
    .with_columns(pl.col("psi").round(4))
    .write_csv(),
    end="",
)
region_shares = (
    comparison.level_distribution.filter(
        (pl.col("feature") == "region") & (pl.col("level") != "__NULL__")
    )
    .select("level", "sample", "share")
    .pivot(on="sample", index="level", values="share")
)
print(region_shares.write_csv(), end="")

feature,psi
age,6.9077
region,6.9077
level,reference,current
north,0.5,0.25
south,0.5,0.25
__UNSEEN__,0.0,0.5

comparison.psi has one score per feature. Larger values mean a greater change in fitted-level shares. level_distribution shows the reference/current counts and shares behind each score. The new "west" category uses the fitted unseen level; numerical bins retain the reference boundaries. Here north and south each fall from 50% to 25%, and unseen categories account for 50% of current rows. Empty levels make the score sensitive to the configured epsilon share floor; this value is an arithmetic demonstration, not a universal alert threshold.

Call analysis.compare(next_sample) for later batches. Re-fitting on each batch would change the reference. For temporal distributions, set PSIConfig(period="week") (default "month") and provide aligned Date/Datetime timestamps with time= in both fit and compare. The original ranges must satisfy max(reference_time) <= min(current_time). Equal endpoints are allowed; overlap beyond the shared endpoint and reversed ranges raise ValueError. The split may fall inside one grouping period. Comparisons without timestamps do not have this restriction.

docs.title: Reuse feature levels
docs.text:
LevelTransformer exposes the same fit/transform operations when you need consistent bins for another report. Continue with reference and current above to transform both samples and compare their existing levels:

FeatureLevelConfig supplies the rules for each column. fit(reference) determines categories or numerical intervals from the reference sample; it does not train a prediction model. The resulting feature_levels tuple contains one FeatureLevels per configured column, in the same order. Each result holds its original rules in config, its labels in levels, and its numerical boundaries or categorical categories.

from ml_toolkit.feature_levels import LevelTransformer
from ml_toolkit.psi import compare_psi

levels = LevelTransformer(analysis.config.features, n_bins=2).fit(reference)
reference_levels = levels.transform(reference)
current_levels = levels.transform(current)
assert levels.feature_levels is not None
level_comparison = compare_psi(
    reference_levels, current_levels, feature_levels=levels.feature_levels
)
print("Age boundaries:", levels.feature_levels[0].boundaries)
print(
    "Current region levels:", current_levels["region"].cast(pl.String).to_list()
)
print("Same PSI scores:", level_comparison.psi.equals(comparison.psi))

Age boundaries: (35.0,)
Current region levels: ['north', 'south', '__UNSEEN__', '__UNSEEN__']
Same PSI scores: True

Configured columns become Polars Categorical columns; other columns retain their values and order. Reuse the fitted transformer for subsequent samples. Calling fit again replaces its levels; previously returned comparison results retain their original immutable rules and levels.

docs.title: How PSI and observed/fitted share levels
docs.text:
During training, PSI and ObservedFitted receive the same ReportingConfig.features rules and ReportingConfig.n_bins. Each report uses levels fitted on the same training rows for that fit. PSI reuses the fitted transformer from the model's baseline when that model is being saved; ObservedFitted creates its own transformer. PSI and observed/fitted do not share a fitted transformer with each other.

The same rules, bin count and reference data produce identical categories and numerical boundaries for matching features. Identical configuration alone is insufficient when the reference data differs. ObservedFitted(features=...) can select a subset of the shared feature definitions without changing how those features are binned.

Each report applies its training-fitted levels to both train and validation/test rows. Held-out rows do not influence the learned levels. Every enabled fit learns levels afresh from its own training rows, so boundaries can differ across folds and the final fit. See the observed/fitted guide for the corresponding prediction report.

docs.title: Compare recorded weather and calendar features
docs.text:
Prepare the Bike Sharing cache. These figures fit levels on 2011 training hours and compare 2012 test hours. Calendar changes can be expected; PSI measures distribution differences, not their cause. Shares count rows, independent of model weights.

from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
partition = Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01").get_test()
train, test = partition.train, partition.heldout
assert test is not None
output = Path("figures")
figure = FigureConfig(dpi=150)
print(f"2011 train hours: {len(train)}; 2012 test hours: {len(test)}")

2011 train hours: 8645; 2012 test hours: 8734

from ml_toolkit.plots import psi

categorical_features = {
    "hour",
    "working_day",
    "weekday",
    "holiday",
    "season",
    "weather",
    "month",
}
weather_analysis = PSIAnalysis(
    PSIConfig(
        features=tuple(
            FeatureLevelConfig(
                name,
                "categorical" if name in categorical_features else "numerical",
            )
            for name in train.X.columns
        ),
        n_bins=10,
    )
).fit(train.X, time=train.time)
weather_comparison = weather_analysis.compare(test.X, time=test.time)
psi.feature_psi_plot(
    weather_comparison.psi, output / "psi-scores.png", figure=figure
)
print(
    weather_comparison.psi.sort("psi", descending=True)
    .head(5)
    .with_columns(pl.col("psi").round(3))
    .write_csv(),
    end="",
)

feature,psi
humidity,0.048
temperature,0.036
feels_like_temperature,0.033
weather,0.004
wind_speed,0.004

The bars show one PSI score per feature. Inspect its level shares to understand which values contribute to the difference; a universal alert cutoff is not implied by this illustration.

psi.time_psi_level_distribution(
    weather_comparison.time_distribution,
    "temperature",
    output / "psi-time.png",
    figure=figure,
)

Each bar shows period-specific shares on the fitted levels. The dashed boundary marks the first current bar. When the split falls inside a period, that period has two equal-width bars, reference then current; the separator marks their visual boundary, not the exact split date. Entirely missing periods stay empty. Both plotting calls return None; their tables come from PSIAnalysis.

docs.title: Enable PSI during training
docs.text:
from ml_toolkit.config import ReportingConfig

reporting = ReportingConfig(
    psi=True, features=weather_analysis.config.features, n_bins=10
)

Pass this reporting config to TrainingConfig(reporting=reporting). The workflow compares train with the current held-out sample, writes psi/scores.png and per-feature time distributions, and saves the score and distribution tables as JSON. PSI uses feature values and timestamps only; no predictions are passed to the analysis. A train-only fit has no PSI report. features=None infers feature rules from both Pool.X and Pool.auxiliary_features; features=() disables feature diagnostics. Explicit FeatureLevelConfig entries can select columns from either table, including categorical codes and continuous numerical values. Numerical quantile boundaries are fitted on train only and applied unchanged to the held-out sample. PSI counts rows without exposure weights. epsilon is the PSI share floor, and period sets temporal grouping. Scheduling and shared figure settings are described in the data analysis overview.

docs.title: Persist a reference for monitoring
docs.text:
PSIBaseline stores fitted feature rules and aggregate counts rather than retaining a row-level reference frame. Continue with the small reference and current samples above to save and reload it locally without MLflow:

from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from polars.testing import assert_frame_equal
from ml_toolkit.psi import PSIBaseline

baseline = PSIBaseline.from_reference(
    reference, config=analysis.config
)
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    baseline.save(directory)
    restored = PSIBaseline.load(directory)

result = restored.compare(current)
assert_frame_equal(result.psi, comparison.psi)
assert_frame_equal(result.level_distribution, comparison.level_distribution)

Numerical boundaries, typed categories, missing/error sentinels and feature order survive serialization. LevelTransformer.to_dict() and from_dict() also expose the fitted transformation state separately. Loading does not refit any levels.

compare returns the existing PSIResult with feature scores and reference/current distributions. Counts are unweighted, and epsilon floors shares independently without renormalization, exactly as in PSIAnalysis. The batch must be nonempty and contain all configured features; extra columns are allowed.

time= in from_reference records the reference date range as metadata. The baseline's time_distribution is empty: compare each incoming monitoring window separately against the same fixed reference. Existing temporal reports in PSIAnalysis and training remain available.

During training, enabled PSI is bundled automatically with saved models. See loading a model's baseline.

Training baselines can include model and auxiliary columns. For a current pool, call baseline.compare(current_pool.to_analysis_frame()). All configured diagnostic columns must be present, even when prediction needs only X; missing columns are listed in the error. Numerical boundaries and category definitions remain fixed after loading.

Nonempty Series of discrete reference levels, compared after casting to String. Bin continuous numerical values before calling.

required current Series

Nonempty Series of discrete current levels, compared after casting to String; sample sizes may differ. Null is counted as a separate level.

required epsilon float

Minimum share strictly between zero and one used to avoid logarithms of zero.

1e-6

Returns:

Type Description float

Sum of (current_share - reference_share) * log(current_share / reference_share) over the union of observed levels.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

Either sample is empty or epsilon is invalid.

Notes

Shares are floored independently without renormalization. Use LevelTransformer or PSIAnalysis to bin raw numerical values first.

Examples:

Compare category shares: north falls from 75% to 25%, while south rises.

>>> import polars as pl
>>> from ml_toolkit.psi import psi
>>> reference = pl.Series(["north"] * 3 + ["south"], dtype=pl.Categorical)
>>> current = pl.Series(["north"] + ["south"] * 3, dtype=pl.Categorical)
>>> round(psi(reference, current), 4)
1.0986

docs.title: Inspect chronological windows
docs.text:
Run from an installed checkout after python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike. The imported prepare_training() loads the original Bike Sharing hours, model parameters and local MLflow settings described in the training example. Targets are rentals per hour; weights are one per recorded hour.

from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_frequency
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
splitter = Holdout(data, val_size=0.25, test_size=0.2)

import pandas as pd
from ml_toolkit.data import Pool
from ml_toolkit.training import Splitter, TimeSeriesCV


def split_table(strategy: Splitter[Pool]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows = []
    for part in strategy.get_validation():
        assert part.heldout is not None
        for sample, pool in (("train", part.train), ("val", part.heldout)):
            rows.append(
                (
                    str(part.index),
                    sample,
                    len(pool),
                    str(pool.time[0])[:10],
                    str(pool.time[-1])[:10],
                )
            )
    final = strategy.get_test()
    for sample, pool in (("train", final.train), ("test", final.heldout)):
        if pool is not None:
            rows.append(
                (
                    "final",
                    sample,
                    len(pool),
                    str(pool.time[0])[:10],
                    str(pool.time[-1])[:10],
                )
            )
    return pd.DataFrame(
        rows, columns=["fold", "sample", "rows", "first date", "last date"]
    )


print("Holdout")
print(split_table(splitter).to_string(index=False))
cv = TimeSeriesCV(data, n_splits=3, test_size=0.2, gap=24)
print("\nTimeSeriesCV")
print(split_table(cv).to_string(index=False))

    1  train 10427 2011-01-01 2012-03-15
    1    val  3476 2012-03-15 2012-08-07
final  train 13903 2011-01-01 2012-08-07
final   test  3476 2012-08-07 2012-12-31

TimeSeriesCV
