    1  train  3454 2011-01-01 2011-05-28
    1    val  3475 2011-05-29 2011-10-22
    2  train  6929 2011-01-01 2011-10-21
    2    val  3475 2011-10-22 2012-03-15
    3  train 10404 2011-01-01 2012-03-14
    3    val  3475 2012-03-15 2012-08-07
final  train 13903 2011-01-01 2012-08-07
final   test  3476 2012-08-07 2012-12-31

The tables show calendar dates for compact display. Counts use the exact hourly observations; adjacent samples can begin and end on the same date without sharing rows.

Each CV fold leaves 24 recorded rows between training and validation. They are included again in the main train. Rows need not be equally spaced in clock time: integer gap, integer sizes and max_train_size count observations.

test_size accepts a row count, fraction of the original pool, calendar date, YYYY-MM-DD string, or None. Dates start test inclusively in the data's timezone; when a date has no observations, the next observation starts test. Datetimes are not accepted. Fractions round upward, and both resulting samples must be nonempty. Validation fractions use only the retained non-test rows.

TimeSeriesCV.val_size=None divides the retained rows into equal validation blocks. max_train_size limits each CV training window, but not final training; skip_splits omits initial folds and preserves their original one-based indices. Without test, built-in final training uses the entire pool.

docs.title: Use a duration gap
docs.text:
Pass datetime.timedelta directly; no conversion to milliseconds is needed.

from datetime import timedelta

duration_cv = TimeSeriesCV(data, n_splits=3, test_size=0.2, gap=timedelta(days=1))
for part in duration_cv.get_validation():
    assert part.heldout is not None
    assert part.train.time[-1] <= part.heldout.time[0] - timedelta(days=1)

gap=timedelta(seconds=1) is also supported. Preceding rows are retained when time <= validation_start - gap, including equality. Zero duration matches zero row gap. The duration measures elapsed time across timezone/DST changes; Date values represent midnight and sub-day gaps are not rounded. A duration of 30 days is exactly 30 days, not a calendar month.

Validation windows and the test boundary stay unchanged. CV applies max_train_size after excluding the gap. Negative gaps or an empty train in a used fold raise ValueError. Gap rows remain available for later fitting. parameters() stores row gaps as integers and durations as {"type": "timedelta", "microseconds": N}.

docs.title: Fit outside the workflow
docs.text:
Continue with splitter, params and the model imported above:

part = next(splitter.get_validation())
assert part.heldout is not None
model = CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel(params).fit(part.train, part.heldout)
final = splitter.get_test()
final_model = CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel(model.get_refit_params()).fit(
    final.train
)
assert final.heldout is not None
prediction = final_model.predict_pool(final.heldout)
print("Final test predictions:", prediction.shape)

Final test predictions: (3476,)

Each get_validation() call creates a fresh iterator. Direct use leaves iteration, metrics and logging to the caller. train_model consumes one pair at a time and calls get_test() once after validation, so test pools are not retained during validation. With fit_on_test=True, it calls get_final() after test evaluation for an additional full-data fit.

docs.title: Implement a splitter
docs.text:
Subclass Splitter and implement two methods. get_validation() yields Split(train, heldout, index) with a nonempty validation heldout and positive, unique indices. Iterator order determines execution order. At least one pair is required. get_test() returns Split(train, heldout) where heldout is optional test; its index is ignored. Its train contains every eligible non-test row, or the entire eligible pool when test is absent. The separate get_final() method defaults to self.data; override it to customize the full pool used for additional training including test. It returns a pool, not a Split.

This reusable example uses explicit positional boundaries:

Complete implementation 
"""Project-defined row boundaries for validation and final fitting."""

from collections.abc import Iterator

from ml_toolkit.data import Pool
from ml_toolkit.training import Split, Splitter


class ProjectSplitter(Splitter[Pool]):
    def __init__(self, data: Pool, *, validation_start: int, test_start: int):
        super().__init__(data)
        if not 0 < validation_start < test_start < len(data):
            raise ValueError(
                "Boundaries must leave nonempty train, validation and test"
            )
        self.validation_start = validation_start
        self.test_start = test_start

    def get_validation(self) -> Iterator[Split[Pool]]:
        yield Split(
            self.data.take(range(self.validation_start)),
            self.data.take(range(self.validation_start, self.test_start)),
            index=1,
        )

    def get_test(self) -> Split[Pool]:
        return Split(
            self.data.take(range(self.test_start)),
            self.data.take(range(self.test_start, len(self.data))),
        )

    def parameters(self) -> dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "validation_start": self.validation_start,
            "test_start": self.test_start,
        }

Use it in the ordinary workflow:

from examples.custom_splitter import ProjectSplitter

project_splitter = ProjectSplitter(
    data, validation_start=len(data) // 2, test_start=3 * len(data) // 4
)
project_result = train_model(
    splitter=project_splitter,
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    metric=metrics_frequency,
    run_name="project-splits",
    config=config,
)
print("ProjectSplitter")
print(split_table(project_splitter).to_string(index=False))
print("Validation folds fitted:", len(project_result.validation.splits))

ProjectSplitter
 fold sample  rows first date  last date
    1  train  8689 2011-01-01 2012-01-02
    1    val  4345 2012-01-02 2012-07-02
final  train 13034 2011-01-01 2012-07-02
final   test  4345 2012-07-02 2012-12-31
Validation folds fitted: 1

Keep the original pool in self.data; generate a fresh iterator on each call. The workflow checks valid pools, matching feature schemas and declarations within each pair, and selected-feature availability in final data. Your splitter owns sample membership and leakage prevention. IDs are optional and may repeat; no ID-based overlap check is performed. Preserve row metadata by using Pool.take.

parameters() defaults to {}. Override it with explicit JSON-compatible settings to log them alongside the class name in configuration/splitter.json. Do not return data, generators or fitted models. The splitter supplies data; model fitting, refitting and serving belong to the model adapter.

docs.title: Tracking
docs.text: train_model records its experiment in MLflow. Set the tracking URI and experiment before calling it; the toolkit uses the active run as a parent when one already exists. The same table helpers also work outside training.

docs.title: Inspect a training run
docs.text:
A workflow has a parent named by run_name, a validation run containing validation/split_<index> runs, and a test run when test exists. Without test, the main fit is final_fit; with test and fit_on_test=True, a separate final_fit follows test evaluation. Selection history is stored in selection/history.json inside each split. Built-in selectors also write a main plot alongside it: selection/rfe_progress.png, selection/top_k_ranking.png, or selection/forward_progress.png. Forward also writes selection/forward_improvement.png when rounds can be compared. All three write selection/best_iteration.png when iteration data is available. These figures use the current split's single search history. Figure configuration can change the format to SVG/PDF. Selection plots are automatic, including when validation reporting is disabled, and use no extra model fits. See feature selection. Tuning uses nested tuning and trial_<number> runs. The final fit uses the last yielded split's settings and the final data supplied by the splitter.

Where to look Contents Parent configuration/requested.json Shared training configuration Parent configuration/splitter.json Splitter class and explicit parameters Parent configuration/evaluators.json Prediction evaluator classes, names and parameters Parent configuration/data_analyzers.json Data analyzer classes, names and parameters Parent configuration/resolved.json Final selected features and model settings validation Averages of primary validation metrics validation/split_<index> Train/validation metrics, optional selection, trials and reports test Main model train/test metrics, reports and optional model final_fit All-data train metrics, applicable reports and optional model; no independent test metrics

Primary metrics drive training and tuning; evaluator and analyzer metrics are additional named measurements. See Evaluation and Data analysis for report scheduling, metric names and artifact paths. The complete task recipe shows selection, tuning, SHAP and final model packaging together.

TrackingConfig controls packaging for trials, validation, test and final fitting. log_test_model=True saves the test-stage main model; log_final_model=True saves the final-fit model, including when test is absent. Registration selects the additional model when trained, otherwise the main model, and requires that model's logging flag. It never falls back to the other model. Each stage logs its own row counts and timestamp ranges. Model methods preserve their prediction transformation when saving and loading; use the model serving guide or the custom adapter guide for that contract.

docs.title: Prepare a fitted model
docs.text:
This independent example uses recorded Bike Sharing hours. The last 20% are held out; the preceding data contains a trailing 25% validation window. Run python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike from the checkout once.

import numpy as np
from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
splitter = Holdout(data, val_size=0.25, test_size=0.2)
part = next(splitter.get_validation())
test = splitter.get_test().heldout
assert test is not None
model = CatBoostRegressionModel(
    {
        "iterations": 40,
        "depth": 4,
        "loss_function": "RMSE",
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    }
).fit(part.train, part.heldout)

docs.title: Save a table in MLflow
docs.text:
import mlflow
import polars as pl

from ml_toolkit.tracking import log_polars_table

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("ml-toolkit-examples")
predictions = model.predict_pool(test)
table = (
    test.X.select("working_day")
    .with_columns(
        pl.Series("absolute_error", np.abs(test.y.to_numpy() - predictions))
    )
    .group_by("working_day")
    .agg(
        pl.col("absolute_error").mean().round(3).alias("mae"),
        pl.len().alias("hours"),
    )
    .sort("working_day")
)
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="segment-metrics") as run:
    log_polars_table(table, "tables/segment-metrics.json")
    saved = mlflow.artifacts.load_dict(
        f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/tables/segment-metrics.json"
    )
    print(saved)

{'rows': [{'working_day': 0, 'mae': 89.048, 'hours': 1127}, {'working_day': 1, 'mae': 101.836, 'hours': 2349}]}

The table summarizes held-out absolute error in rentals per hour by the recorded working-day flag, alongside the number of hours in each group. The call creates a local MLflow database if needed and writes a JSON artifact containing the table's rows under the active run. The example reads back the saved payload to verify its contents. docs.title: Load a model's PSI baseline
docs.text:
With ReportingConfig(psi=True), each saved model includes a psi_baseline artifact containing fitted feature levels and unweighted reference counts. The existing TrackingConfig.log_trial_models, log_validation_models, log_test_model, and log_final_model switches control this packaging; no additional tracking switch is needed. ReportingConfig.on_* controls reports, so disabling a stage's reports does not remove the saved model's baseline. features=() explicitly disables both levels and their baseline.

The training workflow prepares this artifact automatically. For the model fitted above outside the workflow, attach it explicitly when logging:

from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from ml_toolkit.config import FeatureLevelConfig
from ml_toolkit.psi import PSIBaseline, PSIConfig

reference = PSIBaseline.from_reference(
    part.train.X,
    config=PSIConfig(
        features=tuple(
            FeatureLevelConfig(
                name,
                "categorical" if name in part.train.cat_features else "numerical",
            )
            for name in part.train.X.columns
        )
    ),
    time=part.train.time,
)
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    reference.save(directory)
    with mlflow.start_run(run_name="psi-monitoring"):
        info = model.log(
            part.train, extra_artifacts={"psi_baseline": directory}
        )

Use the same immutable model URI for serving and monitoring. The saved package remains available after the temporary source directory has been removed:

from polars.testing import assert_frame_equal
from ml_toolkit.tracking import load_psi_baseline

model_uri = info.model_uri
served = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(model_uri)
baseline = load_psi_baseline(model_uri)

# Use the original training feature representation for monitoring.
current_X = test.X
current_levels = baseline.transformer.transform(current_X)
result = baseline.compare(current_X)
assert_frame_equal(result.psi, reference.compare(current_X).psi)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    served.predict(test.to_model_input(categorical_as_strings=True)),
    model.predict_pool(test),
)

The loader also accepts a registered version such as models:/risk_model/17 or a local model package. It reads the named artifact from MLmodel without loading native model weights or executing serving code. Install a compatible ml-toolkit in the monitoring environment. Use a fixed model version instead of independently resolving a mutable registry alias for serving and monitoring.

Each baseline uses all training rows after feature selection, independently of input_example_rows. Validation/test rows are excluded unless they are part of the subsequent final fit's training population. A train-only final fit still packages its baseline. Inflation-adjusted models include the same reference in both their native and wrapper packages.

The package contains manifest.json (format version, scoring settings and reference metadata), levels.json (typed fitted transformation rules), and reference_counts.parquet (feature/level counts, including zero counts). It contains no source rows and requires no separate PyFunc model. Graphs and evaluation distributions remain run artifacts. Missing baselines raise FileNotFoundError; malformed or unsupported state raises ValueError. Existing models remain loadable for predictions without migration.

docs.title: Training
docs.text: train_model runs validation, optional feature selection and parameter tuning, then fits a main model and evaluates optional test data. A splitter supplies the rows for each fit.

docs.title: Run a holdout experiment
docs.text:
Run this page from an installed repository checkout after python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike. The shared examples.training_setup.prepare_training loads all 17,379 original UCI Bike Sharing hours from 2011–2012, with eleven weather/calendar features, rental counts as targets and unit weights. Inputs exclude count components that reveal the target. It configures a local mlflow.db and disables automatic model packaging. The model uses a Poisson loss; predictions are rentals per recorded hour.

from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_frequency
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
splitter = Holdout(data, val_size=0.25, test_size=0.2)
result = train_model(
    splitter=splitter,
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    metric=metrics_frequency,
    run_name="frequency-holdout",
    config=config,
)
print(
    "Validation Poisson deviance:",
    round(result.validation.mean_metrics["mean_poisson_deviance"], 4),
)
assert result.test_metrics is not None
print(
    "Test Poisson deviance:",
    round(result.test_metrics["mean_poisson_deviance"], 4),
)

Validation Poisson deviance: 118.8938
Test Poisson deviance: 111.7045

The latest 20% of rows are test; the last 25% of the remaining rows are validation. This Holdout uses all non-test rows for its test-stage fit. Fractions round upward. The workflow logs metrics and configuration to MLflow.

docs.title: Understand the run
docs.text:
1. Consume each validation pair in the splitter's iterator order.
  2. Select columns and tune parameters when those extensions are supplied.
  3. Fit the validation model and run enabled prediction reports and data analysis.
  4. Request splitter.get_test() once and fit a fresh main model on its train, including former validation and gap rows, and evaluate its optional heldout as test. This stage is test when heldout exists, otherwise final_fit.
  5. With fit_on_test=True, request splitter.get_final() after test evaluation and fit a separate model on that full pool, including test.

The last yielded validation split supplies the final features, parameters, iteration budget and classification threshold. The splitter determines final training rows; they need not match the last validation train. The workflow obtains the main training/test pair after validation; your splitter owns sample separation. Requesting fit_on_test=True without test raises ValueError at that point, before the main fit. Validation fits and their MLflow runs have already completed. Reporting stage flags control additional reports; primary metrics always run.

docs.title: Use the result
docs.text:
Result Meaning result.model Main adapter fitted on all non-test rows, or all rows when test is absent result.final_model Additional model including test when fit_on_test=True, otherwise None result.params Last validation split's refit settings, shared by both models result.features Selected columns in fitted order result.validation.splits Validation results in execution order result.validation.mean_metrics Mean validation metrics across splits result.test_metrics Independent test metrics from the main model, or None without test result.feature_selection, result.tuning Last split's optional search results

Selection and tuning scores measure the data used to choose settings. The optional test scores describe independent held-out performance. Evaluator and analyzer metrics are logged separately and are not part of these result summaries.

docs.title: Optionally train including test
docs.text:
TrainingConfig(fit_on_test=True) adds a fresh fit on all eligible data after independent test evaluation. Both models reuse the last validation split's features, iteration budget, threshold and parameters, without another search. Learned baselines and inflation state are fitted anew for each model.

Test sample fit_on_test Stages after validation model final_model Present False test All non-test rows None Present True test, then final_fit All non-test rows All eligible rows Absent False final_fit All eligible rows None Absent True ValueError after validation, before the main fit — —

For example, reuse the holdout setup above:

from dataclasses import replace

full_result = train_model(
    splitter=splitter,
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    metric=metrics_frequency,
    run_name="frequency-including-test",
    config=replace(config, fit_on_test=True),
)
assert full_result.final_model is not None

test_metrics always belongs to the main model and is never replaced with in-sample scores from the additional model. final_fit logs train metrics and applicable train-only custom reports; held-out comparisons are skipped. ReportingConfig.on_test and on_final_fit independently enable additional reports; primary metrics are always calculated.

TrackingConfig.log_test_model controls test-stage packaging, and log_final_model controls final_fit packaging, including the no-test case. Both default to True. registered_model_name applies to the additional model when requested, otherwise the main model, only if that model's packaging flag is enabled. Disabling its packaging never registers the other model instead.

docs.title: Configure the workflow
docs.text:
Pass a model factory, metric and prepared splitter. TrainingConfig controls tuning, shared reporting and packaging. The task recipes show complete combinations.

Training shows stage progress and an evaluation summary by default. Use TrainingConfig(verbosity="verbose") for split sizes, date ranges, per-split metrics and tuning trials, or TrainingConfig(verbosity="silent") to disable automatic ml-toolkit output. With an existing configuration, use replace(config, verbosity="verbose"). See the four verbosity levels for details and their relationship to Python logging and backend output.

Need Guide Holdout, time-series CV or custom windows Data splitting Select columns or provide a ranker Feature selection Supply an Optuna search space or a standalone objective Parameter tuning Add prediction reports or custom metrics/artifacts Evaluation Analyze feature distributions and drift Data analysis Implement a training adapter Models Save, reload or inspect MLflow artifacts Tracking

docs.title: train_model
docs.text:
train_model(
    *,
    splitter: Splitter[Pool],
    params: ModelParams,
    model_factory: Callable[[ModelParams], Model],
    metric: Metric,
    run_name: str,
    config: TrainingConfig,
    feature_selector: FeatureSelector | None = None,
    param_space: (
        Callable[[Trial], ModelParams] | None
    ) = None,
    prediction_evaluators: (
        PredictionEvaluator
        | list[PredictionEvaluator]
        | None
    ) = None,
    data_analyzers: (
        DataAnalyzer | list[DataAnalyzer] | None
    ) = None,
    model_evaluators: (
        ModelEvaluator | list[ModelEvaluator] | None
    ) = None
) -> TrainingResult

Tune, validate, refit and optionally test a complete training workflow.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default splitter Splitter

Supplies numbered validation pairs and final training/test data. Pools must have aligned features and metadata, ascending timestamps, finite targets and nonnegative weights with positive total. Raw categorical values must not stringify to the reserved "unknown".

required params ModelParams

Base constructor parameters, copied without mutating the input.

required model_factory Callable[[ModelParams], Model]

Creates fresh adapters implementing fit, predict_pool, native_model, best_iteration, feature_importances, get_refit_params and log.

required metric Callable

Receives targets, predictions and weights; returns named scalar scores.

required run_name str

Enclosing MLflow experiment run name.

required config TrainingConfig

Parameter tuning, console verbosity, reporting and model packaging settings.

required feature_selector FeatureSelector or None

Selects features independently before tuning on each split. None keeps all columns. The selector owns its settings and must not retain fitted state.

None param_space Callable or None

Optuna trial overrides; required when tuning is enabled.

None prediction_evaluators PredictionEvaluator, list[PredictionEvaluator], or None

Named evaluators called in list order with one combined pool and aligned train and optional val or test labels per fit. Names are unique ignoring case; object IDs are optional. ReportingConfig stage flags gate all reports. None or an empty list disables evaluator calls, not data analysis or PSI/SHAP.

None data_analyzers DataAnalyzer, list[DataAnalyzer], or None

Data reports receiving the same pool and split labels without predictions. Called in list order after prediction/model evaluators, using the same stage flags and selected features. Names must be unique across all report lists and enabled PSI/SHAP. None or [] disables custom data reports, not PSI.

None model_evaluators ModelEvaluator, list[ModelEvaluator], or None

Reports receiving the fitted adapter, task metric and aligned data/split labels. Run after prediction evaluators and before data analyzers, under the same reporting stage flags. Names are unique across all reports.

None

Returns:

Type Description TrainingResult

Main model, split results, optional test scores and additional final model.

Notes

Each split independently selects features using the base parameters, tunes on its validation rows, then fits the winning settings once for reporting. Validation averages are reports, not Optuna objectives. The main model fits splitter.get_test().train using the last split's features and refit parameters. With held-out test data this is the test stage; otherwise it is final_fit. fit_on_test adds a fresh final_fit on splitter.get_final() after test evaluation, without replacing the main model or its scores. No selection or tuning is repeated. MLflow configuration is caller-owned.

See Also

ml_toolkit.training.Holdout : A trailing validation window and optional test. ml_toolkit.training.TimeSeriesCV : Chronological validation windows.

Examples:

For executable data preparation, configuration, fitting and interpretation of held-out scores, see the documentation's Training guide, "Run a holdout experiment". The Feature selection, Parameter tuning and Evaluation guides show how to extend that workflow with independently prepared examples.

docs.title: Parameter tuning
docs.text: Use an Optuna search-space callback with train_model, or call tune_optuna with your own scalar scoring callback. Both paths create a TuningResult with the best parameter dictionary, score and zero-based trial number.

docs.title: Tune in the training workflow
docs.text:
Run from an installed checkout after python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike. The imported prepare_training() loads the original Bike Sharing hours, model parameters and local MLflow settings described in the training example. Targets are rentals per hour; weights are one per recorded hour.

from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_frequency
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
splitter = Holdout(data, val_size=0.25, test_size=0.2)

from dataclasses import replace

from optuna import Trial

from ml_toolkit.config import TuningConfig
from ml_toolkit.feature_selection import RFESelector
from ml_toolkit.training import importance_ranker
from ml_toolkit.types import ModelParams


def param_space(trial: Trial) -> ModelParams:
    return {"depth": trial.suggest_int("depth", 1, 3)}


search_config = replace(
    config,
    tuning=TuningConfig(
        metric="mean_poisson_deviance",
        direction="minimize",
        n_trials=2,
        seed=42,
    ),
)
searched = train_model(
    splitter=splitter,
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel,
    metric=metrics_frequency,
    run_name="frequency-search",
    config=search_config,
    feature_selector=RFESelector(
        min_features=3,
        metric="mean_poisson_deviance",
        direction="minimize",
        max_fits=2,
        ranker=importance_ranker,
    ),
    param_space=param_space,
)
assert searched.feature_selection is not None and searched.tuning is not None
assert searched.test_metrics is not None
print("Selected features:", searched.features)
print(
    "Visited subset sizes:",
    [len(step.features) for step in searched.feature_selection.steps],
)
print("Best depth:", searched.tuning.best_params["depth"])
print(
    "Independent test deviance:",
    round(searched.test_metrics["mean_poisson_deviance"], 4),
)

Selected features: ('temperature', 'feels_like_temperature', 'humidity', 'wind_speed', 'hour', 'working_day', 'weekday', 'holiday', 'season', 'weather', 'month')
Visited subset sizes: [11, 3]
Best depth: 3
Independent test deviance: 121.16

The metric name must be a key returned by metric(...).to_dict(). Selection and tuning use validation rows, so their best scores are search results. Use searched.test_metrics for the independent future test evaluation. Each CV window repeats this process; the final fit reuses the last window's settings. See feature selection for selector and ranker options.

docs.title: Tune outside the workflow
docs.text:
This standalone callback fits each trial on earlier development rows and returns only its validation score. The reserved test tail is not passed in.

from ml_toolkit.training import tune_optuna

partition = next(splitter.get_validation())


def score(candidate_params: ModelParams) -> float:
    candidate = CatBoostLogLinkRegressionModel(candidate_params).fit(
        partition.train, partition.heldout
    )
    return metrics_frequency(
        partition.heldout.y.to_numpy(),
        candidate.predict_pool(partition.heldout),
        partition.heldout.weight.to_numpy(),
    ).mean_poisson_deviance


tuned = tune_optuna(
    base_params=params,
    param_space=param_space,
    score=score,
    config=TuningConfig(
        metric="mean_poisson_deviance",
        direction="minimize",
        n_trials=2,
        seed=42,
    ),
)
print("Best depth:", tuned.best_params["depth"])
print("Validation deviance:", round(tuned.best_score, 4))

Best depth: 3
Validation deviance: 129.3511

The callback owns each trial's model and must return one finite score in the configured direction. Copy or merge parameter dictionaries rather than retaining a fitted model between trials. The search space receives optuna.Trial; use its suggest_* methods to propose settings. n_trials, timeout_seconds and seed control the budget and sampler; metric identifies the objective in workflow metrics. The standalone callback itself chooses its scalar score.

The result's best_params includes the base settings and winning suggestions; best_trial is zero-based. Trial parameters and objective scores are logged in nested MLflow runs. Test data must remain outside both the search-space and scoring callbacks.

docs.title: Data analysis
docs.text:
Analyze input data independently of model predictions. Use data_analyzers for distributions and custom data reports, and prediction_evaluators for reports that compare or explain model predictions. Data analysis covers exploratory data analysis (EDA) as well as comparisons and drift monitoring.

Question Guide Interface How does a numerical feature change over time? Numerical distributions NumericalFeatureDistributions How have feature shares changed? PSI and feature levels PSIAnalysis directly; ReportingConfig(psi=True) in training How do I produce project-specific data metrics or files? Build a data analyzer DataAnalyzer How accurate or well calibrated are predictions? Evaluation PredictionEvaluator

Observed/fitted reports belong to Evaluation even when grouped by feature: their quantities depend on predictions. Feature importance and SHAP explain a fitted model and also remain there. Feature levels are shared infrastructure for both observed/fitted reports and PSI; their API stays in ml_toolkit.feature_levels. Both reports share configuration and training rows, and independently fit their own transformers. The feature-level contract explains how their levels remain consistent.

docs.title: Add reports to training
docs.text:
This function accepts a prepared Pool and model parameters. Set your MLflow tracking URI and experiment before calling it. The two report lists make their responsibilities explicit:

from ml_toolkit import Pool, train_model
from ml_toolkit.config import ReportingConfig, TrackingConfig, TrainingConfig
from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import NumericalFeatureDistributions
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import ObservedFitted
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from ml_toolkit.types import ModelParams
from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae


def train_with_reports(data: Pool, params: ModelParams):
    return train_model(
        splitter=Holdout(data, test_size=0.2),
        params=params,
        model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
        metric=weighted_mae,
        run_name="data-and-predictions",
        config=TrainingConfig(
            reporting=ReportingConfig(psi=True),
            tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False),
        ),
        prediction_evaluators=[ObservedFitted()],
        data_analyzers=[NumericalFeatureDistributions(period="month")],
    )

PSI keeps its existing configuration and artifact paths. The distribution report still writes numerical_feature_distributions/<index>_<feature>.png. No statistical calculations or plot formats change in this separation.

docs.title: Inputs, outputs and scheduling
docs.text:
Pass one DataAnalyzer, a list, None, or []. Each hook receives an aligned Pool and non-null String split labels: train plus at most one of val or test. There is no prediction or model argument. The existing Pool container still includes targets, weights and timestamps; no new data container is needed. Direct calls can analyze prepared data before fitting any model.

During training, analyzers run after prediction evaluators on the same selected features and combined rows. They use train + val for tuning and validation, and train + test for the test stage. The final_fit stage supplies train-only rows, either when no test sample exists or for the additional full-data model requested with TrainingConfig(fit_on_test=True). ReportingConfig.on_tuning, .on_validation, .on_test and .on_final_fit gate both interfaces and PSI/SHAP. Their defaults are false, true, true and true. These switches do not change core training metrics. Reports requiring a held-out comparison skip final_fit.

Like evaluators, analyzers may return finite scalar metrics from evaluate() and selected files from write_artifacts(). Either hook can be omitted. Metrics use <name>/<key>; artifacts use <name>/. They do not enter CV averages, training results or optimization objectives. Instances are reused across fits and must not retain data or fitted state or mutate inputs.

Names must be unique ignoring case across both report lists. Enabled PSI and SHAP reserve psi and shap. Names start with an ASCII letter or digit and contain only ASCII letters, digits, underscores, hyphens or dots. Only returned files inside artifact_dir are uploaded; temporary directories are removed on success and failure. The shared artifact contract and figure/time settings apply. Errors identify the analyzer and training stage.

Settings are recorded separately in configuration/data_analyzers.json and configuration/evaluators.json; each contains names, classes and explicit parameters. None or [] disables custom analyzers, while PSI remains governed by ReportingConfig.psi.

docs.title: Update existing distribution reports
docs.text:
Import NumericalFeatureDistributions from ml_toolkit.data_analysis, move the instance from prediction_evaluators to data_analyzers, and omit prediction in direct hook calls. Keep your existing settings and artifact paths.

The old ml_toolkit.evaluation.NumericalFeatureDistributions import remains a compatibility adapter with its previous prediction-based signature. Existing PredictionEvaluator subclasses and other built-in evaluators remain usable without changes. New data reports should implement DataAnalyzer.

docs.title: Example data
docs.text: Follow the source data preparation once. The distribution and PSI guides load the cached observations directly and compare 2011 with 2012 without fitting a prediction model.

docs.title: Build a data analyzer
docs.text: Implement DataAnalyzer when project-specific metrics or files depend on input data, not predictions. Use PredictionEvaluator when predictions are part of the calculation. Both interfaces support optional evaluate(), write_artifacts() and parameters() hooks.

docs.title: Implement the contract
docs.text:
This example counts rows by sample and writes a per-feature null-count table. It is an example extension, not an additional built-in analyzer:

"""Example data measurements and a table without model predictions."""

from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig
from ml_toolkit.data import Pool
from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import DataAnalyzer
from ml_toolkit.feature_levels import FeatureLevelConfig


class DataAudit(DataAnalyzer):
    """Count sample rows and save per-feature null counts."""

    def evaluate(self, *, data: Pool, split: pl.Series) -> dict[str, float]:
        return {
            f"{part}/rows": float((split == part).sum())
            for part in split.unique(maintain_order=True)
        }

    def write_artifacts(
        self,
        *,
        data: Pool,
        split: pl.Series,
        artifact_dir: Path,
        figure: FigureConfig,
        features: tuple[FeatureLevelConfig, ...] | None,
        n_bins: int,
    ) -> list[Path]:
        artifact_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        path = Path("null_counts.csv")
        data.X.null_count().write_csv(artifact_dir / path)
        return [path]

The method signatures contain no model or prediction input. Keep instances stateless; override parameters() if your analyzer has settings to record. The default is {}. Return explicit JSON-compatible values, not fitted state.

docs.title: Use it without fitting a model
docs.text:
Prepare the cached observations, then run:

from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from examples.custom_data_analyzer import DataAudit
from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
partition = Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01").get_test()
assert partition.heldout is not None
split = pl.Series(
    "split",
    ["train"] * len(partition.train) + ["test"] * len(partition.heldout),
)
analyzer = DataAudit(name="data_audit")
print(analyzer.evaluate(data=data, split=split))
files = analyzer.write_artifacts(
    data=data,
    split=split,
    artifact_dir=Path("data-audit"),
    figure=FigureConfig(),
    features=None,
    n_bins=10,
)
print([path.as_posix() for path in files])

{'train/rows': 8645.0, 'test/rows': 8734.0}
['null_counts.csv']

Direct calls return values and file paths; they do not log to MLflow. To use the same instance during training, pass data_analyzers=analyzer or data_analyzers=[analyzer] to train_model. Training logs data_audit/train/rows, data_audit/val/rows or data_audit/test/rows, and data_audit/null_counts.csv. Train-only calls still produce a row count and table in this example; each analyzer decides whether it needs a comparison pair.

The reporting contract covers names, stage switches, shared settings, metric validation and artifact cleanup.

docs.title: DataAnalyzer dataclass
docs.text:
DataAnalyzer(*, name: str)

Named data metrics and artifacts, independent of model predictions.

Implement either hook or both. During training, finite metrics are logged under <name>/<key> and only returned files are uploaded under <name>/. These metrics do not become CV averages or optimization objectives. Names must be unique across analyzers and prediction evaluators.

docs.title: evaluate

docs.title: Numerical distributions
docs.text: Inspect the location and spread of a measured numerical feature over time. NumericalFeatureDistributions compares train and held-out rows on their recorded calendar axis. Its statistics are unweighted, independent of Pool.weight, and use original feature values rather than fitted levels.

docs.title: Prepare observations
docs.text:
Run from the installed repository checkout after the data preparation. The example compares recorded 2011 hours with 2012 hours. Humidity is the source's normalized measurement. No model fitting or predictions are needed.

from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig

data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
partition = Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01").get_test()
train, test = partition.train, partition.heldout
assert test is not None
split = pl.Series("split", ["train"] * len(train) + ["test"] * len(test))
output = Path("figures")
figure = FigureConfig(dpi=150)
print(f"2011 train hours: {len(train)}; 2012 test hours: {len(test)}")

2011 train hours: 8645; 2012 test hours: 8734

docs.title: Add a distribution report
docs.text:
Use reports as data_analyzers in training, or write the reports directly:

from ml_toolkit.data_analysis import NumericalFeatureDistributions

reports = [
    NumericalFeatureDistributions(features=("humidity",), period="month")
]
files = reports[0].write_artifacts(
    data=data,
    split=split,
    artifact_dir=output / reports[0].name,
    figure=figure,
    features=None,
    n_bins=10,
)
print([path.relative_to(output).as_posix() for path in files])

['numerical_feature_distributions/000_humidity.png']

The x-axis shows calendar periods and the y-axis normalized humidity. Shaded bands contain the 5th–95th and 25th–75th percentiles; lines mark the median and mean. Here reference means 2011 train and current means 2012 test. Read seasonal variation separately from a lasting distribution shift.

features=None selects numeric columns of Pool.X and Pool.auxiliary_features; a tuple restricts the selection. Explicit missing or nonnumeric features raise an error. An empty selection produces no figures. quantile_bands, show_mean, and show_median control the visible summaries, and period sets the calendar grouping. Shared feature-level definitions and n_bins are unused.

print(

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Use prediction_evaluators to add reports to train_model, or call plotting functions directly with predictions you already have. Choose a report by the question you want to answer. For feature distributions, drift, or custom reports that do not use predictions, see Data analysis:

Question Guide Reports Which probability threshold balances precision and recall? Are probabilities calibrated? Classification PrecisionRecall, F1Threshold, Calibration Where do predicted means differ from observations? Observed versus fitted ObservedFitted, TimeObservedFitted How are errors distributed, and which rows contribute most? Residuals and large errors Residuals How much outcome is captured in the highest-ranked rows? Ranking Gains, Lift How are known positives ranked among unlabeled rows? Positive-unlabeled PUScoreDistribution, PUPositiveCapture How do metrics vary by segment? Metrics by group GroupedMetrics How does quality change across calendar windows? Metrics over time MetricTrend How do metrics change with fewer boosting iterations? Model shrink curves model_evaluators=[ShrinkCurve(...)] Which inputs support held-out model quality? Permutation importance model_evaluators=[PermutationImportance(...)] How sensitive is quality to missing or changed inputs? Input robustness model_evaluators=[RobustnessCurve(...)] Which features contribute to predictions? Feature importance and SHAP ReportingConfig(shap=ShapConfig(...)) and direct plots

Every family guide places evaluator configuration beside the resulting figures, interpretation, and direct plotting functions. Build an evaluator when you need an additional metric or artifact.

Install example dependencies from a source checkout and explicitly cache the original sources before running recipes:

python -m pip install -r requirements-examples.txt
python -m examples.prepare_data

docs.title: Add reports to training
docs.text:
Pass one evaluator, a list, None, or []. This example uses hourly bike rental counts and records feature-level and monthly comparisons in each enabled run.

from pathlib import Path

import mlflow

from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.config import ReportingConfig, TrackingConfig, TrainingConfig
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import ObservedFitted, TimeObservedFitted
from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

mlflow.set_tracking_uri(f"sqlite:///{Path('mlflow.db').resolve()}")
mlflow.set_experiment("evaluation-examples")
data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
reports = [ObservedFitted(features=("temperature",)), TimeObservedFitted()]
result = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01"),
    params={
        "iterations": 80,
        "depth": 5,
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    },
    model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    run_name="bike-evaluation",
    config=TrainingConfig(
        reporting=ReportingConfig(on_validation=False, on_test=True),
        tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False),
    ),
    prediction_evaluators=reports,
)
print("Test MAE (rentals/hour):", round(result.test_metrics["mae"], 2))

Test MAE (rentals/hour): 91.4

The observed/fitted guide shows these two report types and how to inspect their aggregate tables. It uses a fixed direct fit to make the illustrations independently reproducible.

docs.title: Reporting inputs and outputs
docs.text:
Each call receives one aligned Pool, one finite prediction per row, and a non-null String split Series containing train and at most one of val or test. The split labels are separate from model features; object IDs are optional. Training passes train + val during validation and tuning, and train + test during the test stage. The final_fit stage receives only train rows.

For reports that need the fitted adapter and task metric, pass model_evaluators. These run after prediction evaluators and before data analyzers, using the same stage switches and shared namespace rules.

Classification, ranking, and PU reports use only the held-out rows. Comparison reports show train and held-out rows together and skip incomplete pairs. GroupedMetrics also supports train-only data and exports additional metrics and a typed table. Other built-in evaluators produce graphical output and return {} from evaluate(). Prediction evaluators use supplied predictions; SHAP uses the fitted native model.

ReportingConfig.on_tuning, .on_validation, .on_test, and .on_final_fit control both methods of every evaluator and data analyzer, plus PSI/SHAP. Defaults are false, true, true, and true. Reports that require held-out rows skip final_fit. Core training metrics are calculated independently. PSI and SHAP are opt-in. Feature-selection search plots are also independent of these stage switches: they are always written to each split's existing selection/ folder when a built-in selector runs. See selection plots. Shared figure, feature-level definitions, and n_bins come from that config; each report page explains which settings it uses.

Names must be unique across prediction/model evaluators and data analyzers ignoring case, start with an ASCII letter or digit, and contain only ASCII letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, or dots. Enabled PSI and SHAP reserve psi and shap. Give repeated report instances distinct names. Extra metrics are logged as <name>/<key>, and do not enter CV averages, training results, or optimization objectives.

Only returned files are uploaded beneath <name>/. Single-sample reports use val/ or test/ subdirectories; comparison reports use their report root. The family pages show exact filenames. Temporary directories are removed on success and failure. Evaluators may return PNG, SVG, PDF, CSV, Parquet, JSON, or HTML files. Errors include evaluator and training-stage context.

docs.title: Figure settings and time
docs.text:
FigureConfig sets dimensions, DPI and format="png", "svg", or "pdf". Saving functions create parent directories, write the figure, and close it. Direct functions return their documented tables or None; binary_curves calculates a table without saving a figure.

Temporal reports accept minute, hour, day, week, month, quarter, and year; the default is month. Grouping uses the input timezone, which must match across the pair. Weeks begin on Monday and quarters are calendar quarters. Minute/hour require Datetime. period_start is the beginning of the calendar period in the input timezone.

Original timestamps must satisfy max(train_time) <= min(heldout_time). Equal endpoints are allowed. Splits inside a calendar period are supported; line plots retain two sample points at that period start. Missing periods have no computed markers, and lines connect neighboring observed periods.

docs.title: Example data
docs.text:
Most figures use the UCI Bike Sharing dataset (Hadi Fanaee-T, CC BY 4.0): 17,379 recorded hourly observations. The model fits 2011, and all 2012 hours are held out. Dates combine the recorded date and hour. Targets are hourly rental counts; each hour has weight one. The eleven weather and calendar predictors exclude casual and registered, whose sum reveals the target. Temperature and humidity retain the source's normalized scales. Classification defines a positive hour as at least 200 rentals before fitting. The PU guide uses recorded Cora citations and unverified candidate links.

The reusable loader owns the exact model parameters and chronological split; it never downloads missing data during recipe execution.

Inspect data preparation and model fitting 
"""Fit chronological Bike Sharing examples used by the evaluation gallery."""

from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit.data import Pool
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostClassificationModel, CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from ml_toolkit.types import FloatArray, ModelParams


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BikeEvaluation:
    """Keep the fitted model and aligned train/test report inputs together."""

    data: Pool
    train: Pool
    test: Pool
    model: CatBoostClassificationModel | CatBoostRegressionModel
    prediction: FloatArray
    split: pl.Series


def fit_bike_evaluation(*, classification: bool = False) -> BikeEvaluation:
    """Fit 2011 hours and predict all recorded hours, retaining 2012 as test.

    The optional binary target means at least 200 rentals in a recorded hour.
    This fixed threshold defines the task before splitting. Source timestamps,
    feature values and unit hourly weights are unchanged. Requires the explicit
    cache preparation described in the documentation; never downloads data.
    """
    data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
    if classification:
        data = data.with_target((data.y >= 200).cast(pl.Float64))
    final = Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01").get_test()
    train, test = final.train, final.heldout
    assert test is not None
    params: ModelParams = {
        "iterations": 80,
        "depth": 5,
        "learning_rate": 0.1,
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    }
    model = (
        CatBoostClassificationModel({**params, "loss_function": "Logloss"})
        if classification
        else CatBoostRegressionModel({**params, "loss_function": "RMSE"})
    )
    model.fit(train)
    prediction = np.concatenate((model.predict_pool(train), model.predict_pool(test)))
    split = pl.Series("split", ["train"] * len(train) + ["test"] * len(test))
    return BikeEvaluation(data, train, test, model, prediction, split)

Regenerate all figures and captured outputs with python -m examples.render_plots; add --check to detect stale outputs or images without rewriting documentation. The broader python -m examples.render_examples --check also checks the remaining guides.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: Inspect a binary classifier's probability thresholds and calibration on held-out observations. The target must contain confirmed 0/1 labels; predictions must be finite positive-class probabilities in [0, 1]. These reports do not apply to unverified PU labels.

docs.title: Prepare predictions
docs.text:
Run from the installed repository checkout after the data preparation. The example fits recorded 2011 hours and evaluates 2012 hours. A positive hour means at least 200 rentals. All curves below use only the 2012 test probabilities; the model never fits those rows.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig

example = fit_bike_evaluation(classification=True)
data, prediction, split = example.data, example.prediction, example.split
train, test = example.train, example.test
train_prediction = prediction[: len(train)]
test_prediction = prediction[len(train) :]
output = Path("figures")
figure = FigureConfig(dpi=150)
print(f"2011 train hours: {len(train)}; 2012 test hours: {len(test)}")

2011 train hours: 8645; 2012 test hours: 8734

docs.title: Reports in training
docs.text:
Use the following list as prediction_evaluators=reports in the training call. To inspect the exact reports without a tracking server, call their artifact methods on the prepared inputs:

from ml_toolkit.evaluation import PrecisionRecall, F1Threshold, Calibration

reports = [PrecisionRecall(), F1Threshold(), Calibration()]
for report in reports:
    files = report.write_artifacts(
        data=data,
        prediction=prediction,
        split=split,
        artifact_dir=output / report.name,
        figure=figure,
        features=None,
        n_bins=10,
    )
    print(report.name, [path.relative_to(output).as_posix() for path in files])

precision_recall ['precision_recall/test/precision_recall.png']
f1_threshold ['f1_threshold/test/f1_threshold.png']
calibration ['calibration/test/calibration.png']

docs.title: Precision and recall
docs.text:
The x-axis is recall: the fraction of positive rows captured. The y-axis is precision: the positive fraction of flagged rows. Each curve point corresponds to a probability threshold. The dashed line shows positive prevalence, and the marked point identifies the best F1 on this sample. Tied scores enter together, with prediction >= threshold defining a positive prediction.

PrecisionRecall(max_curve_points=1000) limits rendered points, preserving the full threshold table from the direct function. Draw the same figure directly:

from ml_toolkit.plots import classification

observed, probabilities = test.y.to_numpy(), test_prediction
precision_recall_table = classification.precision_recall(
    observed,
    probabilities,
    output / "direct-precision-recall.png",
    weight=test.weight.to_numpy(),
    figure=figure,
)
curve = classification.binary_curves(
    observed, probabilities, weight=test.weight.to_numpy()
)
print(
    curve.iloc[np.linspace(0, len(curve) - 1, 6, dtype=int)]
    .round(3)
    .to_string(index=False)
)
assert curve.equals(precision_recall_table)

 threshold  precision  recall    f1
     0.981      1.000   0.000 0.000
     0.729      0.995   0.391 0.561
     0.234      0.967   0.767 0.855
     0.051      0.831   0.981 0.900
     0.014      0.616   0.999 0.762
     0.003      0.486   1.000 0.654

docs.title: F1 by threshold
docs.text:
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. This plot identifies threshold tradeoffs on the supplied sample; adding the evaluator does not change the model's decision threshold. Select a threshold using validation rather than optimizing it on the test figure.

f1_table = classification.f1_threshold(
    observed,
    probabilities,
    output / "direct-f1-threshold.png",
    weight=test.weight.to_numpy(),
    figure=figure,
)
assert f1_table.equals(curve)

F1Threshold(max_curve_points=1000) has the same rendering limit and full-table return behavior as precision/recall.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
The calibration curve compares mean predicted probability with the observed positive rate within score quantiles. The diagonal represents perfect calibration. The accompanying histogram shows where prediction mass lies. Here most points lie above the diagonal: the model underestimates the positive rate in those test-score bins.

calibration_table = classification.calibration(
    observed,
    probabilities,
    output / "direct-calibration.png",
    weight=test.weight.to_numpy(),
    n_bins=10,
    histogram_bins=30,
    figure=figure,
)
print(calibration_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))

 bin  observed_rate  predicted_rate  count  weight_sum
   0          0.002           0.006    874       874.0
   1          0.002           0.011    873       873.0
   2          0.001           0.016    873       873.0
   3          0.037           0.024    874       874.0
   4          0.372           0.068    873       873.0
   5          0.599           0.153    873       873.0
   6          0.904           0.297    874       874.0
   7          0.951           0.545    873       873.0
   8          0.990           0.813    873       873.0
   9          1.000           0.940    874       874.0

Calibration(n_bins=10, histogram_bins=30) controls calibration quantiles and histogram bins independently. Its n_bins is distinct from shared feature-level binning in ReportingConfig.

Precision, recall, F1, prevalence, AP, calibration means and histograms use row weights. Zero-weight rows are ignored. Calibration boundaries remain unweighted quantiles of positive-weight rows; count counts those rows and weight_sum reports their total weight. The direct calibration call returns this full table.

docs.title: Use probabilities from another dataset
docs.text:
Direct functions also accept non-temporal data. The original handwritten digits example uses scikit-learn's 1,797 images, with digits 0–4 as class 0 and 5–9 as class 1. A fixed stratified split trains on 1,078 images and evaluates the other 719; no artificial dates or Pool are needed to calculate its curve.

from examples.gallery_data import load_gallery_data

digits, _ = load_gallery_data(download_if_missing=False)
digits_curve = classification.binary_curves(
    digits.observed, digits.probabilities
)
print(
    f"Training images: {len(digits.train_indices)}; held-out images: {len(digits.observed)}"
)
print(
    digits_curve.iloc[np.linspace(0, len(digits_curve) - 1, 6, dtype=int)]
    .round(3)
    .to_string(index=False)
)

None

>>> print(curve.iloc[[0, 2]].round(3).to_string(index=False))

docs.title: Build an evaluator
docs.text: Implement PredictionEvaluator when a report needs project-specific metrics or files based on predictions. For metrics and files derived from input data alone, use a DataAnalyzer. The two hooks have empty defaults: implement either or both. This example records held-out weighted MAE and the prediction rows behind it.

docs.title: Implement the contract
docs.text:
The canonical implementation is importable from the source checkout:

"""Additional held-out metrics and a prediction table for a training run."""

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig
from ml_toolkit.data import Pool
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import PredictionEvaluator
from ml_toolkit.feature_levels import FeatureLevelConfig
from ml_toolkit.types import FloatArray


class PredictionAudit(PredictionEvaluator):
    """Log weighted held-out MAE and save the rows behind that score."""

    def evaluate(
        self, *, data: Pool, prediction: FloatArray, split: pl.Series
    ) -> dict[str, float]:
        mask = (split != "train").to_numpy()
        if not mask.any():
            return {}
        part = split.filter(split != "train")[0]
        error = np.abs(data.y.to_numpy()[mask] - prediction[mask])
        value = float(np.average(error, weights=data.weight.to_numpy()[mask]))
        return {f"{part}/mae": value}

    def write_artifacts(
        self,
        *,
        data: Pool,
        prediction: FloatArray,
        split: pl.Series,
        artifact_dir: Path,
        figure: FigureConfig,
        features: tuple[FeatureLevelConfig, ...] | None,
        n_bins: int,
    ) -> list[Path]:
        mask = split != "train"
        if not mask.any():
            return []
        part = split.filter(mask)[0]
        relative = Path(part) / "predictions.csv"
        destination = artifact_dir / relative
        destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        pl.DataFrame(
            {
                "timestamp": data.time.filter(mask),
                "observed": data.y.filter(mask),
                "predicted": prediction[mask.to_numpy()],
                "weight": data.weight.filter(mask),
            }
        ).write_csv(destination)
        return [relative]

evaluate() returns finite scalar values keyed by sample and metric. write_artifacts() receives the same aligned inputs plus an output directory and shared plotting settings. Here it writes one CSV and returns its relative path. The evaluator skips train-only calls and leaves the inputs unchanged. It retains no rows or predictions on the instance; the workflow reuses that instance for subsequent fits.

docs.title: Use it in training
docs.text:
Prepare the real example data, then run:

from pathlib import Path

import mlflow
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from examples.custom_evaluator import PredictionAudit
from examples.gallery_data import load_bike_pool
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.config import ReportingConfig, TrackingConfig, TrainingConfig
from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

mlflow.set_tracking_uri(f"sqlite:///{Path('mlflow.db').resolve()}")
mlflow.set_experiment("custom-evaluator")
data = load_bike_pool(download_if_missing=False)
result = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01"),
    params={
        "iterations": 40,
        "depth": 4,
        "random_seed": 42,
        "thread_count": 2,
        "verbose": False,
        "allow_writing_files": False,
    },
    model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    run_name="prediction-audit",
    config=TrainingConfig(
        reporting=ReportingConfig(on_validation=False),
        tracking=TrackingConfig(log_test_model=False, log_final_model=False),
    ),
    prediction_evaluators=PredictionAudit(name="audit"),
)
client = mlflow.MlflowClient()
experiment = mlflow.get_experiment_by_name("custom-evaluator")
assert experiment is not None
runs = client.search_runs([experiment.experiment_id])
final_run = next(
    run for run in runs if run.data.tags["mlflow.runName"] == "test"
)
print("Additional metric:", round(final_run.data.metrics["audit/test/mae"], 3))
files = client.list_artifacts(final_run.info.run_id, "audit/test")
print("Artifact:", files[0].path)
local = client.download_artifacts(
    final_run.info.run_id, "audit/test/predictions.csv"
)
table = pl.read_csv(local, try_parse_dates=True)
print(
    table.head(4).with_columns(pl.col("predicted").round(2)).write_csv(), end=""
)
assert len(table) == int((data.time.dt.year() == 2012).sum())
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    np.average(
        abs(table["observed"] - table["predicted"]), weights=table["weight"]
    ),
    final_run.data.metrics["audit/test/mae"],
)

Additional metric: 92.809
Artifact: audit/test/predictions.csv
timestamp,observed,predicted,weight
2012-01-01T00:00:00.000000,48.0,55.46,1.0
2012-01-01T01:00:00.000000,93.0,36.53,1.0
2012-01-01T02:00:00.000000,75.0,10.85,1.0
2012-01-01T03:00:00.000000,52.0,11.54,1.0

The core metric= drives training results; audit/test/mae is the additional logged metric. The CSV contains the actual test timestamps, targets, predictions, and weights, so its rows reproduce the extra score.

Use a different name for each instance. Override parameters() only when your report has settings to record; return explicit JSON-compatible values rather than internal data or fitted state. This evaluator needs no override. See the shared contract for names, formats, scheduling, temporary paths, and error behavior.

docs.title: Feature importance and SHAP
docs.text: Native feature importance summarizes how a fitted model uses its inputs. SHAP explains the features' contribution to individual raw predictions. Neither method establishes a causal effect.

docs.title: Prepare a fitted model
docs.text:
Run from the installed repository checkout after the data preparation. The example fits recorded 2011 hours and evaluates 2012 hours. The following figures explain the rental-count regressor on real held-out hours. Native contributions work without the optional shap package; the SHAP plots require that extra.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig

example = fit_bike_evaluation(classification=False)
data, prediction, split = example.data, example.prediction, example.split
train, test = example.train, example.test
train_prediction = prediction[: len(train)]
test_prediction = prediction[len(train) :]
output = Path("figures")
figure = FigureConfig(dpi=150)
print(f"2011 train hours: {len(train)}; 2012 test hours: {len(test)}")

2011 train hours: 8645; 2012 test hours: 8734

docs.title: Native feature importance
docs.text:
from ml_toolkit.plots import explainability

importance = example.model.feature_importances(train)
importance_table = explainability.feature_importance(
    list(importance),
    np.array(list(importance.values()), dtype=float),
    output / "feature-importance.png",
    max_features_display=11,
    figure=figure,
)
print(importance_table.head(6).round(3).to_string(index=False))

               feature  importance
                  hour      65.566
           working_day      11.751
           temperature       6.428
feels_like_temperature       5.513
                season       3.491
                 month       2.572

The bars rank supplied importance values. Their scale depends on the backend's importance definition. The function returns a pandas table sorted and limited to displayed features; it accepts names and values, without requiring a model.

docs.title: Reconstruct individual raw predictions
docs.text:
from ml_toolkit.explainability import shap_contributions

names, features, contributions = shap_contributions(
    example.model.native_model, test.X.head(3)
)
feature_effects = contributions[:, :-1]
base_values = contributions[:, -1]
reconstructed = base_values + feature_effects.sum(axis=1)
np.testing.assert_allclose(reconstructed, example.model.predict_pool(test)[:3])
print("Base rental count:", base_values.round(2).tolist())
print("Total feature effect:", feature_effects.sum(axis=1).round(2).tolist())
print("Reconstructed predictions:", reconstructed.round(2).tolist())

Base rental count: [143.82, 143.82, 143.82]
Total feature effect: [-111.95, -129.17, -139.38]
Reconstructed predictions: [31.87, 14.65, 4.43]

There is one contribution per feature followed by a base-value column. Their sum reconstructs the native raw score. For this RMSE model, that is the predicted rental count. For classifiers and log-link models the raw score scale differs from the transformed probability or mean prediction.

docs.title: SHAP importance
docs.text:
from ml_toolkit.config import ShapConfig
from ml_toolkit.explainability import calculate_shap_values, top_shap_features

shap_config = ShapConfig(max_samples=600, max_display=11, seed=42)
explanation = calculate_shap_values(
    example.model.native_model, test.X, config=shap_config
)
explainability.shap_importance(
    explanation,
    output / "shap-importance.png",
    config=shap_config,
    figure=figure,
)
print("Contribution array:", explanation.values.shape)
print("Top three features:", top_shap_features(explanation, top_n=3))

Contribution array: (600, 11)
Top three features: ['hour', 'feels_like_temperature', 'temperature']

The bars average absolute contributions, so they show magnitude, not direction. Calculation samples at most max_samples rows with the supplied seed; max_display limits visible features. Defaults are 10,000 samples and seed 0. The explanation retains sampled feature values, raw contributions, and base values.

docs.title: SHAP beeswarm
docs.text:
explainability.shap_beeswarm(
    explanation,
    output / "shap-beeswarm.png",
    config=shap_config,
    figure=figure,
)

Each point is one hour's contribution. Its horizontal position gives the signed raw-score effect; color shows the feature value. Spread and color patterns show how contributions differ between observations, beyond the average importance.

docs.title: SHAP dependence
docs.text:
explainability.shap_dependence(
    explanation,
    "temperature",
    output / "shap-temperature.png",
    figure=figure,
)

The x-axis is the actual feature value and the y-axis its raw-score contribution. Color can reveal a feature interaction. All three SHAP plotting calls return None; reuse the same shap.Explanation for consistent sample comparisons.

docs.title: Enable SHAP during training
docs.text:
SHAP uses the fitted model, so configure it through reporting rather than a prediction evaluator:

from ml_toolkit.config import ReportingConfig

reporting = ReportingConfig(
    shap=ShapConfig(max_samples=600, max_display=11, seed=42)
)

Pass TrainingConfig(reporting=reporting) to the training workflow. SHAP explains held-out rows and writes shap/val/importance.png and shap/val/beeswarm.png during validation, with test/ for the final test run. Dependence plots are written for configured features. A train-only final fit has no SHAP report. Shared stage flags and figure settings are described in the overview.

docs.title: Metrics over time
docs.text:
MetricTrend shows how the task's quality changes across calendar periods. Each metric has a separate train, validation, or test curve, with the total observation weight of each window below it. Use it to investigate whether a good aggregate score hides months or weeks with worse predictions.

The report consumes existing predictions through prediction_evaluators. Pass the same metric callback used by train_model so that the report and ordinary scores use the same definitions and weights.

docs.title: Calculate a monthly trend
docs.text:
This example uses all recorded UCI Bike Sharing hours. The model fits 2011 and holds out 2012; MAE is measured in rentals per hour, with unit row weights. Cache the source first with python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike. The recipe never downloads missing data.

from pathlib import Path

from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import MetricTrend
from ml_toolkit.plots.metric_trend import metric_trend

example = fit_bike_evaluation()
output = Path("plots")
output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

report = MetricTrend(metric=weighted_mae, period="month", min_rows=100)
table = report.calculate(
    data=example.data,
    prediction=example.prediction,
    split=example.split,
)
table.write_parquet(output / "metric-trend-metrics.parquet")
metric_trend(
    table,
    metric="mae",
    period="month",
    save_fig=output / "metric-trend-mae.png",
)
assert table.height == 24
assert table["status"].unique().to_list() == ["ok"]
assert table["sum_weight"].sum() == len(example.data)

The upper panel shows MAE in each recorded month; the lower panel shows its total weight, which equals the number of observed hours in this example. Compare scores alongside that support. A short or low-volume period can have a less stable metric than a larger one. The train and test curves describe different samples of the same fitted model.

calculate() returns a long Polars table with one row per metric, split, and observed period. The columns are:

Column Meaning period_start Beginning of the endpoint's calendar bucket window_start Beginning of the first calendar bucket included in that window split train, val, or test n_rows All rows in the window n_positive_weight_rows Rows with positive weight sum_weight Sum of observation weights metric Name returned by the task callback value Metric value, or null when unavailable status ok, undefined, zero_weight, or insufficient_rows

Zero-weight windows and windows below min_rows do not call the metric. Their support is retained and their values are null. Nonfinite callback results are stored as null with status undefined; callback exceptions propagate with the evaluator, split, and period endpoint. If every window is skipped, metric names remain null and the report exports the table without metric figures.

docs.title: Use trailing calendar windows
docs.text:
window counts calendar buckets, including the current bucket. For a monthly report, window=3 includes the current month and the preceding two months. Each score is recalculated from all rows in that window, preserving their original weights. It is not an average of separately calculated monthly scores.

rolling = MetricTrend(metric=weighted_mae, period="month", window=3, min_rows=100)
rolling_table = rolling.calculate(
    data=example.data,
    prediction=example.prediction,
    split=example.split,
)
assert rolling_table.height == table.height
assert rolling_table["n_rows"].max() > table["n_rows"].max()

Windows are calculated independently for each split, including a split boundary inside a calendar period. A test window never borrows train rows. Initial windows use the available rows from their own sample; min_rows applies to positive-weight rows. Missing calendar periods have no calculated endpoints and appear as gaps in the figures. Trailing windows count elapsed calendar buckets, so a missing month still uses one position in a three-month window.

Supported periods are minute, hour, day, week, month, quarter, and year. Minute/hour need Datetime timestamps. Other periods accept Date or Datetime; weeks begin on Monday, quarters are calendar quarters, and grouping preserves the input timezone, including daylight saving transitions.

docs.title: Add the report to training
docs.text:
from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
result = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01"),
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    run_name="bike-metric-trend",
    config=config,
    prediction_evaluators=[
        MetricTrend(metric=weighted_mae, period="month", window=3, min_rows=100),
    ],
)
assert result.test_metrics is not None

Each enabled fit exports metric_trend/metrics.parquet and one indexed figure per callback score, such as metric_trend/000_mae.png. Shared FigureConfig controls output dimensions, resolution, and format. Stage switches, unique report names, and artifact paths follow the evaluation reporting contract. The report calculates the table once while writing artifacts and adds no scalar scores to training results, validation averages, or tuning objectives.

For quality by an exact-value segment, use GroupedMetrics. For comparisons of observed and predicted means over time, use TimeObservedFitted.
