docs.title: Model evaluation and shrink curves
docs.text: Use model_evaluators for reports that need the fitted adapter and the task's metric callback. ShrinkCurve shows how those metrics change when retaining fewer boosting iterations. It evaluates prefixes of the existing ensemble; the original model and training results stay unchanged.

docs.title: Add a shrink report to training
docs.text:
This example uses the prepared UCI Bike Sharing data and the same weighted MAE for training and the shrink report. Cache the source first with python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike; recipes never download it.

from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.model_evaluation import ShrinkCurve
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
result = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01"),
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    run_name="bike-shrink",
    config=config,
    model_evaluators=[ShrinkCurve(max_points=12)],
)
assert result.test_metrics is not None

Each enabled fit exports shrink/metrics.parquet and one indexed figure per metric, such as shrink/000_mae.png. All scores returned by the task callback are included, with separate curves for train and validation or test. Final fits without held-out rows produce train-only curves. Undefined metric values are null in the table and gaps in the figures. Prediction and metric errors propagate with evaluator, iteration, and training-stage context.

docs.title: Choose how many sizes to evaluate
docs.text:
Setting Retained iteration counts ShrinkCurve() Up to 50 evenly spaced integer sizes, including 1 and the fitted size ShrinkCurve(max_points=20) Up to 20 evenly spaced sizes, with the same endpoints ShrinkCurve(step=100) 1, multiples of 100, and the fitted size ShrinkCurve(step=1) Every fitted size ShrinkCurve(sizes=(10, 50, 200)) Those sizes, sorted, plus the fitted size

Specify at most one sampling option. max_points is at least two; a model with one iteration produces one point. Explicit sizes must be unique positive integers within the actual fitted size, which may be smaller than the requested training budget after early stopping. Fixed steps adapt to that fitted size.

Sizes count boosting iterations. They equal tree counts for the bundled single-tree-per-iteration models. The original fitted size always appears, so its curve values can be compared with the ordinary training metrics. A reduced copy is held only while its scores are calculated; up to 50 points still require up to 50 prediction passes per sample, so use a coarser grid for expensive data.

docs.title: Calculate and plot directly
docs.text:
The standalone example fits 80 iterations on 2011 hours and evaluates prefixes on both 2011 and the untouched 2012 hours. It shares the original pool and split labels with the existing evaluation examples.

from pathlib import Path

from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.plots.model_evaluation import shrink_curve

example = fit_bike_evaluation()
output = Path("plots")
output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

report = ShrinkCurve(max_points=12)
table = report.calculate(
    model=example.model,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    data=example.data,
    split=example.split,
)
table.write_parquet(output / "shrink-metrics.parquet")
shrink_curve(table, metric="mae", save_fig=output / "shrink-mae.png")
assert table.height == 24
assert table["n_iterations"].max() == example.model.n_iterations == 80
smaller_model = example.model.shrink(20)
assert smaller_model.n_iterations == 20
assert example.model.n_iterations == 80

The horizontal axis is the retained iteration count and the vertical axis is MAE in rentals per hour. Compare the held-out curve with the train curve to judge whether additional iterations help on these data. The report does not choose a model size or reselect a classification threshold.

calculate returns a Polars table with n_iterations (Int64), split (String), metric (String), and nullable value (Float64). Held-out-only and train-only inputs work too. Splits must align with the pool and may contain train plus at most one of val or test. Predictions use the adapter's original target units and each split's row weights.

docs.title: Optional model capability
docs.text:
All bundled CatBoost adapters support n_iterations and shrink(k), including PU classification, log-link/Gamma regression, and inflation-adjusted models. LightGBMServingModel supports these operations and predict_pool for direct evaluation; it remains a serving adapter without a training interface.

shrink(k) returns an independent fitted copy retaining the first k iterations. It preserves fitted baselines, prediction transformations, classification thresholds, and inflation state. Reduced copies clear stale validation F1, return None when the historical best iteration was removed, and use the retained size as their refit budget. These settings survive model serialization. A subsequent fit resets the retained-size override.

Custom adapters may implement the structural ShrinkableModel protocol without inheriting from it. Keep all fitted preprocessing and inverse transformations in the returned adapter, and validate k as an integer from 1 through the current size. The existing Model contract does not require this capability. An enabled ShrinkCurve raises TypeError with implementation guidance when it is missing; disabling the report does not inspect model capabilities.

docs.title: Build another model evaluator
docs.text:
Subclass ModelEvaluator and override either method as needed. evaluate receives keyword arguments model, metric, data, and split, and returns additional finite scalar metrics. write_artifacts receives those same inputs plus artifact_dir and figure, and returns only the files to upload. parameters() describes JSON-compatible settings. Instances retain settings only and may be reused across folds.

Pass one evaluator, a list, None, or []. Reports run after prediction evaluators and before data analyzers, under the same ReportingConfig stage switches. Names must be unique across all report lists and enabled PSI/SHAP. Settings are saved in configuration/model_evaluators.json. Additional scalar scores and artifacts use the evaluator's namespace and do not enter training results, CV averages, or tuning objectives. Shared figure settings and artifact path checks match the prediction evaluation contract.

Both methods receive the fitted adapter, the training metric callback and aligned data/split labels. Do not mutate inputs or retain fitted state: evaluator instances are reused across folds. Scalar results are additional reports, never training objectives or validation averages. Only returned artifact paths inside artifact_dir are uploaded beneath name/.

docs.title: Observed versus fitted
docs.text: Compare actual and predicted weighted means to find segments or time periods where a model systematically overpredicts or underpredicts. Each figure shows train and one held-out sample together. Returned tables include the volume supporting each group.

docs.title: Prepare predictions
docs.text:
Run from the installed repository checkout after the data preparation. The example fits recorded 2011 hours and evaluates 2012 hours. Targets and predictions are rentals per hour. The RMSE model can produce negative predictions; the reports display its raw outputs.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig

example = fit_bike_evaluation(classification=False)
data, prediction, split = example.data, example.prediction, example.split
train, test = example.train, example.test
train_prediction = prediction[: len(train)]
test_prediction = prediction[len(train) :]
output = Path("figures")
figure = FigureConfig(dpi=150)
print(f"2011 train hours: {len(train)}; 2012 test hours: {len(test)}")

2011 train hours: 8645; 2012 test hours: 8734

docs.title: Compare feature levels
docs.text:
ObservedFitted(features=("temperature",)) requests a temperature report. Its feature list selects what to show; shared FeatureLevelConfig rules and n_bins control how levels are learned. Fit levels on train only and apply the same boundaries to test. Numerical quantiles, categories, missing values, and unseen categories follow the feature-level rules.

Pass reports to training, or write the same reports directly from aligned predictions:

from ml_toolkit.config import FeatureLevelConfig
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import ObservedFitted, TimeObservedFitted

features = (FeatureLevelConfig("temperature", "numerical"),)
reports = [
    ObservedFitted(features=("temperature",)),
    TimeObservedFitted(period="month"),
]
for report in reports:
    files = report.write_artifacts(
        data=data,
        prediction=prediction,
        split=split,
        artifact_dir=output / report.name,
        figure=figure,
        features=features,
        n_bins=10,
    )
    print([path.relative_to(output).as_posix() for path in files])

['observed_fitted/000_temperature.png']
['time_observed_fitted/time.png']

The x-axis is the ordered feature level. Curves show weighted observed and fitted means for train and test; bars show total row weight. A curve above the observed mean indicates overprediction. A sparse group's mean is less well supported. Here fitted train means closely follow observations, while fitted test means fall below observed rental demand across most temperature levels. Missing levels and groups with zero total weight have zero volume and no mean.

Get the aggregate table with the direct function:

from ml_toolkit.feature_levels import LevelTransformer
from ml_toolkit.plots import regression

levels = LevelTransformer(features, n_bins=10).fit(train.X)
train_levels, test_levels = levels.transform(train.X), levels.transform(test.X)
assert levels.feature_levels is not None
by_level = regression.observed_fitted_by_level(
    train_levels["temperature"],
    train.y.to_numpy(),
    train_prediction,
    test_levels["temperature"],
    test.y.to_numpy(),
    test_prediction,
    output / "direct-observed-fitted.png",
    level_order=levels.feature_levels[0].levels,
    feature_name="temperature",
    reference_weight=train.weight.to_numpy(),
    current_weight=test.weight.to_numpy(),
    current_label="Test",
    figure=figure,
)
print(by_level.head(5).round(2).to_string(index=False))
print(by_level.groupby("sample")[["volume"]].sum().to_string())

   sample        level  observed  fitted  volume
reference [-inf, 0.22)     51.63   55.86   720.0
reference  [0.22, 0.3)     64.96   64.98   892.0
reference  [0.3, 0.36)     94.29   94.58   929.0
reference [0.36, 0.42)    114.84  113.37   796.0
reference  [0.42, 0.5)    130.35  130.63   925.0

sample

The pandas table uses reference/current sample keys even when the legend says Train/Test. During training, O/F and PSI use separate LevelTransformer instances fitted on the same training rows, ReportingConfig.features rules and ReportingConfig.n_bins. PSI reuses its model baseline transformer when packaging is enabled. O/F and PSI produce identical levels for matching features, but do not share fitted state with each other. A direct LevelTransformer fit also reproduces those levels when both its reference data and settings match. See how levels are shared for fitting and reuse across samples and folds. features=None displays all shared feature definitions; an empty selection produces no feature figures. Explicit unknown feature names raise an error.

docs.title: Compare calendar periods
docs.text:
TimeObservedFitted(period="month") summarizes targets and predictions by recorded calendar period. The lines show weighted means; the returned table also reports total weight. TimeObservedFitted(by=("season",)) creates a separate panel for each exact-value group. Names may refer to Pool.X or Pool.auxiliary_features. Multiple names group by their combinations; an empty tuple gives an overall plot. For continuous values, prepare a categorical band column as shown in the data guide. max_groups=50 limits the number of combinations across train and held-out rows.

The time plot's legend uses reference/current for the two samples. Here those mean 2011 train and 2012 test. Dates, timezone, ordering, and incomplete periods follow the shared temporal rules.

temporal = regression.time_observed_fitted(
    train.time.to_list(),
    train.y.to_numpy(),
    train_prediction,
    test.time.to_list(),
    test.y.to_numpy(),

docs.title: Metrics by group
docs.text:
GroupedMetrics applies an ordinary metric function to each group and split. It accepts the same exact-value by selection as the time report, independently of shared numerical level settings. No metric function changes are required.

from ml_toolkit.evaluation import GroupedMetrics
from ml_toolkit.metrics import metrics_regression

grouped_report = GroupedMetrics(
    name="metrics_by_season",
    metric=metrics_regression,
    by=("season",),
    min_rows=30,
)
grouped_table = grouped_report.calculate(
    data=data, prediction=prediction, split=split
)
assert grouped_table.filter(pl.col("status") == "ok").height > 0

Pass this evaluator through prediction_evaluators to log finite scalar scores and upload metrics.parquet beneath its report name. The table preserves typed grouping columns and includes group_id, split, n_rows, n_positive_weight_rows, sum_weight, metric, value, and status. group_id identifies the same group across splits within that report; identifiers are local to the report and are not persistent segment IDs across folds.

min_rows=1 by default counts positive-weight rows. Each represented split includes every observed group, even if that split has no rows in the group. Statuses are ok, empty, zero_weight, insufficient_rows, or undefined. Skipped and nonfinite results have null values; if every group is skipped, metric names are null too. A single-class group's ROC AUC is undefined, while its other valid scores remain available. Exceptions raised by the metric function propagate with report context. Only finite scores are logged under <name>/<split>/<group_id>/<metric_key>; the table retains original metric names. Unusual metric names are encoded into collision-free tracking keys. Grouping column names must not conflict with the table's metadata columns; give such a diagnostic column a distinct name before grouping.

Grouped metrics are additional diagnostics, including on train-only fits. They do not change training metrics, CV averages, or optimization objectives.

The table exposes period_start for each group. Optional weights affect means and volume. Feature-level plots use shared n_bins; the time plot has its own period and does not use feature-level settings.

docs.title: Compare two held-out periods directly
docs.text:
Direct plotting can compare two evaluation periods without including model training rows. This independent Bike model fits January–June 2011; the reference is July–December 2011 and the current period is 2012. Both plotted samples are held out. Fitting feature levels on the reference makes the comparison answer how its relationships generalize to the subsequent year.

from examples.gallery_data import load_gallery_data

_, bikes = load_gallery_data(download_if_missing=False)
reference, current = bikes.reference.features, bikes.current.features
reference_y, current_y = bikes.reference.observed, bikes.current.observed
reference_prediction, current_prediction = (
    bikes.reference.prediction,
    bikes.current.prediction,
)

from ml_toolkit.plots import regression
from ml_toolkit.config import FeatureLevelConfig
from ml_toolkit.feature_levels import LevelTransformer

heldout_levels = LevelTransformer(
    (FeatureLevelConfig("temperature", "numerical"),), n_bins=10
).fit(reference)
reference_levels = heldout_levels.transform(reference)
current_levels = heldout_levels.transform(current)
assert heldout_levels.feature_levels is not None
heldout_by_level = regression.observed_fitted_by_level(
    reference_levels["temperature"],
    reference_y,
    reference_prediction,
    current_levels["temperature"],
    current_y,
    current_prediction,
    output / "observed-fitted-levels.png",
    level_order=heldout_levels.feature_levels[0].levels,
    feature_name="Normalized temperature",
    reference_label="Jul–Dec 2011",
    current_label="2012",
    figure=figure,
)
print(heldout_by_level.groupby("sample")[["volume"]].sum().to_string())
print(heldout_by_level.head(4).round(2).to_string(index=False))

sample

docs.title: Permutation importance
docs.text: PermutationImportance measures how much a fitted model's held-out score changes when selected feature values are shuffled. It uses the same prediction adapter and task metric as training, including fitted transformations and row weights. Positive importance means worse quality after shuffling; negative importance means better quality on this sample.

docs.title: Add the report to training
docs.text:
The example uses the cached UCI Bike Sharing data and weighted MAE in rentals per hour. Prepare the source once with python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike before running recipes.

from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.model_evaluation import PermutationImportance
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
result = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01"),
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    run_name="bike-permutation",
    config=config,
    model_evaluators=PermutationImportance(
        score="mae",
        direction="minimize",
        features=("hour", "humidity", "wind_speed"),
        groups=(("temperature", "feels_like_temperature"),),
        n_repeats=3,
        max_samples=4000,
    ),
)
assert result.test_metrics is not None

Each enabled validation/test run exports permutation_importance/importance.parquet and importance.png. Train-only fits are skipped. Supply a score name returned by the task callback and its preferred direction: minimize for MAE or deviance, maximize for AUC. Each instance evaluates one score; separate instances can use different scores and report names. No model is retrained or selected.

docs.title: Calculate and plot directly
docs.text:
This example fits 80 boosting iterations to 2011 hours and measures importance on unseen 2012 hours. Temperature and feels-like temperature are shuffled as one group, using the same row permutation to preserve their relationship.

from pathlib import Path

from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.plots.permutation_importance import permutation_importance

example = fit_bike_evaluation()
output = Path("plots")
output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

report = PermutationImportance(
    score="mae",
    direction="minimize",
    features=("hour", "humidity", "wind_speed"),
    groups=(("temperature", "feels_like_temperature"),),
    n_repeats=3,
    max_samples=4000,
    seed=42,
)
importance = report.calculate(
    model=example.model,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    data=example.data,
    split=example.split,
)
permutation_importance(importance, save_fig=output / "permutation-mae.png")
assert importance.height == 12
assert importance["n_rows"].unique().to_list() == [4000]

Bars show the mean score deterioration; error bars show the standard deviation over repeated permutations. These are repeat variability, not confidence intervals. The chart measures the fixed model's reliance on these inputs on this sample. Correlated alternatives may mask individual importance, so group features when their joint contribution is the relevant question. Permutation can also create feature combinations absent from the original data; interpret results with the feature relationships in mind.

docs.title: Sampling, grouping and outputs
docs.text:
features=None evaluates every model column not already included in groups. Use features=() to evaluate only the configured groups. Feature groups must be nonempty and disjoint, and explicitly selected individual columns cannot also belong to a group. Auxiliary columns are never passed to the model.

max_samples limits positive-weight held-out rows with uniform sampling without replacement; zero-weight rows are excluded from the permutation population. All permutations and the baseline use the same sampled rows, original targets and original weights. seed makes both sampling and permutations reproducible. For G groups and R repeats, the report needs 1 + G * R prediction passes on that sample. It retains no fitted state.

calculate returns one row per group/repeat with columns split, group_id, features (a list of column names), repeat (zero-based), metric, baseline, value, importance, n_rows, and sum_weight. Importance is shuffled minus baseline for minimization and baseline minus shuffled for maximization. Nonfinite scores are null, with unavailable importances shown explicitly in the figure. Missing score names and prediction/metric failures raise errors.

The report follows the shared model evaluation stage switches, namespace, figure configuration, and artifact upload rules.

docs.title: Positive-unlabeled
docs.text:
Use the original LINQS Cora archive for an observed-link retrieval example: 2,708 real papers, their 1,433 binary word indicators, and all 5,429 recorded directed citations. Recorded links are known positives. The loader selects 20,000 distinct unrecorded directed pairs as unverified candidates; their citation status is unknown.

Scores are cosine similarities between the source word vectors. They are retrieval scores in [0, 1], without a probability interpretation or fitted PU classifier. Cora's published document classes are unused. This constructs an open-world citation retrieval example; the sampled candidate ratio does not estimate citation prevalence.

From an installed source checkout, prepare the original citation source first:

python -m pip install -r requirements-examples.txt
python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset cora

from pathlib import Path
from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig

output = Path("figures")
figure = FigureConfig(dpi=150)

from examples.citation_data import load_citation_gallery
from ml_toolkit.plots import pu

citations = load_citation_gallery(download_if_missing=False)
pu_labels, pu_scores = (citations.labels, citations.scores)
pu.score_distribution(
    pu_labels, pu_scores, output / "pu-distribution.png", figure=figure
)
print(
    f"Cora: {citations.paper_count} papers, {citations.known_citation_count} recorded citations, {citations.unlabeled_pair_count} unverified candidate pairs"
)

Cora: 2708 papers, 5429 recorded citations, 20000 unverified candidate pairs

Inspect Cora records, candidate selection, and similarity scoring 
"""Real observed-link ranking data from the original LINQS Cora archive.

Recorded citations are positive observations. Other directed paper pairs are
unlabeled candidates: a missing record is not evidence of a confirmed negative.
This is an open-world retrieval illustration, not an author-provided PU
benchmark. Scores are cosine similarities between the original binary word
vectors, not calibrated citation probabilities or a fitted PU classifier.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256
from io import BytesIO
import logging
from pathlib import Path
from tarfile import TarInfo, open as open_tar
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from urllib.error import URLError
from urllib.request import urlopen

import numpy as np

from ml_toolkit.types import FloatArray, IntArray

CORA_URL = "https://linqs-data.soe.ucsc.edu/public/lbc/cora.tgz"
CORA_MIRROR = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tkipf/pygcn/"
    "1600b5b748b3976413d1e307540ccc62605b4d6d/data/cora"
)
CORA_FILE_HASHES = {
    "cora.content": "b8ebed0fd45e53995abafd1b70cf6a9fcc8f86abc5826d69b97fe6ca46e9c8ee",
    "cora.cites": "ec1a372391b7f0f60a6aff0084e8abd8f19f0faa7e1f2441a41c492042d5945e",
}
DEFAULT_CITATION_CACHE = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / ".cache/linqs-cora"
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CitationGallery:
    """Store recorded citations and unverified candidates with content scores.

    Attributes
    ----------
    labels : FloatArray
        One for recorded citations and zero for unlabeled candidate pairs.
    scores : FloatArray
        Aligned cosine word-vector similarities in [0, 1].
    pairs : tuple[tuple[str, str], ...]
        Directed (citing paper ID, cited paper ID) pairs. Recorded links precede
        candidates; no pair is repeated and no paper is paired with itself.
    known_citation_count, unlabeled_pair_count : int
        Numbers of preserved source links and sampled candidate pairs.
    paper_count, feature_count : int
        Number of real source papers and binary word indicators per paper.
    """

    labels: FloatArray
    scores: FloatArray
    pairs: tuple[tuple[str, str], ...]
    known_citation_count: int
    unlabeled_pair_count: int
    paper_count: int
    feature_count: int


def citation_cache_available(cache_dir: Path | None = None) -> bool:
    """Check for the source archive without downloading or writing files.

    Parameters
    ----------
    cache_dir : pathlib.Path or None, default None
        Cache directory; None uses .cache/linqs-cora in the repository.

    Returns
    -------
    bool
        Whether the selected directory contains cora.tgz.
    """
    directory = DEFAULT_CITATION_CACHE if cache_dir is None else cache_dir
    return (directory / "cora.tgz").is_file()


def _download_source(path: Path) -> None:
    try:
        with urlopen(CORA_URL, timeout=30) as response:
            original = response.read()
    except (URLError, TimeoutError) as error:
        logger.warning("Cora source unavailable (%s); using pinned pygcn mirror", error)
        with open_tar(path, "w:gz") as archive:
            for name, expected in CORA_FILE_HASHES.items():
                with urlopen(f"{CORA_MIRROR}/{name}", timeout=30) as response:
                    content = response.read()
                if sha256(content).hexdigest() != expected:
                    raise ValueError(f"Cora mirror checksum mismatch for {name}")
                member = TarInfo(f"cora/{name}")
                member.size = len(content)
                archive.addfile(member, BytesIO(content))
    else:
        path.write_bytes(original)


def _source_records(
    cache_dir: Path, download_if_missing: bool
) -> tuple[tuple[str, ...], FloatArray, IntArray]:
    path = cache_dir / "cora.tgz"
    if not path.is_file():
        if not download_if_missing:
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"Cora data is not cached at {path}")
        cache_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with TemporaryDirectory(prefix="cora-download-", dir=cache_dir) as temporary:
            downloaded = Path(temporary) / "cora.tgz"
            _download_source(downloaded)
            downloaded.replace(path)
    with open_tar(path, "r:gz") as archive:
        content = archive.extractfile("cora/cora.content")
        citations = archive.extractfile("cora/cora.cites")
        if content is None or citations is None:
            raise ValueError("The Cora archive must contain its content and citation files")
        rows = [line.split() for line in content.read().decode("utf-8").splitlines()]
        raw_links = [line.split() for line in citations.read().decode("utf-8").splitlines()]
    paper_ids = tuple(row[0] for row in rows)
    if len(set(paper_ids)) != len(paper_ids):
        raise ValueError("Cora paper IDs must be unique")
    features = np.asarray([row[1:-1] for row in rows], dtype=np.float64)
    if features.ndim != 2 or not len(features) or features.shape[1] == 0:
        raise ValueError("Cora word vectors must be a nonempty matrix")
    if not np.isin(features, [0.0, 1.0]).all() or (features.sum(axis=1) == 0).any():
        raise ValueError("Cora word vectors must be binary and have positive norm")
    positions = {paper_id: index for index, paper_id in enumerate(paper_ids)}
    # The source README stores each citation as (cited ID, citing ID).
    # Retain source order and remove exact duplicate directed records only.
    links = tuple(dict.fromkeys((positions[citing], positions[cited]) for cited, citing in raw_links))
    if any(citing == cited for citing, cited in links):
        raise ValueError("Cora recorded citations must not contain self-links")
    return paper_ids, features, np.asarray(links, dtype=np.int64)


def _candidate_pairs(
    observed: IntArray, paper_count: int, count: int
) -> IntArray:
    recorded = {tuple(pair) for pair in observed.tolist()}
    available = paper_count * (paper_count - 1) - len(recorded)
    if not 1 <= count <= available:
        raise ValueError("unlabeled_pair_count must fit the unrecorded non-self pairs")
    generator = np.random.default_rng(42)
    candidates: list[tuple[int, int]] = []
    selected: set[tuple[int, int]] = set()
    while len(candidates) < count:
        draws = generator.integers(0, paper_count, size=(2 * (count - len(candidates)), 2))
        for citing, cited in draws.tolist():
            pair = (citing, cited)
            if citing != cited and pair not in recorded and pair not in selected:
                selected.add(pair)
                candidates.append(pair)
                if len(candidates) == count:
                    break
    return np.asarray(candidates, dtype=np.int64)


def load_citation_gallery(
    *,
    cache_dir: Path | None = None,
    download_if_missing: bool = True,
    unlabeled_pair_count: int = 20_000,
) -> CitationGallery:
    """Score real citations and unverified candidate pairs by word similarity.

    Parameters
    ----------
    cache_dir : pathlib.Path or None, default None
        Cache directory for the original archive. None uses .cache/linqs-cora.
    download_if_missing : bool, default True
        Allow downloading the LINQS archive, with a pinned, checksum-verified
        pygcn mirror as fallback. False raises for a missing cache without
        making network requests or writing files.
    unlabeled_pair_count : int, default 20000
        Number of distinct absent directed pairs sampled uniformly with seed 42.
        Must be positive and fit the available non-self, unrecorded pairs.

    Returns
    -------
    CitationGallery
        All 5,429 recorded citations and sampled unverified candidate pairs,
        aligned with cosine similarity scores from 1,433 source word indicators.

    Notes
    -----
    Reads only cora.content and cora.cites; archive paths are never extracted.
    Topic labels are ignored. Candidate sampling never alters or hides observed
    citation labels and never uses the similarity scores. No prior prevalence,
    supervised labels, invented dates, or simulated feature values are used.
    A sampled candidate set does not estimate the prevalence of real citations.
    """
    directory = DEFAULT_CITATION_CACHE if cache_dir is None else cache_dir
    paper_ids, features, observed = _source_records(directory, download_if_missing)
    candidates = _candidate_pairs(observed, len(paper_ids), unlabeled_pair_count)
    pairs = np.concatenate((observed, candidates))
    norms = np.linalg.norm(features, axis=1)
    scores = np.empty(len(pairs), dtype=np.float64)
    # Batches keep the two indexed word-vector matrices bounded in memory.
    for start in range(0, len(pairs), 1024):
        batch = pairs[start:start + 1024]
        left, right = batch[:, 0], batch[:, 1]
        numerator = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", features[left], features[right])
        scores[start:start + len(batch)] = numerator / (norms[left] * norms[right])
    scores = np.clip(scores, 0.0, 1.0)
    return CitationGallery(
        labels=np.concatenate((np.ones(len(observed)), np.zeros(len(candidates)))),
        scores=scores,
        pairs=tuple((paper_ids[int(citing)], paper_ids[int(cited)]) for citing, cited in pairs),
        known_citation_count=len(observed),
        unlabeled_pair_count=len(candidates),
        paper_count=len(paper_ids),
        feature_count=features.shape[1],
    )

pu.positive_capture(
    pu_labels, pu_scores, output / "pu-capture.png", figure=figure
)

Both calls return None. Histograms normalize the recorded-link and candidate sets separately. Capture plots show recorded citations recovered as the unverified review fraction increases. Missing records are not confirmed negative citations, and capture on this graph does not establish recall for all real citations. Both axes show percentages; tied scores enter together.

docs.title: Reports in a PU training workflow
docs.text:
PUScoreDistribution(histogram_bins=30) separates score distributions for known positives and unlabeled rows, normalizing each group independently. PUPositiveCapture() plots known-positive capture against the unlabeled fraction reviewed. Both use row weights and only the current held-out split. They require both groups to have positive total weight. The distribution's histogram_bins controls score bins; capture processes tied scores together.

For an existing project PU workflow, add the following evaluators. The callable below requires your actual chronologically ordered PU pool, model parameters, and population prior; the Cora illustration above supplies no training dates or population prior and is not used to fabricate a PU training run.

from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.config import TrainingConfig
from ml_toolkit.data import Pool
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import PUScoreDistribution, PUPositiveCapture
from ml_toolkit.metrics import PUMetric
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostPUClassificationModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout
from ml_toolkit.types import ModelParams


def train_pu_reports(data: Pool, *, prior: float, params: ModelParams):
    return train_model(
        splitter=Holdout(data, val_size=0.2, test_size=0.2),
        params={**params, "pu_prior": prior, "loss": "nnPU"},
        model_factory=CatBoostPUClassificationModel,
        metric=PUMetric(prior=prior, loss="nnPU"),
        run_name="pu-reports",
        config=TrainingConfig(),
        prediction_evaluators=[PUScoreDistribution(), PUPositiveCapture()],
    )

In a test run the files are pu_score_distribution/test/pu_score_distribution.png and pu_positive_capture/test/pu_positive_capture.png; validation uses val/. The displayed Cora figures illustrate the same direct plotting functions used by those evaluators, using the stated retrieval scores rather than a fitted PU model. A prior is a population prevalence assumption, not the labeled fraction.

docs.title: PUScoreDistribution dataclass
docs.text:
PUScoreDistribution(
    *,
    name: str = "pu_score_distribution",

docs.title: Ranking
docs.text: Rank rows by their predicted outcome and measure how much observed outcome falls within a limited review or service capacity. Gains and Lift require finite, nonnegative targets and a positive weighted observed total. They use confirmed outcomes; PU capture has a different meaning.

docs.title: Prepare predictions
docs.text:
Run from the installed repository checkout after the data preparation. The example fits recorded 2011 hours and evaluates 2012 hours. The target is rentals per hour and each row has unit exposure, so capacity is a fraction of hours. The reports rank only the 2012 test hours.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.config import FigureConfig

example = fit_bike_evaluation(classification=False)
data, prediction, split = example.data, example.prediction, example.split
train, test = example.train, example.test
train_prediction = prediction[: len(train)]
test_prediction = prediction[len(train) :]
output = Path("figures")
figure = FigureConfig(dpi=150)
print(f"2011 train hours: {len(train)}; 2012 test hours: {len(test)}")

2011 train hours: 8645; 2012 test hours: 8734

docs.title: Gains and lift reports
docs.text:
Use this list as prediction_evaluators=reports in training. These calls produce the same report files from existing predictions:

from ml_toolkit.evaluation import Gains, Lift

reports = [Gains(), Lift()]
for report in reports:
    files = report.write_artifacts(
        data=data,
        prediction=prediction,
        split=split,
        artifact_dir=output / report.name,
        figure=figure,
        features=None,
        n_bins=10,
    )
    print([path.relative_to(output).as_posix() for path in files])

['gains/test/gains.png']
['lift/test/lift.png']

docs.title: Gains
docs.text: The x-axis is cumulative exposure after sorting from highest to lowest score. The y-axis is the share of total observed × exposure captured. The diagonal shows uniform selection. A curve above it captures more outcome with the same capacity; the marked 10% point summarizes a common operating capacity.

docs.title: Lift
docs.text: Lift divides captured outcome share by the exposure share. A value of 2 means capturing twice the outcome expected from uniform selection at that capacity.

docs.title: Inspect the curves and selected capacities
docs.text:
from ml_toolkit.metrics import ranking_metrics
from ml_toolkit.plots import ranking

ranked = ranking_metrics(
    test.y.to_numpy(), test_prediction, test.weight.to_numpy()
)
ranking.gains_curve(ranked, output / "direct-gains.png", figure=figure)
ranking.lift_curve(ranked, output / "direct-lift.png", figure=figure)
print(
    [
        (point.percent, round(point.gain, 3), round(point.lift, 3))
        for point in ranked.selected_points
    ]
)
selected = ranking_metrics(
    test.y.to_numpy(),
    test_prediction,
    test.weight.to_numpy(),
    selected_percents=(10.0, 20.0),
)
print(
    [
        (point.percent, round(point.gain, 3), round(point.lift, 3))
        for point in selected.selected_points
    ]
)

[(10.0, 0.277, 2.767)]
[(10.0, 0.277, 2.767), (20.0, 0.473, 2.367)]

ranking_metrics returns cumulative arrays and selected points; plotting calls return None. Selected points interpolate at the requested exposure fraction. Zero-exposure rows are omitted and tied predictions retain input order. The evaluator classes use the default 10% point; direct plotting accepts any RankingMetrics result, including other selected capacities.

docs.title: Residuals and large loss contributions
docs.text: Use Residuals to inspect the shape of regression errors, systematic bias at different prediction levels, and observations contributing most to the chosen loss. The report uses predictions already calculated by the training workflow.

docs.title: Add the report to training
docs.text:
This complete workflow uses recorded UCI Bike Sharing hourly counts and dates. Cache the source with python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike before running recipes; examples never download it implicitly.

from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.evaluation import Residuals
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
trained = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01"),
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    run_name="bike-residuals",
    config=config,
    prediction_evaluators=Residuals(loss="squared", n_bins=12, max_rows=15),
)
assert trained.test_metrics is not None

The evaluator follows the shared ReportingConfig stage switches and figure settings. Each enabled fit writes rows.parquet, bins.parquet, worst.parquet, and residuals.png beneath residuals/. The parquet rows include observed outcomes and optional object IDs.

docs.title: Read the residual diagnostics
docs.text:
For a reproducible direct example, fit 80 iterations on the recorded 2011 hours and evaluate those predictions on both 2011 and untouched 2012 observations. Every hour has weight one; outcomes and predictions are rentals per hour.

from pathlib import Path

from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.plots.residuals import residual_diagnostics

example = fit_bike_evaluation()
output = Path("plots")
output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

report = Residuals(loss="squared", n_bins=12, max_samples=1500, max_rows=15)
diagnostics = report.calculate(
    data=example.data,
    prediction=example.prediction,
    split=example.split,
)
residual_diagnostics(
    diagnostics,
    save_fig=output / "residuals-diagnostics.png",
    loss=report.loss,
    max_samples=report.max_samples,
)
assert diagnostics.rows.height == len(example.data)
assert diagnostics.worst.height == 30
assert diagnostics.worst["weight"].min() > 0

Positive residuals mean overprediction; negative residuals mean underprediction. The first panel shows the share of each split's total row weight in common residual bins. The scatter panel reveals whether errors change with prediction size. Its uniformly sampled points are bounded by max_samples per split; marker sizes represent relative row weights. Sampling affects only that panel.

The last panel shows the weighted median, interquartile band, and weighted mean residual in prediction bins. Cutoffs are fitted from positive-weight train predictions when present and shared across splits. Held-out-only calls use the supplied positive-weight predictions. Repeated quantile cutoffs collapse, so a constant prediction produces one bin. Extreme predictions fall into the first or last bin. Train and test curves are compared at each split's weighted mean prediction within the shared bin; their horizontal coordinates can differ.

docs.title: Inspect the tables
docs.text:
calculate returns a ResidualResult containing three Polars tables:

Table Contents rows Every original row, with position, split, timestamp, target, prediction, weight, residual, unit loss, weighted contribution, and prediction-bin ID. Includes object_id when the pool supplies it. bins Populated split/bin pairs with bounds, positive-weight row count, total weight, weighted mean prediction/residual/loss, total contribution, and residual quantiles. worst Up to max_rows positive-weight rows per split, ordered by decreasing weighted contribution, with original row order breaking ties. 
largest = diagnostics.worst.select(
    "split", "time", "observed", "prediction", "weight", "contribution"
)
largest.write_parquet(output / "residuals-largest.parquet")
assert diagnostics.bins["sum_weight"].sum() == example.data.weight.sum()

Quantiles use the inverse weighted empirical CDF: the smallest residual whose cumulative weight reaches the requested share. p05, p25, p50, p75, and p95 correspond to 5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 95%. Zero-weight observations remain in rows for positional alignment but do not enter statistics, figures, or the largest-contribution table. Missing object IDs are not fabricated.

docs.title: Choose the loss and residual scale
docs.text:
loss Residual Individual weighted contribution "squared" Prediction minus observed target Weight × squared error "absolute" Prediction minus observed target Weight × absolute error "poisson" Signed square root of Poisson unit deviance Weight × Poisson unit deviance "gamma" Signed square root of Gamma unit deviance Weight × Gamma unit deviance

Poisson requires nonnegative observations and strictly positive predicted means. At observed zero its unit deviance is twice the predicted mean. Gamma requires strictly positive observations and predicted means. Both deviance residuals retain the prediction-minus-observation sign and equal zero at a perfect fit. These domains apply to every supplied row, including rows with zero weight. Squared and absolute error support signed outcomes and predictions.

Choose a loss explicitly for the regression task. The evaluator does not infer it from the model's training parameters or from the metric callback. A Poisson loss report therefore needs predictions on the positive mean scale, rather than raw log predictions. The report supports train-only or held-out-only data, preserves inputs, and adds no scalar optimization objectives.

Poisson requires nonnegative targets and positive predictions; Gamma requires both targets and predictions to be strictly positive.

Maximum number of weighted prediction-quantile bins. Repeated cutoffs collapse. Positive-weight train rows define cutoffs when available; held-out-only calls use their supplied positive-weight rows.

Keep aligned observations, weighted bin summaries, and worst rows.

Name Type Description rows DataFrame

Every input row in its original order, including zero-weight rows. Contains row_index, split, time, observed, prediction, weight, residual, loss, contribution, and prediction_bin, plus object_id when supplied. contribution is row weight multiplied by the nonnegative unit loss.

docs.title: Input robustness
docs.text: RobustnessCurve measures task metrics after explicit changes to held-out features. Use it to assess missing inputs, measurement noise, reduced precision, or categories absent from the supplied data. The fitted model is reused at every level; its parameters and the original data stay unchanged.

docs.title: Add a stress report to training
docs.text:
The example uses the original UCI Bike Sharing hourly observations, weather features, and rental counts. Cache the source first with python -m examples.prepare_data --dataset bike. It fits on earlier hours and reserves 2012 as test; the report applies the configured scenario only to held-out rows and keeps the task's weighted MAE and original target values.

from examples.custom_metric import weighted_mae
from examples.training_setup import prepare_training
from ml_toolkit import train_model
from ml_toolkit.model_evaluation import RobustnessCurve
from ml_toolkit.models import CatBoostRegressionModel
from ml_toolkit.training import Holdout

data, params, config = prepare_training()
result = train_model(
    splitter=Holdout(data, test_size="2012-01-01"),
    params=params,
    model_factory=CatBoostRegressionModel,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    run_name="bike-input-robustness",
    config=config,
    model_evaluators=RobustnessCurve(
        features=("temperature", "humidity"),
        mode="missing",
        levels=(0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5),
        n_repeats=3,
        seed=42,
    ),
)
assert result.test_metrics is not None

Each enabled validation/test fit exports robustness/metrics.parquet and one indexed figure per metric, such as robustness/000_mae.png. The shared ReportingConfig stage switches and FigureConfig apply. A train-only final fit skips this report. Use distinct report names for several scenarios.

docs.title: Calculate and plot a scenario directly
docs.text:
This fixed model fits 80 iterations on 2011 hours and reports on 2012 hours. The stress scenario independently hides temperature and humidity at each chosen fraction. The resulting points describe this explicit scenario applied to the real held-out rows, rather than a forecast of how the input source will fail.

from pathlib import Path

from examples.evaluation_data import fit_bike_evaluation
from ml_toolkit.plots.robustness import robustness_curve

example = fit_bike_evaluation()
output = Path("plots")
output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

report = RobustnessCurve(
    features=("temperature", "humidity"),
    mode="missing",
    levels=(0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0),
    n_repeats=5,
    max_samples=2500,
    seed=42,
)
table = report.calculate(
    model=example.model,
    metric=weighted_mae,
    data=example.data,
    split=example.split,
)
table.write_parquet(output / "robustness-metrics.parquet")
robustness_curve(table, metric="mae", save_fig=output / "robustness-missing.png")
assert table.height == 31
assert table["n_rows"].unique().to_list() == [2500]

The vertical axis is MAE in rentals per hour. The dashed line uses unmodified features on the same 2,500 sampled hours as every scenario. The solid line is the mean over five random realizations, and the band is one repeat standard deviation. It shows variability of the chosen perturbation, rather than an uncertainty interval for future model quality. Undefined metric values leave gaps.

docs.title: Scenario settings
docs.text:
Mode Meaning of levels Supported features missing Probability in [0, 1] of setting each selected feature value to null Any model feature noise Nonnegative Gaussian-noise scale, in training standard deviations Numerical model features rounding Nonnegative integer decimal places; fewer means coarser precision Numerical model features unknown Probability in [0, 1] of replacing a category with unknown_value Categorical model features

Levels are unique and finite. Masks/noise are reused across levels within each repeat, so larger missing fractions hide nested row sets. n_repeats defaults to three; deterministic rounding is evaluated once per level. max_samples defaults to 10,000 uniformly sampled positive-weight held-out rows; None uses all positive-weight held-out rows. Zero-weight rows are excluded before sampling and perturbation. An all-zero held-out sample raises an error. Row selection occurs once, and targets, weights, dates, IDs, and auxiliary columns remain aligned throughout. seed controls both row selection and perturbations.

Noise uses the weighted population standard deviation of finite, positive-weight training values. It therefore requires train rows even for direct calculation. Constant features have zero noise scale; nulls remain null. Rounding and noise may promote changed numerical columns to Float64.

noise = RobustnessCurve(
    features=("temperature",), mode="noise", levels=(0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0),
    n_repeats=3, max_samples=2500, seed=42,
)
rounding = RobustnessCurve(
    features=("humidity",), mode="rounding", levels=(0.0, 1.0, 2.0),
    max_samples=2500,
)
for scenario in (noise, rounding):
    scenario_table = scenario.calculate(
        model=example.model, metric=weighted_mae,
        data=example.data, split=example.split,
    )
    assert scenario_table["metric"].unique().to_list() == ["mae"]

Unknown mode injects an unseen label, defaulting to "unknown". The label must not already occur in any supplied value of the selected features. Changed categorical columns are converted to String in the temporary input only, including Enum/Categorical and integer-coded categories. Their categorical feature metadata is preserved. CatBoost can predict unseen labels; LightGBM's categorical preparation uses its missing-category behavior for unseen values. Custom adapters must support the chosen scenario through predict_pool.

The following example explicitly treats the recorded weather code as a categorical feature before fitting a separate model:

from dataclasses import replace

import numpy as np

categorical_data = replace(
    example.data,
    cat_features=("weather",),
    numerical_features=tuple(name for name in example.data.X.columns if name != "weather"),
)
categorical_model = CatBoostRegressionModel({
    "iterations": 40, "depth": 4, "random_seed": 42, "thread_count": 2,
    "verbose": False, "allow_writing_files": False,
}).fit(categorical_data.take(np.flatnonzero((example.split == "train").to_numpy())))
unknown = RobustnessCurve(
    features=("weather",), mode="unknown", levels=(0.0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0),
    unknown_value="unknown", n_repeats=3, max_samples=2500, seed=42,
)
unknown_table = unknown.calculate(
    model=categorical_model, metric=weighted_mae,
    data=categorical_data, split=example.split,
)
assert unknown_table.height == 13

docs.title: Calculated values
docs.text:
calculate returns a Polars table containing split, mode, level, repeat, is_baseline, metric, value, delta, n_rows, and sum_weight. n_rows counts the selected positive-weight held-out rows. Baseline rows have null level/repeat and is_baseline=True. Other rows identify the scenario level and zero-based repeat. Values use natural metric units and the original row weights; delta is scenario value minus baseline. Positive delta worsens a minimized metric and improves a maximized metric. Nonfinite scores and deltas become null, while prediction/metric exceptions propagate with scenario context.

Reports calculate the curve once during artifact generation and do not add scalar scores to training results or tuning objectives. parameters() returns the settings, and evaluator instances retain no fitted state.

docs.text:
RobustnessCurve(
    *,
    name: str = "robustness",
    features: tuple[str, ...],
    mode: Literal[
        "missing", "noise", "rounding", "unknown"
    ] = "missing",
    levels: tuple[float, ...] = (0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4),
    n_repeats: int = 3,
    max_samples: int | None = 10000,
    seed: int = 0,
    unknown_value: str = "unknown"
)

Bases: ModelEvaluator

Measure task metrics after controlled changes to held-out features.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default features tuple of str

Nonempty, unique feature names from Pool.X, changed together. Auxiliary columns are never passed to the model or changed by this report.

required mode (missing, noise, rounding, unknown)

Missing injects nulls. Unknown injects unknown_value only in categorical model columns, converting those changed columns to String locally. Noise adds independent Gaussian noise to numerical features, scaled by each feature's weighted population standard deviation on train rows. Rounding rounds numerical features to the requested decimal places.

'missing' levels tuple of float

Unique, finite scenario levels. Missing/unknown use fractions in [0, 1]. Noise uses nonnegative standard-deviation multipliers. Rounding uses nonnegative integer decimal places, with smaller values coarser.

(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4) n_repeats int

Positive number of random realizations per level. Rounding is deterministic and is calculated once per level.

3 max_samples int or None

Positive maximum number of uniformly sampled positive-weight held-out rows. Zero-weight rows are excluded before sampling. Sampling occurs once and retains the same rows, targets and weights at all levels. None evaluates all positive-weight held-out rows.

10000 seed int

Nonnegative seed for row sampling and perturbations. Each realization shares masks/noise across levels so fractions form nested row sets.

0 unknown_value str

Unseen label used by unknown mode. Must not occur in any supplied value of a selected feature. The same label is used for all selected features.

'unknown' name str

Unique report name and artifact namespace.

'robustness' Notes

Evaluates the fitted adapter without refitting or mutating inputs. Requires val or test rows; train-only inputs return an empty table and no artifacts. Noise additionally requires train rows to estimate its scale, excluding zero-weight, null and nonfinite feature values. A constant feature has zero noise scale. Changed numerical columns may be promoted to Float64.

Every named score from the supplied task metric is evaluated with the original held-out targets and row weights. Nonfinite scores become nulls. The unmodified baseline is a separate row with level/repeat=null and is_baseline=True; delta is changed score minus baseline in natural units. A positive delta improves a maximized metric and worsens a minimized one.
